arguments.body:
Pre-read for Monday. Builds on the baseline summary Priya already read. Goal of this doc: lock the measurement spine before we go further on naming, lifecycle, or pricing mechanics.

How to read this doc: the refusal rules, eligibility checks, and tier design we are pre-discovering exist to protect customers from a self-serve setup that won't deliver value for them. If a setup will fail for an account — whether because of permissions, import, billing, or migration complexity, or because the account's needs exceed what self-serve carries — the right move is to route that account to a path where they can succeed, not to push them through a plan they will churn out of. Every refusal rule below should be readable as a customer safeguard first.

Sections:
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
2. Measurement method
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
5. Open questions (lifecycle, instrumentation, support, eng sizing)

—
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
—

"Helio Start" is the working name for the sub-50-seat tier we are pre-discovering. It is internal shorthand only.

Priya's gate (2023-06-14): the name implies nothing customer-facing until all of the following are ready — eligibility rules, refusal rules, instrumentation, lifecycle paths, and support boundaries. Nothing in this doc, in the baseline summary, or in any Slack thread should be read as a launch commitment, a launch date, or a marketing promise.

The framing is protective, not exclusionary: we are pre-discovering whether the tier can be designed so that customers who enter it have a realistic path to activation, and so that customers the tier won't serve are routed to a path that does. If the design can't meet that bar, the right answer is to not ship the tier, not to ship it with weaker rules.

If this tier ships, the working name may change. Anything written here should hold under that.

—
2. Measurement method
—

Cohort definitions (locked):
- Mid-seg v2 = 75–200 seats (default since 2023-04-26). 50–75 = starter band. v1 (50–200) stays in the warehouse for back-compat comps only — we do not roll v1 forward.
- Under-50 / sub-50 = the band this tier work is actually about. We report it separately from mid-seg v2 in every cut going forward.

Activation (locked):
- Activation definition v3: `+ ≥1 in-product event in 14d` (locked 2023-03-16). Target: 60% for mid-seg+ in 14d; the conditional 65% target is tied to sub-50 tier ship in Q3 and is not in scope of this doc.
- Activation KPI is owned by me.

What we measure for the sub-50 work (per the 2023-06-01 small-biz tier scoping):
- Activation deltas (vs. control, vs. mid-seg v2 baseline)
- Support load (tickets / contact rate per activated account, by seat band)
- Gross retention by seat band (we are NOT using ACV as a metric for this tier)

What we explicitly do NOT do in this readout:
- We do not pool 50–75 into mid-seg v2. The 50–75 band is reported on its own line.
- We do not mix sub-50 cuts with the mid-seg v2 cohort for significance. They are separate populations with different effect-size expectations.
- We do not use first-significance-only as evidence. Standing rule from 2023-03-26: first sig on a growth exp does not ship — wait one stab cohort. Pre-registered stab def (same metric, same direction, n ≥ treatment) plus p<0.01 on the second-look cohort must clear before the next peek.

Cuts (per Owen's cadence, locked 2023-02-13): every ruling — in or out — gets a 1-pager with why, cuts, p-value, effect-size, and call. Summary up top, raw attached.

—
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
—

Caveat on what this section shows (Owen, 2023-06-17): the baseline below is descriptive, not causal. It describes what we observe in the data, not what produces activation. In particular, first-week first integration is observed alongside activation in simple deployments — it is not, by itself, established as the cause of activation. We will not promote any framing that treats first-week integration as the lever that "creates" activation until we have a treatment effect in a controlled cut.

Headline: simple under-50 deployments where the customer lands a first integration inside week 1 are already behaving near the target range. The gap is not in the happy path — the gap is in the friction modes around it.

Specifically:
- Near target: first-week first integration on simple under-50 deployments. Activation v3 sits in the band we would expect a healthy sub-50 segment to reach if the deployment stayed simple.
- Lagging by more than 15 points: permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity. Each of these on its own pulls activation v3 down by ≥15 points relative to the simple-deployment baseline.

Read (descriptive): across the sub-50 population we have today, activation v3 is high in the simple-deployment, first-week-first-integration subset and lower in the four friction modes. The descriptive pattern is consistent with — but does not prove — those friction modes being the binding constraint on the segment's activation ceiling. A treatment-effect read (does fixing each mode move activation in a controlled cut?) is the next step.

Implication for scoping: if a future controlled cut confirms the friction-mode pattern as causal, the activation ceiling for sub-50 is gated by those four modes, not by acquisition quality or by the product's ability to deliver value on a clean install. Anything we add on top (lifecycle nudges, expansion plays, pricing-page mechanics) would be downstream of these four. Until that controlled cut lands, we treat the friction modes as the leading candidate spine for what "Helio Start" would need to actually solve — not as a confirmed one.

We are NOT yet calling this finding "shippable." It is a baseline read, not a treatment effect. It needs the second-look cohort and a controlled cut before we promote it.

—
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
—

Framing (Priya, 2023-06-17): the labels below are written so the tier reads as protective for the customer, not as a screen that sorts accounts into a lower tier. We don't say "this account isn't a fit for us." We say "this self-serve setup won't carry this account" — and route them to a path where the setup does carry them. The same framing applies to entry-mechanic choices: trial vs. freemium vs. paid-only entry is about making sure the customer has enough runway and context to succeed, not about offering a cheaper plan.

Pending decisions — to be locked before any customer-facing naming:

Eligibility (open):
- Which seat bands qualify. Band 20–75 is pending as the working envelope; we need a clean ruling on whether 20–50, 50–75, or 20–75 is the in-scope band for the tier. Bands describe what the self-serve setup can carry, not what tier of customer we're willing to take.
- Self-serve vs. sales-assisted boundary for sub-50. Affects refusal-rule design — the question is at what point an account needs a human to succeed, not at what point we choose not to sell to them.
- Trial vs. freemium vs. paid-only entry. The choice is governed by what gives the customer a fair chance to land a first integration and learn whether the product carries their use case — not by offering a lower-priced path.

Refusal rules (open):
- When do we route an account off the self-serve path — at signup, at first-integration miss, at billing-failure, or at migration-complexity flag? Each trigger is a moment where the self-serve setup has stopped carrying the account, and the right response is to move them to a path that does.
- What is the escalation path for routed accounts (sales handoff, hold queue, manual review)? Affects support load metric. The path should make the account feel handed-off, not refused.
- How refusal interacts with the four friction modes: if a customer hits permissions or migration friction, do we route, hold, or sequence? The principle is the same — the self-serve path has stopped carrying the account, so we don't keep them on it.

Implication of the baseline: refusal rules need to be at least as good at catching the four friction modes as they are at catching setup failures generally. A tier that routes on complexity but admits on permissions friction will still miss the activation target, and more importantly will leave customers stuck in a setup that won't deliver for them. The refusal rules protect the customer from that outcome; they are not a filter that protects us from the customer.

Naming implication: until eligibility and refusal rules are locked, "Helio Start" stays internal. We will not surface the name in lifecycle copy, pricing, or sales conversations.

—
5. Open questions
—

Lifecycle:
- What is the in-product nudge cadence for the four friction modes? Standing rule (2023-03-26) applies — first sig does not ship, wait one stab cohort.
- Email vs. in-product vs. PostHog-flagged-only routing for sub-50 expansion plays — must stay disambiguated from email-lift attribution per the expansion_nudge_60d_v1 precedent (launched 2023-05-23, mid-seg v2 only).
- How does the lifecycle path branch when a customer hits a refusal rule? The branch should be a hand-off to a setup that will carry them, not a stop sign.

Instrumentation:
- Are permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity each individually evented in PostHog with sufficient coverage to support the activation v3 cut? Need an audit before we can run the 1-pagers.
- Seat-band tagging at signup — do we have a reliable band-at-signup field, or do we reconstruct it post-hoc? Affects whether eligibility can be measured cleanly.
- Refusal-rule eventing — what fires when a refusal rule trips, and where does it land in the warehouse? Need the same eventing for the routing hand-off, not just the refusal moment.

Support:
- Support load model for the four friction modes — what is the expected ticket volume per activated sub-50 account under each mode? Marcus Vail (CRO) alignment requires this to be explicit before any instrumentation commitments land.
- Support boundary: what does Helio support cover for the tier vs. what falls to self-serve docs / community? The boundary should make it clear to the customer where the hand-off is.
- How refusal escalations hit support load — do they count against the support-load metric for this tier? Need this pinned before we read the load number.

Engineering sizing:
- Daniela (eng) capacity is the binding constraint. Need a clean read on the eng ask for the four friction-mode fixes before we can promise anything to Marcus Vail on a ship window.
- Which of the four friction modes are quick wins vs. multi-quarter work? Determines whether we scope to a v0 of the tier or wait for a fuller build.
- Instrumentation work above — eng sizing depends on what the audit surfaces.

—
End of pre-read. Next step: walk this with Priya Monday, then lock the band decision and start the instrumentation audit.

arguments.body:
Daniela —

Putting EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger in front of you for eng review before we power it on. Flag: lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2, experiment registered today (status: designed).

What it is
- Mid-segment only.
- Control: day-7 onboarding touch fires on literal calendar day-7, as today.
- Treatment: touch fires on the activation event (user crosses the first-use threshold), regardless of calendar day.
- Powered for 2 weeks, target n=400 (200/200).

messages.content: [2023-06-05T12:15:00-05:00] Owen sent me two May activation views that don't line up, and I want to answer him without manufacturing an emergency. The dashboard default is on activation definition v3 and it shows a materially lower activation rate than an older notebook still on v2. My strong guess is definition drift, not a product drop: v3 is completed first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days, while v2 was first integration plus two logins in 14 days. Can you sanity-check how I should explain that mismatch to Owen, and list the specific checks we should run before anyone edits dashboard labels or forwards May activation numbers?

Your read is almost certainly correct, and here's why it's safe to hold the line without escalating:

The direction of the gap matches the ordering of the definitions, not a product regression.

  v3 = first integration + ≥1 in-product event within 14d
  v2 = first integration + 2 logins within 14d

v3 is strictly a subset of v2. Anyone who logged in twice but never fired an in-product event is counted by v2 and dropped by v3. So v3 rate ≤ v2 rate, always. A materially lower number on v3 is what a tightened def produces — it isn't evidence of a drop. That's the one-paragraph version you can give Owen.

The thing that would make it a real emergency is if v3 itself is moving against its own baseline. So the checklist below is sequenced to prove "definition drift" cheaply before anyone touches labels or forwards May numbers.

Checks to run before any edit or external number:

1. Lock the v3 time series for May vs Mar/Apr on the same def.
   This is the single most important check. v3 has been live since 2023-03-16, and your memory note says the lift has been holding since Mar 7+. Pull May v3 activation on the same 75-200 v2 cohort frame and compare to Mar and Apr v3. If May is in line with the prior two months on v3, you have a clean "definition drift, no product signal" answer. If May is materially below, then it's not just drift and you need a deeper cut before forwarding anything.

2. Compute the gap on the same cohort frame, side by side.
   Re-run v2 activation for May on the exact same cohort (75-200 v2, 14d window, same first-event milestone). The delta between v2 and v3 on the same cohort is the "tightening tax" — the share of May activations who logged in twice but never fired an in-product event. That number is the headline Riley-and-Owen can both defend.

3. Confirm both views use the same "first integration" milestone.
   This is the silent failure mode. If the notebook's "integration" is first signup-to-paid and the dashboard's is first API key provisioned, you're comparing two different starts, not just two different endings. Check the milestone event name and timestamp on both sides before you trust anything else.

4. Confirm the cohort band on both sides.
   Your standing rule (Owen 2023-04-26) is v2 cohort = 75-200 default, v1 = 50-200 still preserved for comps. If the notebook is silently on v1 (50-200) and the dashboard is on v2 (75-200), part of the gap is cohort, not definition. Re-tag the notebook's cohort to 75-200 v2 and rerun. This is a known footgun from the April re-tag.

5. Confirm the date frame.
   "May activation" can mean signed-up-in-May, first-active-in-May, or first-event-in-May. Check both views are using the same framing. The notebook being older is more likely to be on a different frame than the dashboard.

6. Check in-product event taxonomy stability Mar → May.
   v3's "in-product event" is only meaningful if the event list didn't change underneath it. Pull a count of distinct event names contributing to "in-product event" in Mar, Apr, May. If a meaningful event was renamed, deprecated, or added mid-May, that's a third source of drift on top of the def change.

7. Sanity-check expansion_nudge_60d_v1 exposure (launched 2023-05-23, 25% on retained mid-seg).
   Only relevant if the gap is on the v3 side and concentrated post-5/23. The nudge changes in-product behavior, which could shift v3 counts in the treatment arm. Unlikely to be the main driver, but cheap to rule out.

8. Quantify the reclassified bucket explicitly.
   Of the May cohort that activates under v2, how many are dropped under v3? Show Owen the count, not just the rate. A concrete reclassification number ("X of Y May activations didn't fire an in-product event") is what kills the "is the product broken?" question in one sentence.

What to do with the output:

  - If checks 1–5 pass and the gap is fully explained by definition drift: dashboard labels stay, the notebook is stale on v2, and you can answer Owen with the side-by-side …

arguments.title: Helio Start pre-discovery readout — measurement spine
arguments.body:
Pre-read for Monday. Builds on the baseline summary Priya already read. Goal of this doc: lock the measurement spine before we go further on naming, lifecycle, or pricing mechanics.

Sections:
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
2. Measurement method
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
5. Open questions (lifecycle, instrumentation, support, eng sizing)

—
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
—

"Helio Start" is the working name for the sub-50-seat tier we are pre-discovering. It is internal shorthand only.

Priya's gate (2023-06-14): the name implies nothing customer-facing until all of the following are ready — eligibility rules, refusal rules, instrumentation, lifecycle paths, and support boundaries. Nothing in this doc, in the baseline summary, or in any Slack thread should be read as a launch commitment, a launch date, or a marketing promise.

If this tier ships, the working name may change. Anything written here should hold under that.

—
2. Measurement method
—

Cohort definitions (locked):
- Mid-seg v2 = 75–200 seats (default since 2023-04-26). 50–75 = starter band. v1 (50–200) stays in the warehouse for back-compat comps only — we do not roll v1 forward.
- Under-50 / sub-50 = the band this tier work is actually about. We report it separately from mid-seg v2 in every cut going forward.

Activation (locked):
- Activation definition v3: `+ ≥1 in-product event in 14d` (locked 2023-03-16). Target: 60% for mid-seg+ in 14d; the conditional 65% target is tied to sub-50 tier ship in Q3 and is not in scope of this doc.
- Activation KPI is owned by me.

What we measure for the sub-50 work (per the 2023-06-01 small-biz tier scoping):
- Activation deltas (vs. control, vs. mid-seg v2 baseline)
- Support load (tickets / contact rate per activated account, by seat band)
- Gross retention by seat band (we are NOT using ACV as a metric for this tier)

What we explicitly do NOT do in this readout:
- We do not pool 50–75 into mid-seg v2. The 50–75 band is reported on its own line.
- We do not mix sub-50 cuts with the mid-seg v2 cohort for significance. They are separate populations with different effect-size expectations.
- We do not use first-significance-only as evidence. Standing rule from 2023-03-26: first sig on a growth exp does not ship — wait one stab cohort. Pre-registered stab def (same metric, same direction, n ≥ treatment) plus p<0.01 on the second-look cohort must clear before the next peek.

Cuts (per Owen's cadence, locked 2023-02-13): every ruling — in or out — gets a 1-pager with why, cuts, p-value, effect-size, and call. Summary up top, raw attached.

—
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
—

Headline: simple under-50 deployments where the customer lands a first integration inside week 1 are already behaving near the target range. The gap is not in the happy path — the gap is in the friction modes around it.

Specifically:
- Near target: first-week first integration on simple under-50 deployments. Activation v3 sits in the band we would expect a healthy sub-50 segment to reach if the deployment stayed simple.
- Lagging by more than 15 points: permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity. Each of these on its own pulls activation v3 down by ≥15 points relative to the simple-deployment baseline.

Read: the activation ceiling for sub-50 is not gated by acquisition quality or by the product's ability to deliver value on a clean install. It is gated by the four friction modes above. Any tier design that does not address those four modes will not move the activation KPI regardless of pricing, naming, or lifecycle cadence.

Implication for scoping: the four friction modes are the spine of what "Helio Start" needs to actually solve. Anything we add on top (lifecycle nudges, expansion plays, pricing-page mechanics) is downstream of these four.

We are NOT yet calling this finding "shippable." It is a baseline read, not a treatment effect. It needs the second-look cohort before we promote it.

—
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
—

Pending decisions — to be locked before any customer-facing naming:

Eligibility (open):
- Which seat bands qualify. Band 20–75 is pending as the working envelope; we need a clean ruling on whether 20–50, 50–75, or 20–75 is the in-scope band for the tier.
- Self-serve vs. sales-assisted boundary for sub-50. Affects refusal-rule design.
- Trial vs. freemium vs. paid-only entry. Affects refusal rules and instrumentation scope.

Refusal rules (open):
- When do we say "this customer is not a Helio Start fit" — at signup, at first-integration miss, at billing-failure, or at migration-complexity flag?
- What is the escalation path for refused accounts (sales handoff, hold queue, manual review)? Affects support load metric.
- How refusal interacts with the four friction modes: if a customer hits permissions or migration friction, do we refuse, route, or sequence?

Implication of the baseline: refusal rules need to be at least as good at catching the four friction modes as they are at catching fit-mismatches. A tier that refuses on fit but admits on permissions complexity will still miss the activation target.

Naming implication: until eligibility and refusal rules are locked, "Helio Start" stays internal. We will not surface the name in lifecycle copy, pricing, or sales conversations.

—
5. Open questions
—

Lifecycle:
- What is the in-product nudge cadence for the four friction modes? Standing rule (2023-03-26) applies — first sig does not ship, wait one stab cohort.
- Email vs. in-product vs. PostHog-flagged-only routing for sub-50 expansion plays — must stay disambiguated from email-lift attribution per the expansion_nudge_60d_v1 precedent (launched 2023-05-23, mid-seg v2 only).
- How does the lifecycle path branch when a customer hits a refusal rule?

Instrumentation:
- Are permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity each individually evented in PostHog with sufficient coverage to support the activation v3 cut? Need an audit before we can run the 1-pagers.
- Seat-band tagging at signup — do we have a reliable band-at-signup field, or do we reconstruct it post-hoc? Affects whether eligibility can be measured cleanly.
- Refusal-rule eventing — what fires when a refusal rule trips, and where does it land in the warehouse?

Support:
- Support load model for the four friction modes — what is the expected ticket volume per activated sub-50 account under each mode? Marcus Vail (CRO) alignment requires this to be explicit before any instrumentation commitments land.
- Support boundary: what does Helio support cover for the tier vs. what falls to self-serve docs / community?
- How refusal escalations hit support load — do they count against the support-load metric for this tier?

Engineering sizing:
- Daniela (eng) capacity is the binding constraint. Need a clean read on the eng ask for the four friction-mode fixes before we can promise anything to Marcus Vail on a ship window.
- Which of the four friction modes are quick wins vs. multi-quarter work? Determines whether we scope to a v0 of the tier or wait for a fuller build.
- Instrumentation work above — eng sizing depends on what the audit surfaces.

arguments.body:
Pre-read for Monday. Builds on the baseline summary Priya already read. Goal of this doc: lock the measurement spine before we go further on naming, lifecycle, or pricing mechanics.

How to read this doc: the refusal rules, eligibility checks, and tier design we are pre-discovering exist to protect customers from a self-serve setup that won't deliver value for them. If a setup will fail for an account — whether because of permissions, import, billing, or migration complexity, or because the account's needs exceed what self-serve carries — the right move is to route that account to a path where they can succeed, not to push them through a plan they will churn out of. Every refusal rule below should be readable as a customer safeguard first.

Sections:
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
2. Measurement method
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
5. Open questions (lifecycle, instrumentation, support, eng sizing)

—
1. Helio Start is a working name, not a launch promise
—

"Helio Start" is the working name for the sub-50-seat tier we are pre-discovering. It is internal shorthand only.

Priya's gate (2023-06-14): the name implies nothing customer-facing until all of the following are ready — eligibility rules, refusal rules, instrumentation, lifecycle paths, and support boundaries. Nothing in this doc, in the baseline summary, or in any Slack thread should be read as a launch commitment, a launch date, or a marketing promise.

The framing is protective, not exclusionary: we are pre-discovering whether the tier can be designed so that customers who enter it have a realistic path to activation, and so that customers the tier won't serve are routed to a path that does. If the design can't meet that bar, the right answer is to not ship the tier, not to ship it with weaker rules.

If this tier ships, the working name may change. Anything written here should hold under that.

—
2. Measurement method
—

Cohort definitions (locked):
- Mid-seg v2 = 75–200 seats (default since 2023-04-26). 50–75 = starter band. v1 (50–200) stays in the warehouse for back-compat comps only — we do not roll v1 forward.
- Under-50 / sub-50 = the band this tier work is actually about. We report it separately from mid-seg v2 in every cut going forward.

Activation (locked):
- Activation definition v3: `+ ≥1 in-product event in 14d` (locked 2023-03-16). Target: 60% for mid-seg+ in 14d; the conditional 65% target is tied to sub-50 tier ship in Q3 and is not in scope of this doc.
- Activation KPI is owned by me.

What we measure for the sub-50 work (per the 2023-06-01 small-biz tier scoping):
- Activation deltas (vs. control, vs. mid-seg v2 baseline)
- Support load (tickets / contact rate per activated account, by seat band)
- Gross retention by seat band (we are NOT using ACV as a metric for this tier)

What we explicitly do NOT do in this readout:
- We do not pool 50–75 into mid-seg v2. The 50–75 band is reported on its own line.
- We do not mix sub-50 cuts with the mid-seg v2 cohort for significance. They are separate populations with different effect-size expectations.
- We do not use first-significance-only as evidence. Standing rule from 2023-03-26: first sig on a growth exp does not ship — wait one stab cohort. Pre-registered stab def (same metric, same direction, n ≥ treatment) plus p<0.01 on the second-look cohort must clear before the next peek.

Cuts (per Owen's cadence, locked 2023-02-13): every ruling — in or out — gets a 1-pager with why, cuts, p-value, effect-size, and call. Summary up top, raw attached.

—
3. Baseline finding (under-50 deployments)
—

Caveat on what this section shows (Owen, 2023-06-17): the baseline below is descriptive, not causal. It describes what we observe in the data, not what produces activation. In particular, first-week first integration is observed alongside activation in simple deployments — it is not, by itself, established as the cause of activation. We will not promote any framing that treats first-week integration as the lever that "creates" activation until we have a treatment effect in a controlled cut.

Headline: simple under-50 deployments where the customer lands a first integration inside week 1 are already behaving near the target range. The gap is not in the happy path — the gap is in the friction modes around it.

Specifically:
- Near target: first-week first integration on simple under-50 deployments. Activation v3 sits in the band we would expect a healthy sub-50 segment to reach if the deployment stayed simple.
- Lagging by more than 15 points: permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity. Each of these on its own pulls activation v3 down by ≥15 points relative to the simple-deployment baseline.

Read (descriptive): across the sub-50 population we have today, activation v3 is high in the simple-deployment, first-week-first-integration subset and lower in the four friction modes. The descriptive pattern is consistent with — but does not prove — those friction modes being the binding constraint on the segment's activation ceiling. A treatment-effect read (does fixing each mode move activation in a controlled cut?) is the next step.

Implication for scoping: if a future controlled cut confirms the friction-mode pattern as causal, the activation ceiling for sub-50 is gated by those four modes, not by acquisition quality or by the product's ability to deliver value on a clean install. Anything we add on top (lifecycle nudges, expansion plays, pricing-page mechanics) would be downstream of these four. Until that controlled cut lands, we treat the friction modes as the leading candidate spine for what "Helio Start" would need to actually solve — not as a confirmed one.

We are NOT yet calling this finding "shippable." It is a baseline read, not a treatment effect. It needs the second-look cohort and a controlled cut before we promote it.

—
4. Eligibility and refusal-rule implications
—

Framing (Priya, 2023-06-17): the labels below are written so the tier reads as protective for the customer, not as a screen that sorts accounts into a lower tier. We don't say "this account isn't a fit for us." We say "this self-serve setup won't carry this account" — and route them to a path where the setup does carry them. The same framing applies to entry-mechanic choices: trial vs. freemium vs. paid-only entry is about making sure the customer has enough runway and context to succeed, not about offering a cheaper plan.

Pending decisions — to be locked before any customer-facing naming:

Eligibility (open):
- Which seat bands qualify. Band 20–75 is pending as the working envelope; we need a clean ruling on whether 20–50, 50–75, or 20–75 is the in-scope band for the tier. Bands describe what the self-serve setup can carry, not what tier of customer we're willing to take.
- Self-serve vs. sales-assisted boundary for sub-50. Affects refusal-rule design — the question is at what point an account needs a human to succeed, not at what point we choose not to sell to them.
- Trial vs. freemium vs. paid-only entry. The choice is governed by what gives the customer a fair chance to land a first integration and learn whether the product carries their use case — not by offering a lower-priced path.

Refusal rules (open):
- When do we route an account off the self-serve path — at signup, at first-integration miss, at billing-failure, or at migration-complexity flag? Each trigger is a moment where the self-serve setup has stopped carrying the account, and the right response is to move them to a path that does.
- What is the escalation path for routed accounts (sales handoff, hold queue, manual review)? Affects support load metric. The path should make the account feel handed-off, not refused.
- How refusal interacts with the four friction modes: if a customer hits permissions or migration friction, do we route, hold, or sequence? The principle is the same — the self-serve path has stopped carrying the account, so we don't keep them on it.

Implication of the baseline: refusal rules need to be at least as good at catching the four friction modes as they are at catching setup failures generally. A tier that routes on complexity but admits on permissions friction will still miss the activation target, and more importantly will leave customers stuck in a setup that won't deliver for them. The refusal rules protect the customer from that outcome; they are not a filter that protects us from the customer.

Naming implication: until eligibility and refusal rules are locked, "Helio Start" stays internal. We will not surface the name in lifecycle copy, pricing, or sales conversations.

—
5. Open questions
—

Lifecycle:
- What is the in-product nudge cadence for the four friction modes? Standing rule (2023-03-26) applies — first sig does not ship, wait one stab cohort.
- Email vs. in-product vs. PostHog-flagged-only routing for sub-50 expansion plays — must stay disambiguated from email-lift attribution per the expansion_nudge_60d_v1 precedent (launched 2023-05-23, mid-seg v2 only).
- How does the lifecycle path branch when a customer hits a refusal rule? The branch should be a hand-off to a setup that will carry them, not a stop sign.

Instrumentation:
- Are permissions, import, billing, and migration complexity each individually evented in PostHog with sufficient coverage to support the activation v3 cut? Need an audit before we can run the 1-pagers.
- Seat-band tagging at signup — do we have a reliable band-at-signup field, or do we reconstruct it post-hoc? Affects whether eligibility can be measured cleanly.
- Refusal-rule eventing — what fires when a refusal rule trips, and where does it land in the warehouse? Need the same eventing for the routing hand-off, not just the refusal moment.

Support:
- Support load model for the four friction modes — what is the expected ticket volume per activated sub-50 account under each mode? Marcus Vail (CRO) alignment requires this to be explicit before any instrumentation commitments land.
- Support boundary: what does Helio support cover for the tier vs. what falls to self-serve docs / community? The boundary should make it clear to the customer where the hand-off is.
- How refusal escalations hit support load — do they count against the support-load metric for this tier? Need this pinned before we read the load number.

Engineering sizing:
- Daniela (eng) capacity is the binding constraint. Need a clean read on the eng ask for the four friction-mode fixes before we can promise anything to Marcus Vail on a ship window.
- Which of the four friction modes are quick wins vs. multi-quarter work? Determines whether we scope to a v0 of the tier or wait for a fuller build.
- Instrumentation work above — eng sizing depends on what the audit surfaces.

—
End of pre-read. Next step: walk this with Priya Monday, then lock the band decision and start the instrumentation audit.

messages.content: [2023-03-16T11:00:00-05:00] with Owen on this now. shipping activation def v3 as `first integration` plus at least one in-product event inside day 14. v2 stays in the warehouse as `first integration + logged in twice in 14 days` -- that's been the cut since Nov 2022 -- and v1 is still there too, just `first integration in 14 days` from Aug 2022. not deleting any of it. versioned tables so I can still pull historical cohort comps across all three without the usual "wait which definition was live then" mess. leaning right call -- post-pricing-page wobble, login-twice was giving us too much fake comfort and not enough product proof.

That lands. Two quick things:

1. Versioned tables — good call by Owen. Preempts the "which def was live then" mess cleanly. The fact that he kept v1 around too (not just v2) is the move — that's where most teams get lazy and end up splicing definitions across cohort history.

2. v3 rate will read lower than v2. The post-pricing-page-wobble crowd is exactly the group that logged in twice without ever touching a feature — they hit v2, miss v3. When v3 becomes metric-of-record, expect the 60% KPI to take a hit. Saving v3 to memory.

Helio lifecycle documentation — design lineage note (2028-01-01)

Author: Riley Tanaka
Purpose: Distinguish two parallel threads that touch the lifecycle stack so future readers do not conflate them. Both ship dates are in the same month (March 2023) and both reference "activation," but they answer different questions and are owned separately.

────────────────────────
THREAD 1 — Onboarding email trigger change
────────────────────────

What changed
The day-7 onboarding email stop condition was changed from a calendar trigger to a behavior trigger.

- Experiment: EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger
- Flag: lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2 (rolled 2023-03-13; mid-seg only; 50% rollout; 50–200 seat v1 bucket; target n=400 over 2 weeks)
- Control arm: day-7 touch fires on literal calendar day-7, as before
- Treatment arm: day-7 touch fires on the activation event (first-use threshold), regardless of calendar day
- Hypothesis: week-1 retention lifts ≥ +2 pts when the email lands after the user has crossed the first-use threshold rather than mid-setup
- Eng review: closed by Daniela 2023-03-12 (1 day late vs. planned ship)
- Suppression logic (dedupe against the existing day-7 scheduler): one touch per user, on whichever trigger fires first; late-activation cap at day-14 to avoid dropping a "you crossed activation" email on a user who has been active for two weeks

Why this thread exists
The trigger change is a lifecycle mechanic. It changes when the email goes out. It does not change what counts as activation, does not change the metric-of-record, and does not change the activation rate itself. Any read on this flag is a read on lifecycle cadence; it is not a read on product engagement.

Scope discipline
Pinned as scope-disjoint from pricing_page_2026q2_rev (different cohort, different metric-of-record) in the launch doc so later attribution does not get mashed.

────────────────────────
THREAD 2 — Activation definition review (separate thread)
────────────────────────

Why the definition was reviewed
The previous metric-of-record (v2: first integration + 2 logins within 14d, live Nov 2022 – Mar 2023) was contaminated by the 2023 pricing-page wobble. Login-twice is an attendance metric. The pricing-page wobble pulled in shoppers who logged in twice without ever firing a product event, which v2 counted as activation. That gave a falsely comfortable number and not enough product proof.

The review's conclusion was that login-twice was a weak signal post-wobble and that the metric needed to be re-anchored on real product engagement — not on whether a user happened to open the app twice.

What the successor metric direction was intended to be
Move activation from an attendance basis to a usage basis within the 14d window, while keeping the first-integration milestone as the gate and preserving all earlier definitions for historical comparison.

- v1 (Aug 2022): first integration in 14d
- v2 (Nov 2022 – Mar 2023): first integration + 2 logins in 14d
- v3 (2023-03-16, with Owen): first integration + ≥1 in-product event in 14d — the metric-of-record going forward

Direction (read this as a single sentence): from "the user showed up twice" → to "the user did something in the product." v3 is a strict subset of v2 — anyone who logged in twice but never fired an in-product event counts under v2 and is correctly dropped under v3. As a consequence, v3 rate reads lower than v2; this is intentional tightening, not a regression, and was flagged in the launch note for that reason.

Versioned tables, not deletions
v1 and v2 are not deleted. They live in versioned tables so historical cohort comps (e.g., "what was the activation rate in Aug 2022 cohorts?") remain answerable without splicing definitions across cohort history. The rule going forward is: pick the version that matches the time window of the cohort being read, and do not blend.

────────────────────────
Why these two threads must not be treated as one combined change
────────────────────────

- Different questions. Thread 1 changes when a lifecycle email fires. Thread 2 changes what counts as activation.
- Different surfaces. Thread 1 touches lifecycle tooling (trigger / scheduler / suppression). Thread 2 touches the events model and the metric-of-record in the warehouse.
- Different scopes of evaluation. Thread 1 is read on week-1 retention in mid-seg. Thread 2 is read on activation rate (target 60% mid-seg+ in 14d) across the versioned tables.
- Different drift modes. Thread 1 drift = mid-run reads before the 2-week exposure window completes (rule: no result narrative mid-run). Thread 2 drift = dashboards/notebooks silently running on v2 instead of v3, producing a definition mismatch that looks like a product drop (May 2023 sanity check is the canonical example).
- Different downstream effects. Thread 1 affects cohort experience (when they get the email). Thread 2 affects every metric that uses activation as input, including the activation KPI itself, and is the input into Thread 1's treatment-arm definition.

When in doubt: if you are looking at when an email goes out, you are on Thread 1; if you are looking at whether a user activated, you are on Thread 2; if you are looking at both at once, name which is which in the write-up so the two are not collapsed.

────────────────────────
Pointers
────────────────────────

- Thread 1 source: EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger; flag lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2; ship 2023-03-13; eng review closed 2023-03-12; design discussion 2023-03-01 (event eligibility + dedupe + late-activation cap).
- Thread 2 source: activation definition v3 ship 2023-03-16 (with Owen); versioned tables preserve v1 (Aug 2022) and v2 (Nov 2022 – Mar 2023); review rationale = post-pricing-page-wobble attendance contamination; successor direction = attendance-based login-twice → usage-based in-product event within the 14d window; activation target 60% mid-seg+ held; v3 rate reads lower than v2 as intentional tightening.

==========================================================================================

Scope of this checkpoint
------------------------
This checkpoint records the bounded CS auto-nudge ledger through May 29 against the standing sections 1–8 of this note. It is interim operational evidence for the 2025-06-13 review gate. It is not a reliability verdict, not a maturity claim, and not evidence to retire the legacy configuration. Daniela's coordinated rollback control remains available and unchanged.

1. Primary denominator through May 29
-------------------------------------
641 unique scheduled nudge decisions are now the primary ledger entries in section 1. Each decision appears once in the primary denominator regardless of how many checks, holds, or re-evaluations it accumulated afterward.

Of those 641:
  - 31 stale or conflicting decisions failed closed. This count includes the 12 May 20 decisions affected by the Customer Success refresh delay.

The 12 May 20 decisions count once each in the 641 primary denominator. Their field-specific holds, the post-restore fresh checks, and the final dispositions (8 suppressions, 4 proceeds) remain in those rows' audit histories — not as new primary rows, not as parallel ledger entries. This matches the denominator rule already in this note since 2025-05-15 and the May 23 checkpoint, restated adjacent to the event itself. No primary row is added or duplicated by this checkpoint.

-------------------------------------

---------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------

Observed usage: 2 Ventolin fills in 2026 ($61.80 + $64.25); 24 tier-1 fills (lisinopril + atorvastatin), all $0.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
GUARANTEED PLAN TERMS (verified 11/2/26)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Monthly premium (PDP):  $35.40
  Annual premium:          $35.40 × 12 = $424.80
  Tier 1 generics:         $0 (ded waived) — lisinopril 10mg, atorvastatin 20mg
  Tier 2/brand (Ventolin): subject to $615 annual deductible, then $49 copay

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2027 VENTOLIN PRICE — UNKNOWN / ILLUSTRATIVE
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  The 2027 negotiated pre-deductible price for Ventolin HFA is NOT a
  verified plan term. The two 2026 fills give only an illustrative range:
     Low  : $61.80/fill × 2 = $123.60
     High : $64.25/fill × 2 = $128.50
  Neither figure is a 2027 quote and neither is the $49 post-deductible copay.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
KEY STRUCTURAL POINT
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  2 fills at the high end = $128.50 — well below the $615 deductible.
  At her observed usage, Mom stays in pre-deductible territory all year.
  The $49 post-deductible copay is a paper benefit for this scenario;
  Mom pays full negotiated price on each Ventolin fill.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ILLUSTRATIVE 2027 ANNUAL TOTAL
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Annual premium:        $424.80
  Tier 1 generics (24):    $0.00
  Ventolin — low range:  $123.60  →  TOTAL  $548.40
  Ventolin — high range: $128.50  →  TOTAL  $553.30

  Illustrative 2027 band:  $548.40 – $553.30
  (Excludes any new drug, formulary change, pharmacy switch, or LIS status.)

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
SCOPE NOTES (read these before using the number)
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  • Mom has not chosen coverage; 2027 Medicare OEP closes 12/7/26.
  • This is an illustrative band grounded in 2026 actuals — not a 2027 quote.
  • Holds only if (a) the three drugs and tiers are unchanged, (b) River Park
    Community Pharmacy stays preferred, (c) no new Rx is added, (d) no
    formulary/tier move hits between now and 1/1/27.
  • No enrollment recommendation is made here; decision belongs to Mom by 12/7.

input.body:
Patient: Riley Tanaka
Date of visit: 2027-11-05
Site: Right ankle, reassessment
Clinician-facing record

Reason for visit
Follow-up reassessment of the right ankle. Patient had been progressing through a structured return-to-run protocol and presented for clearance review and plan adjustment.

Findings
- Right ankle tolerating the prescribed loading without symptom recurrence between sessions.
- Each run day followed by a symptom-free next day, meeting the criterion required to advance.
- No new complaints referable to the ankle. Calf and ankle strength work ongoing and well tolerated.

Authorized running plan
- Frequency: two non-consecutive easy runs per week.
- Duration: up to 40 minutes per run, easy intensity.
- Progression rule: each run must be followed by a symptom-free next day before the next run is attempted; do not advance load if any symptoms appear.
- Adjunctive strengthening: ankle and calf strengthening three times per week, on non-running days.

Explicit restrictions
- No third run added to the week.
- No fourth bike day added to the week.
- No run scheduled on a day that also includes a bike session; running and biking remain on separate days.
- Bike sessions remain capped at the previously prescribed duration and intensity (Tuesday and Thursday, easy, ≤25 minutes per leg).

Compliance and escalation
- Patient instructed to hold progression and re-contact the clinic if symptoms recur, if a symptom-free next day is not achieved, or if swelling, pain at rest, or gait change develops.
- Plan to be reviewed at the next scheduled reassessment.

   Comment #1: security owner never approved connector permissions; live setup never finished.
   Mechanism: a stakeholder outside the buying team blocks go-live. Sequence matters (pre-build vs. mid-build) and changes remediation.

B. Post-setup value realization failure — owner: us (activation + seat usage)

D. Workaround adequacy / scope mismatch — owner: us (pricing tiers, fit discovery)
   Comment #4: CSV import covered the one campaign; ongoing plan was more than needed.
   Mechanism: customer found a cheaper substitute that met their narrow need. Distinct from B — they concluded they did not need the product, not that they could not realize value from it.

E. Customer-side implementation guidance gap — owner: us (onboarding content, CS handoff)
   Comment #5: connector worked, but customer could not map lifecycle stages.
   Mechanism: connection succeeded; configuration/mapping guidance failed. Distinct from A (their gate blocked us) and from B (their usage dropped).

F. Champion absence at renewal moment — owner: us (renewal comms, multi-stakeholder confirmation)
   Comment #6: renewal arrived during champion's leave; no successor.
   Mechanism: process timing combined with single-point-of-contact fragility in the customer org.

Cautious synthesis

  - Five of the six themes are independently addressable; only B and E are neighbors, and even they split cleanly (behavior vs. capability).
  - Resist any framing that implies "X% of retained-mid exits are due to setup." We do not have a denominator and six comments are not a representative sample.
  - Resist merging A, B, and E into one "onboarding" bucket. They are three different failure points at three different ownerships (their gate, their behavior, their capability).
  - C is a non-signal for product or GTM action. Worth flagging as macro churn, not as a setup problem.
  - The only cross-cutting hypothesis worth a follow-up: A and F may share an underlying cause — single-point-of-contact fragility in the customer org (a security owner who never engages; a champion who disappears at renewal). This is a hypothesis from these six, not a finding. Treat it as a question for Priya, not a conclusion.

Plain questions for Priya

  Q1. Are these six from a defined cohort/window or a convenience sample? If convenience, do not quote counts. If cohort-defined, what is the denominator?
  Q2. For #1 — what stage of onboarding was the security owner blocking at? Pre-build vs. mid-build changes the remediation path entirely.
  Q3. For #2 and #5 — same customer, or different? If different, the split between adoption and capability is clean. If same, the picture is messier and the comment is doing double duty.
  Q4. For #3 — was the budget cut publicly disclosed (layoff news, earnings call, etc.) so we can identify other a…

arguments.body:
Q2 2027 Helio Start paid-test proposal — working draft
Status: development draft. Not an approved launch plan. Paid traffic remains off through 2027-03-31.

1. Status and what this is
- 2027-03-24: Priya authorized development of a Q2 paid-test proposal for Helio Start. This document is the development draft.
- This draft deliberately does NOT decide launch, budget, traffic allocation, pipeline treatment or pipeline target, forecast credit, eligibility change, lifecycle bypass, launch timing, or a second paid batch. Those are excluded (see §11).
- Owner of this draft: Riley. Routing for decisions: Priya (final). Channel convention preserved (#growth-investigations for churn/cohort; #lifecycle-systems for kickoff/cert).

2. Decisions still required (not made in this draft)
The following are unresolved as of 2027-03-24 and must be decided in a separate, future step before launch:
  a. Launch timing (calendar window and start date).
  b. Budget (paid spend envelope and approval path).
  c. Traffic allocation (channels, mix, partner routing).
  d. Pipeline treatment and pipeline target (whether/how paid admissions enter the forecast or pipeline).
  e. Forecast credit (whether/how paid admissions credit to forecast).
  f. Launch (go/no-go) decision itself.
  g. A second paid batch (whether, when, scope).
  h. Whether to develop a Q3 plan conditional on day-90 read (decision-gate only; no Q3 plan in this draft).
Items (a)–(g) are not approved by this draft. This draft does not bypass, modify, or pre-decide any of them.

3. Batch scope and close rule
- Scope: a single paid-traffic batch of Helio Start admissions routed through the ordinary eligibility flow. Eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and assisted-routing rules are unchanged (see §7).
- Close rule: the batch closes at the EARLIER of (i) $8,000 in paid spend, or (ii) 25 paid admissions. Whichever threshold is hit first ends the batch.
- Trailing-attribution window after close: admissions in flight at close continue to be tracked through day-90 support; no new paid admissions are admitted after the close threshold is met.
- Reporting cadence during the batch: a running tally of admissions vs. 25-admission cap and spend vs. $8,000 cap, refreshed per the standard cadence, so the close trigger is unambiguous when hit.

4. Unsupported-admission stop
- Definition: an "unsupported admission" is an admission to Helio Start that, at admission time, lacks the support posture required by the ordinary assisted-path coverage standard (e.g., missing connector access, missing required lifecycle state, missing external-authority clearance, or any condition that would render day-90 support infeasible within the assisted-path envelope).
- Stop rule: if an unsupported admission is detected during the batch (i.e., before close, before day-90 support is complete), the batch halts at that admission for paid-source routing purposes. The detected admission is not counted toward the 25-admission cap if and only if excluding it preserves assisted-path coverage; otherwise it is counted and a flag is raised for the routing-or-instrumentation pause (see §5).
- Post-detection action: trigger the routing-or-instrumentation pause (§5). Do NOT route around the issue by relaxing eligibility, refusing ordinary users, bypassing lifecycle, or granting connector access out of band.

5. Routing-or-instrumentation pause
- Trigger: an unsupported-admission detection (§4), OR a post-10-admission support-pause breach (§6), OR an attribution reconciliation failure (§6).
- Action on trigger: pause routing new paid admissions AND pause any instrumentation writes specific to the paid-source cohort (read-only audit remains on) until the cause is identified and a written restart condition is documented in this brief or its successor.
- Restart condition: written identification of cause, written fix, and written sign-off. Restart does NOT authorize a second paid batch (§11).
- Scope of pause: paid-source routing and paid-source-specific instrumentation only. Ordinary (non-paid-source) eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, and assisted-routing behavior are unaffected.

6. End-to-end paid-source attribution reconciliation
- Scope: from eligibility-flow start, through admission decision, through assisted routing. Must be auditable at the account level end-to-end.
- Required checkpoints (each must have a recorded source-of-truth and an account-level join key):
  - eligibility-flow start (entry into the eligibility flow, regardless of outcome)
  - eligibility outcome (admit / refuse / hold, with reason)
  - admission (Helio Start admission event, with timestamp)
  - assisted routing (which assisted-path lane the admission was routed to, with timestamp)
- Reconciliation rule: every admitted paid-source account must have a non-empty value at each of the four checkpoints, joined on a single account-level key. Any missing or mismatched value is an attribution reconciliation failure and triggers the routing-or-instrumentation pause (§5).
- Read-only audit access is preserved during any pause to support reconciliation.
- This reconciliation is descriptive and operational. It does NOT modify eligibility, refusal, connector-access, external-authority, lifecycle, instrumentation, or assisted-routing rules (§7).

7. Post-10-admission support pause above 10%
- Definition: a "support pause" is any day on which the assisted-path lane carrying paid-source admissions is paused, throttled, or operating below its ordinary coverage standard for any reason attributable to the paid-source cohort (e.g., capacity, staffing, or instrumentation issue specific to that cohort).
- Threshold: once paid-source admissions exceed 10 in count (i.e., post-10-admission), the share of support-pause days attributable to the paid-source cohort must stay at or below 10% of elapsed batch days.
- Breach: a breach at any rolling read after the 10-admission mark triggers the routing-or-instrumentation pause (§5). A breach does not by itself constitute a refusal decision for any individual account; ordinary assisted-path coverage for affected accounts is preserved or restored per §7.
- Reporting: per-cadence readout of (paid-source-elapsed-days, paid-source-support-pause-days, ratio) once the cohort passes 10 admissions.

8. Day-90 requirements (complete, for paid-active status)
For an admission to count as "paid-active" at day 90, ALL of the following must be true:
  a. The account is admitted to Helio Start via the ordinary eligibility flow with an auditable end-to-end paid-source attribution chain (§6).
  b. Refund-adjusted collected cash from the account is positive at day 90. "Refund-adjusted collected cash" = gross collected cash from the account over the day-90 window, minus refunds issued to the account over the same window. Chargebacks, disputes, and processor fees are reported alongside but are not netted into this metric unless explicitly decided later.
  c. Account-level support effort is recorded as an account-level aggregate over the day-90 window, expressed in the existing support-effort unit, and is reportable per account (not only in aggregate). Support-effort reporting does NOT bypass or relax assisted-path coverage.
  d. The admission has not been flagged as an unsupported admission that broke assisted-path coverage (§4).
  e. The batch was not in a routing-or-instrumentation pause (§5) covering the admission's day-90 window, OR if it was, the pause has a written restart condition and the admission has been re-validated against that restart condition.
The day-90 read is the read that decides whether the development of a Q3 plan proceeds. This draft does NOT decide Q3.

9. Inputs from owners (solicited, not yet committed in this draft)
- Priya: launch-timing decision, budget decision, traffic allocation decision, pipeline treatment/target decision, forecast credit decision, launch go/no-go, second-paid-batch decision, Q3-development go/no-go on day-90 read. None of these are in this draft (§2, §11).
- Daniela: engineering release/rollback posture for any instrumentation touching paid-source routing. Out of scope for this draft until a concrete launch plan exists.
- Owen: cohort cuts on the paid-source cohort at the post-10-admission gate and at day 90. Methodology consistent with existing cohort work; no new methodology in this draft.
- CS / assisted-path coverage owners: capacity and staffing read for the assisted-path lane carrying paid-source admissions; not a coverage-adequacy judgment, an arithmetic + tradeoff input.
This draft does not solicit approval for any of §2 from these owners; it records the inputs that will be required when those decisions are made.

10. Explicit exclusions (not in this draft)
This draft does NOT decide, approve, request approval for, or pre-decide any of the following. Each is reserved for a separate, future step with its own owner and routing:
  a. Budget (paid spend envelope).
  b. Traffic (channels, mix, partner routing, spend pacing).
  c. Pipeline treatment or pipeline target (whether/how paid admissions affect forecast or pipeline).
  d. Forecast credit (whether/how paid admissions credit to forecast).
  e. Launch timing (calendar window, start date).
  f. Launch (go/no-go).
  g. A second paid batch (whether, when, scope).
A fifth shared-state consumer, a lifecycle bypass, an eligibility change, and a refusal change are also excluded by §7 and are not in scope for this draft under any name.

11. Reminders carried into this draft
- Paid traffic remains off through 2027-03-31.
- This is a development draft, not an approved launch plan.
- The CS cert posture (closed 2027-03-17: 45/45 day-90 support windows complete; median 24m, p90 86m, 3 >90m; no unsupported case entered admitted path; future capped run of ≤25 admitted wkspcs w/o displacing ordinary assisted-path coverage; descriptive — no randomized control) is the standing reference for assisted-path coverage in this draft. This draft does not modify that posture.
- The Expansion Assist descriptive posture (descriptive; keep disputed/cross-surface/exec; don't line-edit routine; eng release/rollback → Daniela) applies to any instrumentation or routing write described here.

12. Open questions for the next iteration (not decisions; just unresolved items)
- Exact attribution join key for end-to-end reconciliation (§6). Candidate: existing account-level key. Confirmation needed before launch plan.
- Reporting cadence for §3 close-trigger tally, §6 reconciliation, and §7 10%-breach readout. Default candidate: standard cadence; confirmation needed before launch plan.
- Definition of "support pause day" for §7 (which throttling states count). To be specified before launch plan; not in this draft.
