messages.content:
Verdict: shape is right (4 items, 4 jobs), but three of the four carry protocol jargon that won't survive handoff, and it drops one axis that's been doing real decision work lately — launch vs widening vs controlled-beta move. Owen and Ines will both fill it in honestly and still overclaim.

LIGHTNESS
Four items is genuinely light. The issue isn't length — it's that lightness assumes shared vocabulary. "Hypothesis stack," "stabilization-cohort confirmation," and "first significance" are Riley-protocol words. A borrower will fill them with plausible-but-wrong content. Light without definitions is hand-waving.

CONFUSING (in order of risk)
1. "Hypothesis stack" — undefined. Ordered by what? Is the top one pre-registered, or is this just "list of guesses"? The pre-reg rule (lock direction+metric before peek) isn't surfaced. A borrower lists three guesses and calls it a stack.
2. "Effect size, not just direction" — in what unit, against what baseline, with what MDE? Effect size without baseline is unfalsifiable; without CI it's point-estimate theater.
3. "Decision boundary" — three buckets specific to one protocol. A borrower with no stabilization cohort will collapse "first sig" and "observation" together. And "first sig" without the second-look rule (same metric/direction, n≥treatment, p<0.01 before next peek) is exactly the fake-1st-sig failure mode the protocol exists to prevent — the checklist asks for the bucket but doesn't encode the rule that earns the label.
4. (bonus) "Metric, cohort, window" — no operationalization. Is the cohort starter / mid? Is the window event-time, exposure-time, or calendar? Starter vs mid (v2 75-200, v1 50-200) has been the live segmentation choice; the checklist doesn't force the writer to name which one or whether the result transfers.

OVERCLAIM BY READER

Ines (lifecycle copy):
  - direction without magnitude → "boosts retention" copy on a 0.3pp effect
  - "first sig" bucket read as "ship it" → copy ships before stabilization, which the protocol forbids
  - population misspecification → copy aimed at all users when cohort was mid-segment only
  - window leak → 2-week finding treated as a permanent truth
  - the hard memory rule (rewrite Ines's snippets ONLY from what she pasted in-turn) isn't enforced here — there's no "this finding supports X copy decision and NOT Y" line, so she reconstructs scope from metric/cohort and overgeneralizes

Owen (analyst):
  - generalizes a single cohort to the dashboard without naming the segment cut
  - reads "stabilization-cohort confirmation" as green light without checking the 2nd-look protocol
  - effect size without CI on the readout
  - conflates calendar vs event-time windows in the pull
  - the 10-04 Cust.io fix and 10-05 34-recipient batch were both "controlled-beta move, NOT launch/widening" — the readout needs that axis or it reads a beta move as a launch signal

WHAT'S MISSING IF YOU WANT IT TO ACTUALLY BE REUSABLE (not just Riley-shaped)
  - header: title, owner, date, allowed audience (who can act on this)
  - baseline/control line — effect size is meaningless without it
  - n_treatment, n_control — the protocol gate is real
  - pre-reg line: was direction+metric locked before the peek? if not, mark exploratory
  - explicit "do not act on bucket 3" stamp, or borrowers will
  - scope-out line: population the finding does NOT generalize to
  - launch / widening / controlled-beta axis — separate from significance, recently load-bearing

If you want, I can draft a v2 with these as named fields rather than implied — keeps the same 4-item spine, just operationalizes each one.

messages.content:
PANEL DRAFT — Onboarding change, p=.04, one week
Lane: Riley (judgment-call escalation). Other panelists can probe other lanes; this draft stays in mine.

THE QUESTION (read verbatim to the candidate):
"An onboarding change has p=.04 after one week. The PM wants to ship it. Would you ship it or not? Explain your decision in five minutes."

WHAT IT SHOULD TEST
Whether the candidate treats p=.04 as a decision input or as a decision. A good answer refuses the yes/no frame until they have:
  - denominator (sample size, segment, pooled vs segmented, was it powered)
  - effect size (absolute lift, practical significance — not just "it's significant")
  - cohort stability (week-1 onboarding cohorts are noisy; do later cohorts agree)
  - support risk (onboarding breakage hits new users; reversibility / rollback)
  - first-sig vs stabilization read (single peek at α=.05 is the classic p-hack;
    pre-reg'd stabilization requires same metric/direction, n≥treatment, and
    a p<.01 second-look BEFORE the next peek)

WHY THE GOTCHA IS RISKY
As written, the prompt rewards a confident yes/no answer with a clean narrative. That is exactly the failure mode we are trying to detect. The signal is in what they ask for FIRST. If they answer ship/not inside 30 seconds without asking for any of the five things above, that is the answer — and it is "no, not from this prompt."

Reframe in your head (do not say this aloud): "Does this person know that p=.04 at one week is the kind of number that ends up in a postmortem six months later?" Listen for the moment they slow down and start requesting inputs.

LISTEN-FORS, BY DIMENSION
Denominator:
  "How many users in treatment? Pooled or per-segment? Powered for the effect we care about, or just for any effect?"
Effect size:
  "What is the absolute lift on activation / retention / the actual metric? Is 0.4pp meaningful at our scale, or noise we would never notice?"
Cohort stability:
  "One cohort or several? Do later cohorts look the same? Week-1 onboarding cohorts churn differently than week-2+."
Support risk:
  "What breaks at 100%? Is this behind a flag? Can we roll back in under a day? Has support seen this change yet?"
First-sig vs stabilization:
  "First peek or Nth peek? Was the metric and direction pre-registered? Did the result hold at p<.01 on a second look, or did we just clear .04 once and stop peeking?"

PROBES (use only if they don't surface these on their own; one per dimension, in order)
1. "Walk me through what you would want to know about the test setup before deciding."
2. "What is the absolute effect, separate from the p-value?"
3. "If we waited another week, what would you expect to see?"
4. "What is the rollback path if support gets hit on day 1?"
5. "How many times has someone peeked at this metric? Is this a stabilization read or a first hit?"

STRONG vs WEAK SIGNALS
Strong:
  - Asks for at least 3 of the 5 dimensions before answering ship/not
  - Distinguishes "ship behind a flag to 10%" from "ship to 100%"
  - Names a concrete rollback / kill criterion
  - Distinguishes first-sig from a stabilization read, and treats them differently
  - Calls out peeking / multiple-testing risk
  - Names a concrete escalation path (wait N days, cut, ship to a segment, escalate for a denom review)

Weak / red:
  - Answers yes or no inside 30 seconds with a clean story
  - Treats p=.04 as a decision
  - Cannot articulate effect size apart from p-value
  - Does not ask about rollback or support
  - Treats "PM wants to ship" as a reason to ship
  - Treats "PM wants to ship" as a reason to refuse (politics-blind is also a fail — they will stall every fight)

CALIBRATION
In five minutes, a strong candidate asks for at least 3 of the 5 dimensions unprompted, gives a conditional answer ("I would ship behind a flag to X%, not 100%, IF Y and Z"), and names one thing that would change their mind. That is a clear hire signal for this lane.

A candidate who answers the yes/no in under a minute with conviction…

I have full context now. The user's request is a continuation: identify methodological conflicts in the Growth team's draft method and draft concise revision comments covering four specific requirements:

1. Predeclared metric and powered window
2. Effect size before conclusions
3. No rollout on first significance
4. Stabilization cohort before ship decision

Keep the review about method, not the product hypothesis. The previous turn was already thorough — but the user is now asking for *concise revision comments* (not a long memo). Let me draft that. The previous turn covered all four issues but in a longer form. I'll keep it tight, structured as revision comments, and stay descriptive (per the standing rule). I won't write to the brief unless asked.

Here's the draft. I've structured it as four discrete revision comments so they can be lifted into the doc individually:

---

**Method section — revision comments (concise)**

Scope: method only. Not addressing the product hypothesis.

**1. On the stopping rule — "stop on first p<0.05"**

Conflict: daily peeking across a 7-day run, with no pre-registered spending function, inflates the cumulative Type I error well past the stated 5% (≈ 1 − 0.95⁷, roughly 30% under the null). "Stop and roll out on the first significant read" compounds this: the magnitude observed at stop-time is selected for extremeness, so any reported effect size is biased upward by construction.

Required revision: replace the ad-hoc stopping rule with either (a) a fixed analysis horizon — no interim peeking, single read at day 7 — or (b) a sequential design with a pre-specified alpha-spending function (e.g. O'Brien-Fleming) so the cumulative false-positive rate stays at the intended level. The chosen rule must be written into the method *before* the run starts.

**2. On "effect-size reporting is optional"**

Conflict: optional effect-size reporting is incompatible with the stopping rule above. If early stopping is permitted, the point estimate at the moment of stop is the single most biased quantity in the analysis; treating it as optional is the load-bearing risk in the draft, because the ship decision will be presented as if the lift were stable.

Required revision: effect-size reporting must be *required*, not optional, and reported at the pre-specified analysis horizon — point estimate with a confidence interval, alongside any p-value. Lift claims to leadership without CIs should not survive this section.

**3. On "no separate stabilization cohort is planned"**

Conflict: shipping on the analysis read alone removes the internal replication step. A stabilization cohort (or holdback) exists to verify the effect holds rather than to discover it; skipping it means the conclusion rests on a single draw from the experiment's noise distribution, on a stopping rule that selected for extremeness.

Required revision: ship decisions require a confirmation read — either a pre-defined stabilization cohort held out from the primary analysis and read after the horizon, or an explicit justification for shipping without one (reversibility, low blast radius). Default is cohort, not waiver.

**4. On the missing primary-metric / cohort lock**

Conflict: "check the primary conversion result each day" presupposes a locked primary metric and a locked cohort — neither is stated. If secondary conversions are also being glanced at during those 7 daily reads, the family-wise error rate compounds further; if the cohort definition drifts mid-run, the hypothesis space quietly expands. The method doesn't say either way.

Required revision: predeclare the primary metric, the cohort definition, and the analysis window *before* the run starts. State whether secondary metrics are read at all during the run, and if so under what correction. Lock these at design time so day-1 looks aren't quietly enlarging what's being tested.

---

messages.content:
I can't run a Python sandbox in this shell, so the math below is hand-calculated — but Owen's numbers check out and the conclusion is unambiguous.

---

**Call: do not run. Don't even log it as a designed-but-never-started experiment.**

Owen's power math is right. 446/arm (892 total) is the correct figure for 72→80pp, two-sided α=0.05, 80% power. The eligible pool of 112 gives 56/arm, which is **12.6% of the required sample**. That yields ~17% power to detect an 8pp true lift — worse than a coin flip, and it makes the null result non-informative: a flat renewal curve here tells you nothing about whether the treatment works, only that the test can't see it.

MDE at n=56/arm, 80% power = ~22.5pp absolute. So the test as scoped can only "conclude" on a lift almost 3× the design's stated target.

---

**Why an invite-rate secondary won't rescue an underpowered renewal claim**

Three reasons, and they're structural, not rhetorical:

1. **The primary is still null-by-design.** A 17%-powered test gives you a null on renewal either way (effect present or absent). Treating "secondary moved" as a stand-in for "primary works" requires assuming invite-rate is a valid surrogate for 8-week renewal. It probably isn't — invites can move without changing retention, especially at the small effects we're talking about. You're shipping on a proxy while the primary is silent by construction.

2. **Asymmetric cost flips.** When you "rescue" with a faster signal, you're trading Type II error on the slow metric for Type I error on the fast one. Renewal is the outcome that pays the bills; invite-rate is a leading indicator. Letting the cheaper-to-measure signal override the expensive-to-measure one inverts the cost structure without telling you the cheap signal is actually predictive here.

3. **You lose the ability to learn from the test either way.** A powered null is informative (no effect, stop). An underpowered null is just silence. If we ship on the secondary and renewal stays flat in the next 8 weeks, we have no way to distinguish "secondary was a false rescue" from "treatment takes longer than the window." The whole point of the test is to make a decision; an unpowered primary + secondary rescue makes every future decision harder.

---

**Why first significance still needs a stabilization cohort**

This is the rule you've already locked in, and it matters more, not less, when the secondary is moving early:

- **Single-peek p<0.05 has a known false-positive tail under any look schedule.** Once you've peeked and seen green, your next observation is conditionally sampled on "winner-so-far." The second-look bar (n ≥ treatment-arm + p<0.01) is the structural guard against that. Drop it and you ship on noise that the first peek was guaranteed to produce sometimes.
- **"Fake first significance" is the specific failure mode.** A fast proxy will look significant at first peek because early-treatment accounts are the most engaged, the most recently activated, the most observed. That effect decays. The stabilization cohort is the only mechanism that forces you to wait through the decay.
- **Same metric, same direction, second look.** That's the minimum. A secondary metric moving does not satisfy "same metric." If you let secondary sig at first peek satisfy the bar, you've replaced a falsification rule with a vibes rule.

---

**What I'd actually do**

Three options, in order of preference:

1. **Re-scope the cohort.** The exclusions are doing a lot of work — 28 prior-exposed, 15 in active plans/support, 9 window-limited. The prior-exposed carve-out is the obvious lever; if there's a way to include them (different prompt variant, or accept invite-rate dilution and power for it), you roughly double eligible n. Still short of 446/arm, but directionally better than 56.

2. **Change the metric of record** to something the eligible pool can actually power — invite-rate within 4 weeks, if base rates support a detectable effect at n=112. Be explicit that the me…

arguments.body:
Lifecycle contractor closeout handoff
Date: 2025-02-13
Workspace: Helio Team
Handoff type: final closeout, contractor → Helio
Source of truth: 2025-02-12 closeout inventory + 2025-02-13 owner confirmations
Status: closed at handoff for owner resolution; suppression record accepted under reconstruction for 4 of 31, with 2 of 31 parked as unresolved historical evidence gaps.

This doc is the canonical handoff from the lifecycle contractor to Helio. It tells Helio staff leads exactly what the contractor delivered, what evidence is on file, what remains open, where authority is preserved above the contractor, and what work samples (if any) the contractor may carry forward. The contractor's work-sample is held by Helio; Helio retains the complete handoff. The contractor carries no Helio-specific identifiers forward.

This handoff is the final record for the contractor's engagement. It supersedes the contractor-facing closeout brief dated 2025-02-12 (Lifecycle folder) for any Helio-side reader. The Feb 12 brief remains the contractor-facing working doc; this doc is the Helio-facing handoff.

--------------------------------
0. Why this doc exists (one paragraph)
--------------------------------
The Feb 12 inventory surfaced 31 active lifecycle templates with two failure surfaces: two campaigns with no evidence-backed accountable owner, and six suppression-check records with no contemporaneous proof (four reconstructable from archived manifests plus timestamped audits, two with no contemporaneous proof at all). Between Feb 12 and Feb 13, Helio named the two missing owners and accepted the four reconstructed suppression records. Two suppression gaps remain parked. This doc records the final state, what is and is not certified, where the contractor's boundary stops, and what authority is preserved above the contractor.

--------------------------------
1. The 31 active lifecycle templates
--------------------------------
Total: 31 active templates in scope at the 2025-02-12 snapshot. The canonical roster — 31 template identifiers by inventory index — is held by Helio in the master inventory record and is NOT reproduced in this handoff document. Reason: the contractor's boundary at handoff is preparation-only, and any enumeration of all 31 individual template identifiers in a contractor-held document would breach the work-sample redaction rules in §7.

What this handoff references about the 31:
- Inventory slots are referenced by index (T-01 through T-31) wherever a count or class is needed below.
- The four named-and-known-to-this-doc templates appear by name only where Helio has already named them in current release documentation (Ines-owned onboarding-help series; CS-operations-named renewal reminder; Ines-named integration summary as of 2025-02-13; CS-operations-named trial-expiry education as of 2025-02-13). Other template names live in the Helio-held master inventory.
- The six templates that interact with this handoff directly (the four reconstructed suppression records, the two unresolved historical evidence gaps, plus integration summary and trial-expiry education for owner resolution) are listed by name where they appear below. All other template names are held by Helio and are NOT reproduced here.

--------------------------------
2. Owner resolution at handoff (31 of 31 named)
--------------------------------
At the 2025-02-12 inventory snapshot, 29 of 31 active templates had evidence-backed accountable owners on file. The two exceptions (integration summary, trial-expiry education) lacked approved owners; only adjacent signals were present (old folder creator for integration summary; recent editor for trial-expiry education).

Between Feb 12 and Feb 13, Helio closed the two owner gaps. The Feb 13 state:

  29 templates    Evidenced-backed accountable owner on file at 2025-02-12. Carried forward unchanged.

   2 templates    Accountable owner newly confirmed at handoff (2025-02-13):
                  - Integration summary:
                      Accountable owner: Ines (lifecycle-aud-risk lane).
                      Source: direct owner named in a current release artifact for this campaign. Folder-creator and editor lineage are NOT cited as the source; the direct-evidence chain is what closes the gap. This is a forward event and does not retroactively validate the folder-creator signal.
                  - Trial-expiry education:
                      Accountable owner: Customer Success operations.
                      Source: direct owner named for this campaign at 2025-02-13. Recent-editor lineage is NOT cited as the source; the direct-evidence chain is what closes the gap. This template sits in the HIGHER-RISK `routine education` lifecycle-send class; the owner-naming does NOT bypass the standing reclassification rule (see §4). This is a forward event and does not retroactively validate the editor signal.

Total at handoff: 29 previously evidenced owners + 2 newly-confirmed accountable owners = 31 of 31 templates with a named accountable owner at handoff.

What the contractor did NOT do here:
- Did not infer either of the two owners from adjacent signals (folder creator / recent editor). The owners were named by Helio from the direct-evidence chain.
- Did not certify that the 29 previously-evidenced owners remain correct at handoff. Those are held as recorded in the master inventory; any change since the Feb 12 snapshot is a Helio forward event, not a contractor rewrite.

--------------------------------
3. The four reconstructed suppression-check records
--------------------------------
Four of the 31 templates had suppression-check records missing from the Feb 12 inventory that ARE reconstructable from archived manifests plus timestamped audits. These four are accepted at handoff as fixed-point historical records under the manifest+audit reconstruction carve-out. They are NOT certified as freshly verified.

Evidence-safe label applied to each of the four (exact phrasing):

  "reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available"

Per-record handling:
- Each of the four carries the archived manifest path on file with Helio.
- Each of the four carries the audit timestamp(s) on file with Helio, establishing when the suppression check actually ran.
- Both are filed as the contemporaneous proof on file for that template.
- None carries a generic "verified" stamp. Reconstruction is a distinct evidentiary status.

Why this label, not "verified":
- "Verified" implies a fresh check on file. Reconstruction is not a fresh check; it is an artifact-based recovery of historical evidence. If any of these four templates is re-audited later, the re-audit must treat the historical record as reconstructed, not as a clean verification.
- The reconstruction bound is the archived artifact set, not the live state. If the archived manifests or audits are revised or withdrawn later, the historical record has to be revisited.

Contractor did NOT:
- Re-run the suppression check for any of these four and call the historical record "verified" on the strength of a successful re-run. A successful re-run is forward evidence, not historical evidence.
- Apply the reconstruction label to any record that lacks both an archived manifest AND a timestamped audit. Any such record moved to §4.

The four reconstructed records and their filed proof are held by Helio. The contractor's contribution was to surface the manifest path and audit timestamp for each, with Ines review on the filing.

--------------------------------
4. The two unresolved historical evidence gaps
--------------------------------
Two of the 31 templates have suppression-check records with NO contemporaneous proof on file — no archived manifest, no timestamped audit, no ticket attachment, no pinned Slack confirmation. These two are the historical evidence gaps in the suppression record.

Evidence-safe label applied to each of the two (exact phrasing):

  "unresolved historical evidence gap — no contemporaneous proof available"

Status at handoff: NOT releasable. Parked from any routine send lane. Suppression check is a hard gate.

What "resolved" looks like (forward only, not at handoff):
- A forward remediation owner is named by Ines (lifecycle-aud-risk lane).
- That owner runs a fresh preflight and produces a timestamped suppression audit.
- The new audit is filed as a forward event against the template.
- The Feb 12 (and Feb 13) snapshot is NOT rewritten. The unresolved label stays on the historical record. The new audit is a separate dated entry.

Contractor did NOT:
- Infer the historical record from a later audit. Later audits are forward events.
- Edit either template (copy, send timing, audience) until a fresh preflight is on file.
- Use "reconstructed" or "verified" labels on either of these two records. Neither applies.

The two unresolved historical evidence gaps and their forward remediation ownership are held by Helio. The contractor did not name the forward remediation owner.

--------------------------------
5. Standing rules preserved above the contractor
--------------------------------
The contractor does not have authority over any of the following. Each is held by the named lane owner.

Ines — lifecycle-aud-risk lane (routine authority):
- Names the primary accountable owner and named backup for any template where the direct-evidence chain is incomplete.
- Owns the reclassification gate for the HIGHER-RISK `routine education` lifecycle-send class. Trial-expiry education sits in that class; Ines reclassifies before release, fresh preflight on file, contractor documentation only.
- Names the forward remediation owner for any template with an unresolved historical evidence gap, and signs off on the resulting fresh preflight and audit.
- Routine send-lane cap (≤3 neutral sends per week, max not target; stale fails closed). This is the audit send lane and is unaffected by the contractor closeout.

Owen — shape + measurement/definitions + routine exceptions:
- Owns measurement and definition-level work that touches lifecycle templates (e.g., forecasted vs. descriptive splits, audience-shape changes that cross a definition boundary).

Riley — judgment-escalation + higher-risk + stop authority:
- Judgment-call escalation on any unowned campaign if Ines and the contractor cannot locate the direct-evidence chain.
- Judgment-call escalation on the trial-expiry reclassification if disputed.
- Sign-off on executive-language phrasing about the closeout. Honest phrasing at handoff: "29 of 31 owners evidenced-backed at Feb 12; 2 owners named at Feb 13 (Ines, CS operations); 4 of 31 suppression-check records accepted under reconstruction with provenance labels; 2 of 31 suppression-check records unresolved historical evidence gaps, parked."
- Stop authority on any lifecycle send touching the higher-risk class, regardless of routine send-lane cap.

--------------------------------
6. The contractor's boundary at handoff (preparation-only)
--------------------------------
The contractor's scope for the entire engagement was preparation-only. The boundary held throughout the engagement, and it is the boundary at handoff. The contractor:

  DID deliver:
  - Inventories: the Feb 12 closeout inventory record and any prior weekly inventories.
  - Evidence organization: the 29 prior-evidenced owner rows; the 4 reconstructed suppression records (with manifest path + audit timestamp surfaced per record); the 2 unresolved historical evidence gaps (with no-contemporaneous-proof labels applied per record); the 2 owner gaps as of Feb 12 (with folder-creator / recent-editor signals labeled per campaign).
  - Documentation: the Feb 12 contractor closeout brief; this Feb 13 handoff; prior weekly status notes.

  DID NOT deliver (and was never authorized to deliver):
  - Owner assignment. Owners were named by Helio (Ines for integration summary; CS operations for trial-expiry education). The contractor did not infer either owner from adjacent signals.
  - Audience approval. No audience sign-off; no expansion of any audience list.
  - Send release. No send was released under the contractor's authority. No send ceiling or audit window was set by the contractor.
  - Engineering control. No flag, workflow, manifest, or suppression-check tool was changed under the contractor's authority.
  - Certification of missing history. The contractor did not certify that the 2 unresolved historical evidence gaps were ever suppressed. They were not. The contractor labeled them and parked them.

  DID NOT carry forward (and may not carry forward in any work sample):
  - Helio template identifiers (the 31 inventory slots by name).
  - Owner names (Ines, Owen, Riley, CS operations, or any other named owner in this doc or the master inventory).
  - Internal paths (manifest paths, audit storage paths, workflow paths, ticket IDs, Slack channel or pin identifiers).
  - Send ceilings (the standing ≤3 neutral/wk cap or any per-template cap).
  - Audit windows (the suppression-audit time bounds or the standing audit cadence).
  - Customer rows (any evaluated account ID, cohort slice, or account-level fact from a preflight extract).
  - Company-specific release rules (the `routine education` reclassification gate, the suppression-as-hard-gate rule, the forward-only standard, the standing send-lane cap, the reclassification lane, the contractor-boundary rule itself).

Any contractor work sample produced after handoff must be generic. The rules above apply to the work sample, not just to this doc.

--------------------------------
7. The redaction rule for the contractor's work sample
--------------------------------
Helio retains the complete handoff, including the master inventory, the owner rows, the four reconstructed suppression records with manifest path and audit timestamp, the two unresolved historical evidence gaps, and the rule set in §5. The contractor carries forward only what is permitted below. Any work sample must omit:

  - Helio template identifiers (by name, by slot, or by any internal alias).
  - Owner names (current or former; named or by role).
  - Internal paths (file system, manifest storage, audit log location, workflow export, ticket, Slack pin).
  - Send ceilings (any number that represents a weekly, monthly, per-template, or per-audit send cap).
  - Audit windows (any time bound that defines when a suppression check ran, when it was due, or when the next one is scheduled).
  - Customer rows (any account ID, account name, cohort label, or preflight count tied to a customer or workspace).
  - Company-specific release rules (any rule that is not generic to lifecycle-email operations — including but not limited to the `routine education` reclassification gate, the suppression-as-hard-gate rule, the forward-only standard, the standing send-lane cap, and the contractor-boundary rule).

A work sample may reference generic patterns (e.g., "inventory of active templates in scope," "evidence-backed owner vs. adjacent signal," "reconstructed vs. verified record," "preparation-only boundary," "forward-only standard") without referencing Helio. It may NOT reference Helio by name, by template, by owner, by path, by ceiling, by audit window, by customer, or by release rule.

--------------------------------
8. Configuration-vs.-history rule (held above the contractor)
--------------------------------
The contractor did not, and Helio may not, use current template configuration to claim what occurred in an old release. The rule:

  Current template configuration must not be used to claim what occurred in an old release.

What this rule does:
- A template's current copy, audience, send timing, or suppression state is configuration, not history.
- History is what was true at the time of the old release (manifest, audit, send log, ticket attachment, Slack pin).
- If the historical record is missing (as for the two unresolved historical evidence gaps), the gap is the historical record. The current configuration does NOT fill the gap.
- If the historical record is reconstructed (as for the four reconstructed suppression records), the reconstruction is the historical record. The current configuration does NOT upgrade a reconstructed record to verified.

Why this rule matters at handoff:
- It prevents a silent retroactive rewrite of the closeout by saying "the template looks right now, so it must have been right then."
- It keeps the four reconstructed records labeled as reconstructed, not verified.
- It keeps the two unresolved historical evidence gaps labeled as unresolved, regardless of how the templates are configured at handoff.
- It is consistent with the forward-only standard (see §5): later state is a forward event, not a rewrite of the historical snapshot.

This rule is held above the contractor. The contractor did not apply it; Helio enforces it.

--------------------------------
9. Status summary at handoff
--------------------------------
Owner resolution: 31 of 31 active templates have a named accountable owner at handoff. 29 were evidenced-backed at the Feb 12 snapshot; 2 were named at Feb 13 (Ines for integration summary; CS operations for trial-expiry education).

Suppression-check record:
  - 25 of 31 have a contemporaneous suppression-check record on file at the Feb 12 snapshot. Carried forward unchanged.
  - 4 of 31 are accepted under the manifest+audit reconstruction carve-out, labeled "reconstructed — contemporaneous manifest and timestamped audit available." Filed with provenance, not certified as freshly verified.
  - 2 of 31 are unresolved historical evidence gaps, labeled "unresolved historical evidence gap — no contemporaneous proof available." Parked from any routine send lane.

Total: 25 + 4 + 2 = 31. Consistent with §1.

Executive-language phrasing at handoff (Riley-signed):
"Owner resolution: 31 of 31 named. Suppression record: 25 of 31 on file, 4 of 31 accepted under reconstruction with provenance labels, 2 of 31 unresolved historical evidence gaps parked."

Do NOT write at handoff or thereafter:
- "All 31 verified." (Two are unresolved; four are reconstructed, not verified.)

arguments.body:
# Owen — Q2 growth plan
_Drafted 2025-03-24, Riley. For Wednesday calibration with Priya._

## Summary
Owen's Q2 lane is **executive explanation of the Lifecycle program**, not analyst review. He owns the standard Helio Start report (independent circulation) and Lifecycle Systems reporting semantics + routine exception readouts. Riley retains accountability for disputed semantics, cross-surface decisions, and executive language. The Q1 Lifecycle live result stays **OPEN** — preflight clean ≠ release; nothing in exec or external comms may write it complete before the 03-31 evidence close + Ines reclass + Q-end decision.

## Owen — current strengths (carry into Q2)
- **Owns the standard Helio Start report** and circulates it independently. Deck rule still binding: Helio Start activation + support-load are reported **separate** from Starter / retained mid-segment — no implied shared operating path.
- **Lifecycle Systems reporting semantics**: measurement definitions + drift detection on the state feed. Five-state model (admitted / assisted / ineligible / final-reconciliation / `pending`) is his to police; `pending` is pre-admission, **not** in rate or activation denominators, and resolves forward only.
- **Routine exception readouts**: weekly, fail-closed with field-specific reasons; held stays held; no drift. Standing-lane cadence cap of ≤3 neutral readouts per week holds.
- **Independent circulation discipline**: his Helio Start report does not need my sign-off to ship, which is the point — it's how the program stays legible to a wider audience than my lane.

## Owen — Q2 primary lane (one)
**Lifecycle program — executive explanation & decision framing.**
- Owns the weekly Lifecycle routine readout (state feed + exception reads).
- Owns measurement definitions + drift detection on the 5-state model.
- Q2 deliverable: **Q1-aggregate readout + decision brief**, early April, after the 03-31 evidence close. Format: 1-pager, decision-first, plain questions.

# Helio Start first beta read — Aug 22

Working agenda. Goal: a decision read, not a dashboard tour.

## Activation shape
- Cohort definition + window (per activation KPI v3: ≥1 in-product event in 14d).
- Mid-segment (75–200, v2) curve vs. prior baselines (T6M v1 ≈ 2.1% on 50–200).
- Time-to-first-event distribution; where do beta wsps land on the curve.
- Open: are we reading activation lift, or just confirmation that nothing regressed?

## Support-load mix
- Ticket volume + category mix from the controlled-beta path only (learning coverage — non-public).
- Top failure modes (onboarding, entitlement mismatch, in-product confusion).
- Ines QA tier notes: state-changing = heavy review, mapping/education = light.
- Compare mix against a pre-beta baseline so we don't read absolute volume as a signal.

## Lifecycle education / copy risks
- Email + in-product education surfaces touching beta wsps.
- Copy that could be misread as a launch, pricing move, or paid-acquisition prompt — flag and hold.
- 'Helio Start' framing (2023-07-26): education + manual review only. Anything beyond that needs naming before it ships.

## Instrumentation confidence
- PostHog coverage on the events we'd cite (state-changing vs. mapping/education).
- Entitlement_state capture timing — per Daniela, captured at ws creation, updated on support handoff / billing change. No plan_name inference. Verify this held for the beta cohort.
- Gaps that would block a clean read (e.g. missing billing_account_mode on early-trial wsps — still open from 2023-08-01 review).

## Decision boundary
The only question on the table:

**Keep capped vs. widen later.**

Out of scope for this read:
- Launch framing (we are not launching).
- Pricing-page motion (Marcus's workstream, separate).
- Paid acquisition (not in scope for this cohort).
- Expansion / revenue credit (controlled-beta invites = learning coverage only — no pipeline, forecast, or pricing-page credit; 2023-08-15 Marcus hold still applies).

A widen-later call requires:
- Stab check on the same metric / direction, n ≥ treatment, p < 0.01 second look, before the next peek (standing rule 2023-03-26).
- Documentation of any instrumentation gaps closed, not deferred.

A keep-capped call is the default if activation shape, support load, or instrumentation confidence don't clear.

arguments.title: 2024 Annual Self-Review — Working Draft (for Priya, Mon noon)
arguments.body:
# 2024 Annual Self-Review — Working Draft
**Status:** working draft, not a polished promotion case. For Priya by Mon noon.
**Format:** 1-pager. Summary first. Why / cuts / effect / call. Plain questions at the end.

## Summary (read first)
My year was defined less by shipping launches and more by holding the line on what we actually know before it reaches leadership. The four workstreams below show the same pattern: scope a claim to what evidence supports, separate inputs that look like one input, delegate the routine so judgment stays focused on the non-routine, and correct definitions before they harden into reported numbers.

## 1. Helio Start 60-workspace diagnostic — closed with a scoped finding
- **Why:** The open question was whether workspaces failing connector auth were "not onboarded" in a general sense.
- **What I cut:** I did not let the diagnostic land as a broad onboarding-readiness claim.
- **Effect:** The closed read distinguishes three inputs that were being conflated: (a) Helio admin proof, (b) connector authentication, and (c) external-system authority. External-system authority is a separate readiness input, not a subset of either of the other two, and it has to be evidenced independently.
- **Call:** Scope held. The diagnostic closes on the narrower finding; the broader onboarding claim stays open pending its own evidence.

## 2. Lifecycle release authority — delegated routine, retained judgment
- **Why:** Routine lifecycle releases were consuming attention that should sit on incidents, customer corrections, state-changing sends, ambiguous cases, and higher-risk sends.
- **What I cut:** I handed routine, non-state-changing sends and routine preflights to Ines within her authority. Daniela's engineering release controls stayed with Daniela. Ines has no engineering release-control access.
- **What I kept:** Authority over incident stops, customer corrections, state-changing sends, ambiguous sends, and higher-risk sends.
- **Effect:** Ines owns the volume; I own the call when something is non-routine, customer-visible, or reversible only with cost. The boundary is explicit, not vibe-based.
- **Call:** Delegation worked because the boundary was written down, not implied.

## 3. Stale-retry-manifest correction — handled without overclaiming cause
- **Why:** A stale retry manifest surfaced; the temptation was to attribute it to a single root cause and ship a fix narrative.
- **What I cut:** I did not overstate the cause. The correction went out scoped to what we had actually observed, not to a cause story we hadn't verified.
- **Effect:** The customer-facing correction matched the evidence. A premature cause claim would have created a second correction when the actual cause turned out to be narrower (or different).
- **Call:** Discipline here is cheap; the cost of a second correction is not.

## 4. Metric definitions — corrected before they reached leadership
- **Why:** Several proposed metrics would have read as stronger statements than the underlying data supported.
- **What I cut:** I repeatedly pushed back on definitions — denominators, inclusion windows, "active" thresholds — before they hardened into leadership-facing numbers.
- **Effect:** What reached leadership was scoped to what the data supported. What I stopped did not become someone else's problem later.
- **Call:** This is the cheapest place to add rigor and the easiest place to lose it.

## Improvement area — one, specific
**Reduce late-stage manual interpretation by specifying ownership and evidence boundaries earlier.**
- Today the pattern is: a workstream runs, ambiguous findings surface late, I resolve them by hand because no one else has the context or the authority to call it.
- The fix is upstream: at scoping, name (a) who owns the call, (b) what evidence is in scope, and (c) what evidence is explicitly out of scope. Write it down, not in my head.
- Expected effect: less of my time spent adjudicating in the last mile; cleaner handoffs to Ines on routine work; fewer "Riley said" interpretations that should have been a written boundary.
- This is the one I want to be visibly better at next year, not a list of five.

## What I did NOT do this year (worth naming)
- I did not ship a headline launch. The work was mostly judgment-shaped, and the wins are "we did not overclaim X" rather than "we shipped Y."
- I am calling that out so the review does not get read against a launch-shaped template.

## Open questions for Priya (plain)

Onboarding-trigger v2 — first post-ship checkpoint (evidence card)
Historical observation: 2023-04-13 (CT). Cohort: 2023-04-10.
Anchored to the observation date; not a current rollout-status claim.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
0. What this card is
----------------------------------------------------------------------
A single-cohort snapshot for the onboarding-trigger archive. Covers the
first cohort to enter the post-100% rollout on `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2`,
recorded three days after the cohort started. Dated 2023-04-13. Not a
ship/hold call and not a current rollout-status read; the cohort is a
historical observation, the cohort window has long since closed, and the
flag is no longer in the live registry under this id.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Cohort ↔ rollout
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- Flag: lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2 ("Onboarding day-7 email — trigger
  condition rev"). Owner: Riley.
- Trajectory at the observation date: flipped 2023-03-13 at 50% on mid-seg
  (50–200 seat v1 bucket); 50% ran ~4 weeks; staged rollout to 100% on
  2023-04-10 at 10:00 CT. Cohort dated 2023-04-10 = first cohort to enter
  the post-100% rollout.
- The Apr 10 cohort is therefore the first post-ship cohort, not a 50/50
  spillover and not a pooled-on-flip cohort. Pooling the Apr 10 read into
  the pre-ship 50% read would conflate two different exposure regimes.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Early-retention comparison vs pooled experiment read
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- Apr 10 cohort, day-3 read: week-1 retention +3.2 pts vs baseline.
- Pooled experiment read (the pre-ship 50% mid-seg read, spanning
  2023-03-13 → 2023-04-10): +3.1 pts.
- The Apr 10 cohort sits on top of the pooled read. The two estimates
  agree to within ~0.1 pt. This is the boring case for "trigger is real,
  not us getting lucky for 3 days," and is what we wanted to see on a
  day-3 read.
- Note on scope: this is a day-3 read on one cohort, not a stabilization
  read. Standing rule (2023-03-26) — first significance does not ship,
  wait one stabilization cohort, pre-reg the stabilization def (same
  metric, same effect direction, n ≥ treatment) and the second-look bar
  (p < 0.01) BEFORE the next peek — still applies at this point. The
  Apr 10 read supports "leading indicator looks right," not "fixed."

----------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Data-quality assessment
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- PostHog: clean on `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` at 100%. Path cut
  surfaced nothing gross. The retention delta is therefore unlikely to be
  driven by rollout weirdness (exposure mis-attribution, broken event
  firing, partial rollout residue) and is more likely a cohort-shape read.
- Cohort shape at the observation date: mid-seg (50–200 seat v1 bucket at
  the time). Bucket was being migrated to v2 (75–200 default, 50–75 =
  starter) later, but that move lands after this observation and does not
  affect this read.
- No support-ticket surge, no unsub-rate jump, no mid-seg churn movement
  flagged in the same read. Guardrails clean.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Bounded conclusion on the pre-launch email/template QA noise
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- The QA noise in question: the Apr 10 ship-day QA pass with Ines, which
  covered (i) token fallbacks — empty / malformed {{first_name}},
  {{company}}, {{workspace_url}}, safe-render vs literal "Hi , " / broken
  link; (ii) footer + unsub link — populated merge tags, unsub link not
  pointing at a v1 branch; (iii) old customer.io branches — anything
  still keyed on the v1 trigger (`account_active ≥ 7d`) is dead code
  under v2's event-based trigger. These three surfaces are the only
  places a "QA noise leak" could plausibly contaminate the day-7 email
  read.
- Bounded conclusion: the Apr 10 cohort day-3 read does not show signs
  that any of those three surfaces leaked into the cohort's retention
  metric. The +3.2 read is consistent with the pooled +3.1 read on the
  same metric, PostHog paths are clean, and the retention shape is
  internally coherent. This is a non-leak statement, not a "QA was clean"
  claim; the QA itself was run pre-ship and its outcome is not part of
  this card's evidence.
- What this card does NOT conclude: that the Apr 10 cohort confirms the
  trigger. One cohort at +3.2 does not satisfy the stabilization gate.
  It confirms that the first post-ship cohort is not contaminated by the
  known QA surfaces, and that the point estimate sits where the pooled
  read said it should sit. The "is the trigger real" question is left
  to the stabilization read, not answered here.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
5. What is deliberately not in this card
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- A ship/hold call. The observation date predates the stabilization
  decision and is not one.
- A current rollout-status read. The flag is no longer in the live
  registry under this id; this card describes one historical cohort.
- Effect size in absolute user units, n_treatment / n_control, or a
  confidence interval. The historical observation was a +3.2 pt day-3
  point estimate on a single cohort; none of those fields were part of
  the original read, and inferring them now would be a fabrication.
- A claim about QA outcome. This card only records that the QA noise
  did not appear to leak into the cohort's day-3 retention read; the QA
  itself was Ines's and Riley's pre-ship work and lives elsewhere.
- Any lifecycle-narrative framing. The card is a factual observation,
  not a launch or rollback narrative.

----------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Source anchors
----------------------------------------------------------------------
- 2023-04-10 ship-day QA list w Ines (token fallbacks, footer/unsub,
  old customer.io branches): session 20260912_094329_84d7f5.
- 2023-04-13 day-3 read on the Apr 10 cohort (+3.2 vs baseline,
  pooled +3.1, PostHog clean, QA noise does not look like it leaked):
  session 20260912_095113_ae89a7.
- 2023-04-14 doc-writeup for the boring version (first post-100%
  cohort, +3.2, 50–75 seat slice flagged messy): session
  20260912_095255_93e93b.
- Standing rule (locked 2023-03-26): first significance does not ship;
  wait one stabilization cohort; pre-reg stab def + p<0.01 second-look
  bar BEFORE next peek. Memory: growth standing rule entry.
- Flag trajectory (50% on flip 2023-03-13 → 100% on 2023-04-10):
  `lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2` registry row.

tests.request: Create a focused, reusable review sheet for the new Expansion Assist lifecycle and in-product prompts. Center it on whether each message has a valid current-state reason to act rather than broad style guidance. Then DM Ines and ask her to apply the sheet to the draft set.

input.body:
# Expansion Assist — Message Review Sheet

Purpose: judge each message by whether it gives the reader a valid current-state reason to act. Not a style pass. Lane is descriptive: keep disputed, cross-functional, and exec-flagged wording. Routine line-edits and rel/rb copy are not this sheet's territory (route to rel/rb via Daniela).

## 1. The single gate

Before anything else, answer in one sentence: "This message is warranted because the reader is currently in state ___ and the next reasonable step is ___."

If you cannot finish that sentence with a current state (not a hypothetical, not an aspirational), the message fails the gate. Mark it FAIL and stop. Do not paper over with copy fixes.

## 2. Current-state validity check

For every message, confirm all four:

- State is named, not implied. The reader can recognize themselves in it without inference.
- State is current, not past or projected. "You were admitted" is not a current state; "your account is admitted, your benefit hasn't started" is.
- Admit / assist / ineligible are kept separate. A message that mixes them — or that frames an assist flow as an admission — fails.
- "Conversions" is a paid-platform source label and not used as a generic term for signups. Any draft that conflates the two fails.

State mismatches are the only thing that should cause a hard FAIL on this sheet.

## 3. Reason-to-act check

- The action is the smallest next step the state implies. No upsell, no re-application of an already-completed step.
- Eligibility-flow wording matches the 11/9 ruling: 19+ enters a paid-source eligibility flow; admit / assist / ineligible are reported as separate counts, never collapsed into "admissions/activations."
- Eligibility state changes mid-flow are handled, not flattened. A user whose state changes after the message was drafted is a separate decision, not a copy edit.
- Disputed, cross-functional, and exec-flagged wording is preserved verbatim unless the underlying state is wrong. If the wording is the problem, mark DISPUTED and route, do not rewrite in place.

## 4. Prompt-specific checks (in-product)

- Triggered only on the current state it claims. A tooltip that fires before the state exists fails the gate.
- Dismissible without losing state context the reader still needs. If dismissal hides the state, the prompt is doing two jobs; pick one or split.
- Does not duplicate a lifecycle message sent in the same window. Duplication is a state-reason failure: the reader has no new reason to act.
- Stops cleanly when the state ends. No lingering prompts after the flow resolves.

## 5. What this sheet deliberately does not do

- Voice, tone, or phrasing nits — rel/rb lane, Daniela.
- Disputed or exec-flagged wording — preserved, routed separately.
- Cross-functional phrasing changes — preserved unless the state itself is wrong.
- Routine line-edits — out of scope.

## 6. Verdict format (one line per message)

[ID] state=___  next-step=___  verdict=PASS | FAIL | DISPUTED  reason=___

FAIL needs only the missing piece of the gate sentence. DISPUTED needs the named owner it routes to. PASS needs nothing further.

## 7. Working principles

- State first, copy never. If the copy is fine and the state is wrong, the message is wrong.
- Descriptive lane: describe what the reader is in, do not steer them out of it.
- When in doubt, mark DISPUTED and route. Do not resolve in the sheet.

observed.body:
# Expansion Assist — Message Review Sheet

Purpose: judge each message by whether it gives the reader a valid current-state reason to act. Not a style pass. Lane is descriptive: keep disputed, cross-functional, and exec-flagged wording. Routine line-edits and rel/rb copy are not this sheet's territory (route to rel/rb via Daniela).

## 1. The single gate

Before anything else, answer in one sentence: "This message is warranted because the reader is currently in state ___ and the next reasonable step is ___."

If you cannot finish that sentence with a current state (not a hypothetical, not an aspirational), the message fails the gate. Mark it FAIL and stop. Do not paper over with copy fixes.

## 2. Current-state validity check

For every message, confirm all four:

- State is named, not implied. The reader can recognize themselves in it without inference.
- State is current, not past or projected. "You were admitted" is not a current state; "your account is admitted, your benefit hasn't started" is.
- Admit / assist / ineligible are kept separate. A message that mixes them — or that frames an assist flow as an admission — fails.
- "Conversions" is a paid-platform source label and not used as a generic term for signups. Any draft that conflates the two fails.

State mismatches are the only thing that should cause a hard FAIL on this sheet.

## 3. Reason-to-act check

- The action is the smallest next step the state implies. No upsell, no re-application of an already-completed step.
- Eligibility-flow wording matches the 11/9 ruling: 19+ enters a paid-source eligibility flow; admit / assist / ineligible are reported as separate counts, never collapsed into "admissions/activations."
- Eligibility state changes mid-flow are handled, not flattened. A user whose state changes after the message was drafted is a separate decision, not a copy edit.
- Disputed, cross-functional, and exec-flagged wording is preserved verbatim unless the underlying state is wrong. If the wording is the problem, mark DISPUTED and route, do not rewrite in place.

## 4. Prompt-specific checks (in-product)

- Triggered only on the current state it claims. A tooltip that fires before the state exists fails the gate.
- Dismissible without losing state context the reader still needs. If dismissal hides the state, the prompt is doing two jobs; pick one or split.
- Does not duplicate a lifecycle message sent in the same window. Duplication is a state-reason failure: the reader has no new reason to act.
- Stops cleanly when the state ends. No lingering prompts after the flow resolves.

## 5. What this sheet deliberately does not do

- Voice, tone, or phrasing nits — rel/rb lane, Daniela.
- Disputed or exec-flagged wording — preserved, routed separately.
- Cross-functional phrasing changes — preserved unless the state itself is wrong.
- Routine line-edits — out of scope.

## 6. Verdict format (one line per message)

[ID] state=___  next-step=___  verdict=PASS | FAIL | DISPUTED  reason=___

FAIL needs only the missing piece of the gate sentence. DISPUTED needs the named owner it routes to. PASS needs nothing further.

## 7. Working principles

- State first, copy never. If the copy is fine and the state is wrong, the message is wrong.
- Descriptive lane: describe what the reader is in, do not steer them out of it.
- When in doubt, mark DISPUTED and route. Do not resolve in the sheet.

results.snippet: [2027-08-18T13:10:00-05:00] >>>Owen<<< asked: “The >>>packet<<< and routine >>>source<<<->>>completeness<<< closure are complete. Should we mark the H2 mature-outcome->>>packet<<< goal met now, or wait for the scheduled >>>review<<<?”

messages.content: [2027-08-18T13:10:00-05:00] Owen asked: “The packet and routine source-completeness closure are complete. Should we mark the H2 mature-outcome-packet goal met now, or wait for the scheduled review?”

Wait for the scheduled review. Don't mark it met yet.

Reasoning:

  Packet + routine source-completeness closure are the prerequisites to the review, not the outcome judgment itself. "Mature-outcome" is the conclusion — and it only earns that label after the review confirms Ines's actual outcomes align with the authority granted. Closing the packet just means the evidence is in one place and the routine inputs are clean; it doesn't say the evidence supports a mature verdict.

  Same logic as the growth method: artifact ready ≠ cohort met. We don't ship on "the doc is written and the inputs are complete" — we ship on the powered read + stabilization cohort. Marking the goal met on artifact completeness would lock the state before the review can test it, which is exactly the false-positive pattern the method is built to prevent.

  Concrete call:
    - Status now: keep as "in review, packet closed, source-completeness clean."
    - At review: re-open the question. The review gets to rule on (a) whether the 7/13 ceiling hit stays characterized as ceiling-not-authority given the post-7/13 weeks, and (b) whether one revision + sustained appropriate calls is enough to call H2 mature, or whether we hold for the next cycle.
    - Only flip to met if the review explicitly confirms it. If the review wants more time, the goal stays open — that's a feature, not a slip.

  One thing to flag Owen on before review: confirm the scheduled review actually has Ines's H2 dev eval as a stated agenda item, not bundled under "general." Per your standing rule, dev eval stays separate from routine — keep them that way in the review notes too.

Owen has completed the July monthly sanitized campaign snapshot and the Q2 source lock under his current prep+reporting scope. Q2 board closed with his denom item resolved. Monthly campaign snapshot currently lands at me as exception-summary only (7/2 first post-handoff: 135 campaigns, all status+owner, owner lanes intact). Question on the table: extend a similar handoff to routine source-completeness reviews.

1. FRAMING (5 min) — guardrails on the record
   - This is evaluation only. No new review-closure or claims authority is granted today.
   - I retain authority over: board readiness, causal or revenue claims, forecast treatment, executive language.
   - What we are testing: can routine source-completeness move from line-by-line to exception-summary, mirroring the monthly snapshot handoff.
   - What stays unchanged: missing fields, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies → incomplete, escalate to me.

2. EVIDENCE FIELD AUDIT (12 min) — questions for Owen
   For each field, Owen states how he'd source it, certify it, and flag gaps. I probe the failure mode.
   Q1 — Denominator or exact coverage dates: where does it come from, who owns it, how does it reconcile to last packet's exit state?
   Q2 — Outcome window: how is start/end defined and frozen before the packet opens?
   Q3 — Measurement limits: what does the source cover and not cover?
   Q4 — Exclusions: what is excluded and why; who confirms each exclusion?
   Q5 — Source owner: named per row, single owner per surface.
   Q6 — Reliability evidence: what artifact proves the field is sound on first request?
   Q7 — Revenue and forecast treatment: Owen certifies the source; the call stays with me.
   Q8 — Section certifier: who signs each section; named backup if primary is out.
   Pause rule: any field missing, disputed, or cross-surface mismatched → flag in the packet, do not fill or interpret.

3. OBSERVABLE SUCCESS CRITERIA — over the next several packets (8 min)
   - 3 consecutive packets with all 8 fields complete and a named certifier per section.
   - Zero disputed-semantics reopens (Maya-pattern: snapshot-only items that turned out to be read differently).
   - Zero cross-surface owner drift (Ines-pattern: lifecycle vs. current-owner mismatch).
   - Exceptions surfaced to me within 1 biz day of source release, with the gap named.
   - Reliability evidence reproducible from source on first request, no re-pull.
   - Denominator / coverage dates reconcile against the prior packet's exit state.
   - Revenue and forecast fields carry the explicit handoff note ("source certified by Owen; call retained by Riley").

4. ESCALATION TRIGGERS (5 min)
   - Any missing field on the 8 above → packet is incomplete, escalate.
   - Disputed semantics or cross-surface discrepancy → escalate, do not resolve in packet.
   - Any causal, revenue, forecast, or executive-language content → escalates to me by default.
   - ≥2 consecutive packets with the same exception type → formal review of the pathway, not a third packet.

DECISIONS AVAILABLE AT EXIT
a) Continue current prep+reporting scope, no change.
b) Define a pilot packet class for exception-summary review, gated on the success criteria above.
c) Defer until next quarter; revisit criteria with the same audit questions.

ITEMS I BRING TO THE CONVERSATION
- Which packet class is the right first pilot (monthly sanitized snapshot vs. a defined source-completeness slice).
- Concrete threshold for "next several packets" — proposing 3 consecutive clean packets before re-review.
- Format I want when Owen flags an exception: field name, source, reason, certifier.
- What stays mine regardless of pilot outcome: board readiness, causal/revenue claims, forecast treatment, exec language.
