arguments.body:
# Workload brief — Aug 21 contractor pre-read

Frame: Priya wants the decision structure explicit without a recommendation. This brief describes; Priya decides. Lane ownership (Owen, Ines, Riley, Daniela) is fixed by the 2025-03-24 audit-roles ruling (reaffirmed 2025-08-05) and is not on the table.

---

## 1. Lane anchors (fixed, not negotiated)

- Owen: shape + experiments + Lifecycle Systems semantics + exception readouts + Helio Start report.
- Ines: lifecycle-aud-risk; routine education is higher-risk; review-closure authority unchanged; 2 approved refs.
- Riley: judgment-esc + disputed semantics + cross-surface + exec language.
- Daniela: eng release / rollback control (incl. midsegment tagging controls).
- Expansion Assist: descriptive lane (not prescriptive); not eligible for contractor ownership.
- Standing-lane cap on lifecycle neutrals: ≤3 neutral emails / week.

Workshop out-of-scope (per 2025-08-21 agenda body): adding a fifth consumer; funding Helio Start paid acquisition; broadening Ines's review authority.

---

## 2. Side-by-side matrix

Dimensions are the same across all three cases. Where a case does not apply, the cell is marked n/a.

| Dimension | A. No contractor | B. $36K half-time (Oct 1 start) | C. $48K 4-mo FTE-eq (Nov 1 earliest) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost through Dec | $0 | $36K fixed | $48K prorated; ~$24K through Dec (2 of 4 mo) |
| Start | n/a | 2025-10-01 | 2025-11-01 (no earlier) |
| End horizon | n/a | open-ended at half-time | 4 months from start (~2026-03-01) |
| Capacity through Dec | 0 contractor-hrs | ~13 wks × ~20 hrs/wk ≈ 260 hrs | ~9 wks × ~40 hrs/wk ≈ 360 hrs (2 of 4 mo elapsed by 12/31) |
| Standing-lane lifecycle neutrals (≤3/wk) | stays with current owners | can absorb all 3/wk (≈ 39 hrs through Dec at neutral cadence) | can absorb all 3/wk plus headroom |
| Routine-education enumeration for Ines review | stays with current owners | covers enumeration; Ines retains review-closure | covers enumeration + first-pass review scaffolding; Ines retains review-closure |
| Support-load bucket refresh (no-contact / light / heavier / manual) | stays with current owners | full refresh cycle | full refresh + weekly top-up |
| Cohort-cut prep (Mon mid-segment cuts w Owen) | Owen | prep delegated; Owen keeps the cut | prep delegated; Owen keeps the cut |
| Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration | stays descriptive; no owner change | enumeration only; lane stays descriptive | enumeration + cross-link spotting |
| Owner-leverage gain (qualitative) | none | small: Ines + Owen get the largest time return | larger: Ines + Owen + light pressure-release on Riley's queue for routine enumeration |
| Coordination overhead added (est. hrs/wk) | 0 | ~3–5 hrs/wk (Ines 1–2 review; Owen 1 sign-off; Riley ≤1 dispute escalations; Daniela light touch) | ~5–8 hrs/wk (Ines 2–3 review; Owen 1–2 sign-off; Riley 1 dispute escalations; Daniela 1 cross-check) |
| Net leverage (gain − coord) through Dec | 0 | ≈ 260 − ~170 ≈ ~90 net hrs | ≈ 360 − ~280 ≈ ~80 net hrs (capacity higher, leverage similar because coordination scales) |
| Stays categorically with Owen / Ines / Riley / Daniela | yes — all of it | yes — see §4 | yes — see §4 |
| Risk: stale fail closure | baseline | contractor closes neutral-check fails under Ines sign-off | same, plus weekly stale-fail sweep |
| Risk: crossing into disputed semantics | n/a | watch: contractor must escalate, not adjudicate | same watch, higher volume of edge cases |

---

## 3. Sampled repeatable work each paid case could remove by December

Inputs: 8/5 CS support-load cut on the 52-ws mature cohort (31 no-contact / 15 light ~16-min median / 6 heavier ~41-min median / 0 manual billing-import-migration); standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk; routine education higher-risk under Ines; Expansion Assist descriptive.

B. $36K half-time, Oct 1 start — by 2025-12-31:
- Lifecycle neutral coverage: 3 neutrals × 13 wks ≈ 39 neutrals authored.
- Routine-education enumeration draft for Ines review: ~1 set / 2 wks ≈ 6–7 enumerations.
- Support-load bucket refresh: 1 full cycle ≈ 12–16 hrs; weekly top-ups ≈ 1 hr/wk.
- Mon cohort-cut prep (mid-segment): 1 prep packet / wk ≈ 2 hrs/wk.
- Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration: ~1 pass / 2 wks.
- Total absorbed: ~260 hrs. After coordination overhead (§2), ~90 net hrs land with the four owners.

C. $48K 4-mo FTE-eq, Nov 1 start — by 2025-12-31:
- Lifecycle neutral coverage: 3 neutrals × 9 wks ≈ 27 neutrals authored (more in Jan–Feb).
- Routine-education enumeration draft for Ines review: ~1 set / wk ≈ 9 enumerations + scaffolding.
- Support-load bucket refresh: 1 full cycle + weekly top-ups.
- Mon cohort-cut prep: 1 prep packet / wk.
- Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration: ~1 pass / wk + cross-link spotting.
- Total absorbed: ~360 hrs. After coordination overhead (§2), ~80 net hrs land with the four owners (more capacity, similar net leverage because coordination scales).

---

## 4. Work that remains categorically with each owner

Categorical = by audit-roles ruling, not by case selection. A contractor does not absorb these regardless of hours or cost.

Owen (stays):
- Lifecycle Systems semantic definitions and exception readouts.
- Mon mid-segment cohort cuts (contractor may prep; Owen owns the cut).
- Helio Start report content and shape + experiment design.
- Disputed-semantics calls on Lifecycle Systems semantics.

Ines (stays):
- Lifecycle-audit-risk rulings.
- Review-closure authority on routine education (2 approved refs); contractor enumerates.
- Higher-risk education escalations.
- Stale-fail sign-off (contractor may run the sweep; Ines closes).

Riley (stays):
- Judgment escalations.
- Disputed-semantics calls across surfaces.
- Cross-surface consistency claims.
- Executive language / positioning.
- Final sign-off on Q3 "stop line-editing routine work once checks pass" boundary (reaffirmed 2025-08-05).

Daniela (stays):
- Engineering release and rollback control.
- Midsegment tagging controls and related schema decisions.
- Boundary between release/rollback and lane ownership.

Out-of-scope at the workshop (2025-08-21 agenda body):
- Adding a fifth consumer.
- Funding Helio Start paid acquisition.
- Broadening Ines's review authority.

---

## 5. Evidence tests — owner leverage vs added coordination

For each paid case, run these tests in the first 4 weeks. Pass/fail thresholds are stated; Priya can sharpen them.

Common tests (B and C):
- T1. Lifecycle-neutral coverage. Did the contractor author all 3 standing-lane neutrals in wk 1 without crossing into disputed semantics? Pass = 3/3 wk 1, ≤1 Ines override / wk.
- T2. Routine-education enumeration. Did the contractor produce 1 enumeration set / 2 wks (B) or / wk (C) that Ines signs off without rework? Pass = ≤1 rewrite / enumeration.
- T3. Support-load bucket refresh. Did the full-cycle refresh reproduce the 8/5 cut shape (31 / 15 / 6 / 0) within ±10%? Pass = within ±10%, manual bucket still 0.
- T4. Cohort-cut prep. Did the Mon prep packet reduce Owen's cut time without changing the cut's conclusion? Pass = Owen's cut time ↓ ≥30%, conclusion unchanged.
- T5. Disputed-semantics escalation rate. Of escalations reaching Riley, what fraction originated in contractor-drafted work? Pass = ≤15% (B), ≤25% (C) — higher volume allowed in C.

Coordination tests (both B and C, watching the ceiling):
- T6. Ines review-hours / wk. B target ≤2; C target ≤3. Breaching = leverage has been eaten.
- T7. Owen sign-off-hrs / wk. B target ≤1; C target ≤2. Breaching = same.
- T8. Riley dispute-hrs / wk triggered by contractor work. B target ≤1; C target ≤1.5. Breaching = the contractor is adjudicating when it should be escalating.
- T9. Daniela cross-check / wk. B target ≤0.5; C target ≤1. Cross-check exists because midsegment-tagging edges can show up in enumeration; Daniela stays the release authority.

Decision read at week 4:
- B passes T1–T5 and stays under T6–T9 ceilings → keep.
- C passes T1–T5 and stays under T6–T9 ceilings → keep.
- Either fails T5 ceiling by ≥10 pts OR breaches any coordination ceiling → revisit at the next standing-lane review; do not auto-expand.
- A (no contractor) baseline: tests do not run; standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk cap stays binding on current owners; Expansion Assist stays descriptive.

---

## 6. No-preselection boundary

This brief describes three cases and the evidence that would discriminate between them. It does not select a case. The decision is Priya's, made at or after the 2025-08-21 workshop. Any reading of this brief that treats it as a recommendation is a misread.

Notes for the workshop:
- Priya owns the call. Owen, Ines, Riley, Daniela retain lane ownership under any case.
- The standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk cap and the descriptive-only Expansion Assist lane are not relaxed by selecting a paid case.
- The audit-roles ruling (2025-03-24, reaffirmed 2025-08-05) is the boundary on what can move; the case choice is the boundary on how much can move.

arguments.title: 2027 Lifecycle Systems leadership model — December 4 decision draft
arguments.body:
# 2027 Lifecycle Systems leadership model — December 4 decision draft

Author: Riley Tanaka
Date: 2026-11-18
Status: Decision draft. Not approved. Riley continues attending routine Lifecycle Systems reviews through end of FY26 and until a December 4 decision is recorded.

## 1. Purpose & decision posture

Priya is requesting a 2027 role design that removes Riley from routine monthly Lifecycle Systems preparation and from source-closure attendance, while preserving a concrete monthly hands-on audit so Riley can still test the evidence system directly. Escalation rights on a defined trigger set must be retained. Authority over causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions must not be narrowed.

No role change is approved today. This document is the working draft for the December 4 decision meeting. Riley continues attending routine reviews through end of FY26. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Input the model is built from:
- Owen's November 6 independent source closure (independent prep + source-completeness closure inside the unchanged definition + named-owner certification).
- Riley's November 13 bounded claims decision (bounded instructional wording, precise extension-authority language).
- The November 17 manager calibration was working notes only — not delivered feedback, no authority expansion, no company calibration closure. It is not part of the input set for this role design.

## 2. Delegated monthly cadence

The four lanes and their owners are unchanged from FY26. What changes is *who carries routine prep and routine source-closure attendance*. Riley steps out of those two specific activities; everything else stays.

Lane A — Preparation and source-closure ownership: Owen
- Routine monthly preparation (data pulls, cycle definitions, source-completeness check, named-owner certification on the standard pack).
- Routine source-closure attendance: Owen owns the close on routine packets.
- Source of authority: unchanged from FY26 definition.

Lane B — Lifecycle governance and message-state discipline: Ines
- Routine message-state governance (sending/suppressed/queued state correctness).
- Precise extension-authority language on outbound claims.
- Bounded instructional wording (no expansion of claim scope beyond the approved surface).
- Lifecycle-governance certification.

Lane C — Cross-cycle/strategic: Priya
- Owns the cross-cycle narrative, the broader Lifecycle Systems roadmap, and the December 4 decision package.

Lane D — Final authority: Riley
- Retains decision rights (see §5).
- Stands out of routine prep and routine source-closure attendance.
- Stands in via the monthly hands-on audit (§4) and via escalation (§3).

## 3. Escalation triggers retained (not narrowed)

Riley is escalated into on any of the following six triggers. The set is closed. Adding a trigger is a December 4 decision question; removing one is not on the table.

1. Missing fields in a routine packet.
2. Disputed semantics on a defined term or claim surface.
3. Cross-surface discrepancies (e.g., a number that reconciles in one surface but not another).
4. Customer corrections (a customer has flagged an inaccuracy that affects a routine claim).
5. Incident stops (anything that pauses, rolls back, or quarantines a routine cycle).
6. Executive-language decisions (any claim headed to exec, board, investor, or external comms surfaces).

Escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request for re-prep. Owen/Ines remain the named owners; Riley arbitrates and decides.

## 4. Hands-on audit design (the concrete monthly test)

The audit exists so Riley can test the evidence system directly without redoing routine prep. It is not a second prep pass.

Sampling rule
- One named claim per month, picked by Riley.
- Drawn from a defined stratum: one of {a routine closing claim, a lifecycle-gov claim, a source-completeness close, a certified packet item}.
- Riley names the claim by the 5th business day of the cycle.

Walkthrough checklist (fixed, every month)
1. Pull the source-of-record artifact for the claim. Confirm it exists and is the named source.
2. Re-derive the claim from the source. Confirm the derivation is reproducible.
3. Check the closure cert for that item. Confirm the named owner and the certification date.
4. Check message-state (Lane B) for any related outbound. Confirm state matches the claim.
5. Check instructional wording for any related artifact. Confirm it does not exceed the approved claim surface.
6. Note any cross-surface discrepancy, even one that "reconciles under a convention." Surface it.

Audit artifact
- A one-page audit note per month, posted in the Lifecycle Systems folder by the second business day of the following week.
- Format: claim picked, source used, derivation result, cert check, msg-state check, instructional-wording check, cross-surface note, sign-off.

Failure modes the audit is designed to catch
- Source-completeness closure that was performed but not actually complete.
- Cert signed against a stale source.
- Instructional wording that quietly expanded scope.
- Cross-surface numbers that reconcile by convention but not by derivation.

Time budget
- One audit per month. Half-day at most. Not a substitute for routine prep.

## 5. Decision rights retained (not narrowed)

Riley retains final decision authority on the following five domains. The model must not narrow any of these.

- Causal: any claim of the form "X caused Y" or "because of X" in a routine or strategic surface.
- Revenue: ARR/MRR/expansion/contraction claims, including cohort cuts and segment reads.
- Forecast: forward-looking revenue, retention, or growth projections.
- Board-readiness: anything headed to the board pack or the board pre-read.
- Final-claim: any claim whose authority is the Lifecycle Systems function rather than a named owner.

Note on generalization: the Nov 13 decision was on a *bounded* surface. It is one data point. The model must not assume all routine claims will close the way Nov 13 did. This is why the audit (§4) exists.

## 6. Implementation risks

R1 — False confidence from two clean closes. Nov 6 and Nov 13 are two data points. The model assumes a stable success rate that may not hold. Mitigation: audit (§4) and the closed escalation set (§3).

R2 — Audit becomes performative. If the audit is predictable, it stops testing the system. Mitigation: Riley picks the claim; checklist is fixed but the stratum is wide.

R3 — Escalation under-triggering. Owen/Ines may resolve a trigger informally rather than escalating. Mitigation: the six triggers are closed and escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request to skip Riley.

R4 — Scope creep into causal/revenue/forecast language. Ines owns instructional wording but must not narrow or expand claim scope. Owen owns source closure but must not move into causal/revenue/forecast interpretation. Mitigation: §5 decision rights are explicit; the audit checks instructional-wording scope.

R5 — Cadence drift vs. cross-cycle obligations. Routine monthly cadence must not desynchronize from quarterly board-readiness, customer-correction cycles, or incident response. Mitigation: Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar; audit samples can land on a cross-cycle month.

R6 — Cert completeness decoupling. A named-owner cert can be signed while the underlying source-completeness is not actually complete (the failure mode Owen's Nov 6 close was built to prevent). Mitigation: audit step 3 (§4) explicitly checks the cert against the source.

R7 — Key-person risk. The model depends on Owen and Ines continuing in their roles. Mitigation: if either role is vacant or transitioning, default to *no delegation* — Riley re-attends routine prep and source closure until the role is filled.

R8 — Confusion with the manager-calibration channel. The Nov 17 working notes were not delivered feedback and did not expand authority. The audit is *not* a calibration instrument. Mitigation: the audit note is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not the calibration folder.

## 7. December 4 decision questions

The December 4 meeting should produce a recorded decision on each of the following.

Q1. Approve the model as drafted (delegation in §2, escalation in §3, audit in §4, rights retained in §5)?
- Options: approve / approve with amendments / defer / decline.

Q2. If approving: any amendments to the escalation trigger set (§3)? Adding a trigger requires Riley's sign-off; removing one is off the table.

Q3. If approving: any amendments to the audit (§4)? Specifically: sampling cadence (default monthly), sampling rule (Riley picks, defined stratum), checklist (fixed), artifact (one-page note, Lifecycle Systems folder).

Q4. If approving: any amendments to the decision rights (§5)? The five domains are fixed; the question is whether any are under-articulated and need sharper definition.

Q5. Effective date. Default = first Lifecycle Systems cycle of FY27, with a written handoff and a one-cycle overlap where Riley co-attends. Alternative = a later date. Earliest possible date is the first FY27 cycle, not before.

Q6. Re-decision cadence. Default = re-decide at end of Q2 FY27 (end of June 2027) based on audit notes and escalation volume. Alternative = earlier or later.

Q7. Vacancy / transition rule (R7). Confirm: if Owen or Ines role is vacant or in transition, default is *no delegation* and Riley re-attends until filled.

Q8. Cross-cycle synchronization (R5). Confirm Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar and that audit samples may land on cross-cycle months.

---

End of draft. This document is the working input for the December 4 decision. It is not the decision.

# 2027 Lifecycle Systems leadership model — December 4 decision draft

Author: Riley Tanaka
Status: PROPOSAL — decision draft, not approved. No role change is in effect. Riley's current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance are unchanged through end of FY26 and until a December 4 decision is recorded. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Update log
- 2026-11-18: Initial draft.
- 2026-11-24: Updated after today's 11:00am 1:1 with Owen. Added (a) four preserved-cadence properties in §2 (second-business-day snapshot preparation; named-owner certification before closure; explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing; one closure-and-exception summary instead of informal follow-up fragments); (b) audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4; (c) audit-versus-closure implementation risk R9 in §6; (d) consolidated decision question Q9 in §7.

## 1. Purpose & decision posture

Priya is requesting a 2027 role design that removes Riley from routine monthly Lifecycle Systems preparation and from source-closure attendance, while preserving a concrete monthly hands-on audit so Riley can still test the evidence system directly. Escalation rights on a defined trigger set must be retained. Authority over causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions must not be narrowed.

No role change is approved today. This document is the working draft for the December 4 decision meeting. Riley continues attending routine reviews through end of FY26. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Input the model is built from:
- Owen's November 6 independent source closure (independent prep + source-completeness closure inside the unchanged definition + named-owner certification).
- Riley's November 13 bounded claims decision (bounded instructional wording, precise extension-authority language).
- The November 17 manager calibration was working notes only — not delivered feedback, no authority expansion, no company calibration closure. It is not part of the input set for this role design.
- 2026-11-24 1:1 with Owen: four cadence-preservation properties (see §2) and the audit-evidence sequencing rule (see §4); see also R9 in §6.

## 2. Delegated monthly cadence

The four lanes and their owners are unchanged from FY26. What changes is *who carries routine prep and routine source-closure attendance*. Riley steps out of those two specific activities; everything else stays.

Lane A — Preparation and source-closure ownership: Owen
- Routine monthly preparation (data pulls, cycle definitions, source-completeness check, named-owner certification on the standard pack).
- Routine source-closure attendance: Owen owns the close on routine packets.
- Source of authority: unchanged from FY26 definition.

Lane B — Lifecycle governance and message-state discipline: Ines
- Routine message-state governance (sending/suppressed/queued state correctness).
- Precise extension-authority language on outbound claims.
- Bounded instructional wording (no expansion of claim scope beyond the approved surface).
- Lifecycle-governance certification.

Lane C — Cross-cycle/strategic: Priya
- Owns the cross-cycle narrative, the broader Lifecycle Systems roadmap, and the December 4 decision package.

Lane D — Final authority: Riley
- Retains decision rights (see §5).
- Stands out of routine prep and routine source-closure attendance.
- Stands in via the monthly hands-on audit (§4) and via escalation (§3).

What the delegated cadence preserves (Owen's 11/24 1:1 input)
The delegation transfers *who carries* routine prep and source-closure attendance to Owen and Ines. It does not change the form of the cadence. The following four properties must continue to hold under the delegation; they are part of the proposal's definition of the cadence, not implementation details.

1. Second-business-day snapshot preparation. The monthly snapshot is prepared by the second business day of the cycle, not later, and not on a rolling "when ready" basis. This is a hard date against the calendar, not against completion of any other step.
2. Named-owner certification before closure. Every routine closure carries a named-owner certification — Owen for source completeness, Ines for lifecycle-governance — recorded before the closure is treated as final. No silent closures.
3. Explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing. If a required field is missing or a named-owner certification is not in place, the packet's status is recorded as explicitly incomplete. Not "ready with caveats." Not "closed with notes." Incomplete is incomplete. The closure cannot proceed in that state.
4. One closure-and-exception summary, not informal follow-up fragments. Closure is a single, written closure-and-exception summary per cycle. Disputes, exceptions, and follow-ups are folded into that summary, not carried as informal Slack threads, ad-hoc DMs, or email fragments that drift from the closure record.

Amending or dropping any of these four properties is a December 4 decision question (see §7 Q9), not an implementation detail.

## 3. Escalation triggers retained (not narrowed)

Riley is escalated into on any of the following six triggers. The set is closed. Adding a trigger is a December 4 decision question; removing one is not on the table.

1. Missing fields in a routine packet.
2. Disputed semantics on a defined term or claim surface.
3. Cross-surface discrepancies (e.g., a number that reconciles in one surface but not another).
4. Customer corrections (a customer has flagged an inaccuracy that affects a routine claim).
5. Incident stops (anything that pauses, rolls back, or quarantines a routine cycle).
6. Executive-language decisions (any claim headed to exec, board, investor, or external comms surfaces).

Escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request for re-prep. Owen/Ines remain the named owners; Riley arbitrates and decides.

## 4. Hands-on audit design (the concrete monthly test)

The audit exists so Riley can test the evidence system directly without redoing routine prep. It is not a second prep pass.

Sampling rule
- One named claim per month, picked by Riley.
- Drawn from a defined stratum: one of {a routine closing claim, a lifecycle-gov claim, a source-completeness close, a certified packet item}.
- Riley names the claim by the 5th business day of the cycle.

Walkthrough checklist (fixed, every month)
1. Pull the source-of-record artifact for the claim. Confirm it exists and is the named source.
2. Re-derive the claim from the source. Confirm the derivation is reproducible.
3. Check the closure cert for that item. Confirm the named owner and the certification date.
4. Check message-state (Lane B) for any related outbound. Confirm state matches the claim.
5. Check instructional wording for any related artifact. Confirm it does not exceed the approved claim surface.
6. Note any cross-surface discrepancy, even one that "reconciles under a convention." Surface it.

Audit artifact
- A one-page audit note per month, posted in the Lifecycle Systems folder by the second business day of the following week.
- Format: claim picked, source used, derivation result, cert check, msg-state check, instructional-wording check, cross-surface note, sign-off.

Failure modes the audit is designed to catch
- Source-completeness closure that was performed but not actually complete.
- Cert signed against a stale source.
- Instructional wording that quietly expanded scope.
- Cross-surface numbers that reconcile by convention but not by derivation.

Time budget
- One audit per month. Half-day at most. Not a substitute for routine prep.

Audit-evidence sequencing rule (Owen's 11/24 1:1 input)
Riley declares the audit's evidence scope (the named claim, the source of record, the time window) only after Owen's routine source-completeness decision for that month is recorded. The audit cannot shape the routine sample, and the audit cannot quietly become a second closure review. Concretely:
- Owen records the routine source-completeness decision by the second business day of the cycle (per §2 item 1).
- Riley names the audit claim no earlier than that same day, and only after reading the recorded decision.
- The audit note (§4 artifact) cites Owen's recorded decision and is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not in the routine closure packet.
- If the audit surfaces a finding, it is filed as a separate escalation under §3 or as an input to the next cycle's source-completeness decision — not as an amendment to the current cycle's closure.

## 5. Decision rights retained (not narrowed)

Riley retains final decision authority on the following five domains. The model must not narrow any of these.

- Causal: any claim of the form "X caused Y" or "because of X" in a routine or strategic surface.
- Revenue: ARR/MRR/expansion/contraction claims, including cohort cuts and segment reads.
- Forecast: forward-looking revenue, retention, or growth projections.
- Board-readiness: anything headed to the board pack or the board pre-read.
- Final-claim: any claim whose authority is the Lifecycle Systems function rather than a named owner.

Note on generalization: the Nov 13 decision was on a *bounded* surface. It is one data point. The model must not assume all routine claims will close the way Nov 13 did. This is why the audit (§4) exists.

## 6. Implementation risks

R1 — False confidence from two clean closes. Nov 6 and Nov 13 are two data points. The model assumes a stable success rate that may not hold. Mitigation: audit (§4) and the closed escalation set (§3).

R2 — Audit becomes performative. If the audit is predictable, it stops testing the system. Mitigation: Riley picks the claim; checklist is fixed but the stratum is wide.

R3 — Escalation under-triggering. Owen/Ines may resolve a trigger informally rather than escalating. Mitigation: the six triggers are closed and escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request to skip Riley.

R4 — Scope creep into causal/revenue/forecast language. Ines owns instructional wording but must not narrow or expand claim scope. Owen owns source closure but must not move into causal/revenue/forecast interpretation. Mitigation: §5 decision rights are explicit; the audit checks instructional-wording scope.

R5 — Cadence drift vs. cross-cycle obligations. Routine monthly cadence must not desynchronize from quarterly board-readiness, customer-correction cycles, or incident response. Mitigation: Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar; audit samples can land on a cross-cycle month.

R6 — Cert completeness decoupling. A named-owner cert can be signed while the underlying source-completeness is not actually complete (the failure mode Owen's Nov 6 close was built to prevent). Mitigation: audit step 3 (§4) explicitly checks the cert against the source.

R7 — Key-person risk. The model depends on Owen and Ines continuing in their roles. Mitigation: if either role is vacant or transitioning, default to *no delegation* — Riley re-attends routine prep and source closure until the role is filled.

R8 — Confusion with the manager-calibration channel. The Nov 17 working notes were not delivered feedback and did not expand authority. The audit is *not* a calibration instrument. Mitigation: the audit note is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not the calibration folder.

R9 — Audit versus closure (added 2026-11-24). Even with the sequencing rule in §4, the audit can drift into a parallel closure review: Riley could pick claims that effectively re-litigate Owen's source-completeness decision; Owen could shape the source-completeness decision in anticipation of Riley's audit; or the audit note could quietly become a second closure artifact the routine packet links to. The risk is not that any single audit does this once — it's that over months the audit becomes a structural duplicate of the closure review rather than a system test of it. Mitigation: the audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4 (declare only after Owen's recorded decision; cite the decision; file the audit note separately); the closed escalation set in §3 (audit findings flow through escalation, not back into the routine packet); and a quarterly audit-vs-closure check (see §7 Q9) at the end of Q1 FY27 and again at the re-decision point, on whether the audit is functioning as a system test or as a second closure review. If the latter, the model is failing and the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the audit design is reset.

## 7. December 4 decision questions

The December 4 meeting should produce a recorded decision on each of the following.

Q1. Approve the model as drafted (delegation in §2, escalation in §3, audit in §4, rights retained in §5)?
- Options: approve / approve with amendments / defer / decline.

Q2. If approving: any amendments to the escalation trigger set (§3)? Adding a trigger requires Riley's sign-off; removing one is off the table.

Q3. If approving: any amendments to the audit (§4)? Specifically: sampling cadence (default monthly), sampling rule (Riley picks, defined stratum), checklist (fixed), artifact (one-page note, Lifecycle Systems folder).

Q4. If approving: any amendments to the decision rights (§5)? The five domains are fixed; the question is whether any are under-articulated and need sharper definition.

Q5. Effective date. Default = first Lifecycle Systems cycle of FY27, with a written handoff and a one-cycle overlap where Riley co-attends. Alternative = a later date. Earliest possible date is the first FY27 cycle, not before.

Q6. Re-decision cadence. Default = re-decide at end of Q2 FY27 (end of June 2027) based on audit notes and escalation volume. Alternative = earlier or later.

Q7. Vacancy / transition rule (R7). Confirm: if Owen or Ines role is vacant or in transition, default is *no delegation* and Riley re-attends until filled.

Q8. Cross-cycle synchronization (R5). Confirm Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar and that audit samples may land on cross-cycle months.

Q9. Cadence-preservation rules and audit-versus-closure sequencing (added 2026-11-24). Confirm each of the following as part of the proposal — not as implementation details:
  (a) The four preserved-cadence properties in §2 hold under the delegation: second-business-day snapshot preparation; named-owner certification before closure; explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing; one closure-and-exception summary instead of informal follow-up fragments. Any amendment to one of these properties requires an explicit decision.
  (b) The audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4: Riley declares the audit's evidence scope only after Owen's routine source-completeness decision for that month is recorded. The audit cannot shape the routine sample, and the audit cannot quietly become a second closure review.
  (c) Audit findings flow through the escalation set in §3 and are filed as a separate artifact in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not as an amendment to the routine closure packet.
  (d) A quarterly audit-vs-closure check (R9) at the end of Q1 FY27 and again at the re-decision point, on whether the audit is functioning as a system test or as a second closure review. If it is functioning as a second closure review, the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the audit design is reset.

---

End of draft. This document is the working input for the December 4 decision. It is not the decision.

The audit inspects reliability of the state; it does not acquire decision rights.

## 6. Implementation risks

R1 — False confidence from two clean closes. Nov 6 and Nov 13 are two data points. The model assumes a stable success rate that may not hold. Mitigation: audit (§4) and the closed escalation set (§3).

R2 — Audit becomes performative. If the audit is predictable, it stops testing the system. Mitigation: Riley picks the claim; checklist is fixed but the stratum is wide.

R3 — Escalation under-triggering. Owen/Ines may resolve a trigger informally rather than escalating. Mitigation: the six triggers are closed and escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request to skip Riley.

R4 — Scope creep into causal/revenue/forecast language. Ines owns instructional wording but must not narrow or expand claim scope. Owen owns source closure but must not move into causal/revenue/forecast interpretation. Mitigation: §5 decision rights are explicit; the audit checks instructional-wording scope.

R5 — Cadence drift vs. cross-cycle obligations. Routine monthly cadence must not desynchronize from quarterly board-readiness, customer-correction cycles, or incident response. Mitigation: Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar; audit samples can land on a cross-cycle month.

R6 — Cert completeness decoupling. A named-owner cert can be signed while the underlying source-completeness is not actually complete (the failure mode Owen's Nov 6 close was built to prevent). Mitigation: audit step 3 (§4) explicitly checks the cert against the source.

R7 — Key-person risk. The model depends on Owen and Ines continuing in their roles. Mitigation: if either role is vacant or transitioning, default to *no delegation* — Riley re-attends routine prep and source closure until the role is filled.

R8 — Confusion with the manager-calibration channel. The Nov 17 working notes were not delivered feedback and did not expand authority. The audit is *not* a calibration instrument. Mitigation: the audit note is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not the calibration folder.

R9 — Audit versus closure (added 2026-11-24). Even with the sequencing rule in §4, the audit can drift into a parallel closure review: Riley could pick claims that effectively re-litigate Owen's source-completeness decision; Owen could shape the source-completeness decision in anticipation of Riley's audit; or the audit note could quietly become a second closure artifact the routine packet links to. The risk is not that any single audit does this once — it's that over months the audit becomes a structural duplicate of the closure review rather than a system test of it. Mitigation: the audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4 (declare only after Owen's recorded decision; cite the decision; file the audit note separately); the closed escalation set in §3 (audit findings flow through escalation, not back into the routine packet); and a quarterly audit-vs-closure check (see §7 Q9) at the end of Q1 FY27 and again at the re-decision point, on whether the audit is functioning as a system test or as a second closure review. If the latter, the model is failing and the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the audit design is reset.

R10 — Audit-role boundary drift (added 2026-11-25). Two specific drift modes, each named by the function it would collapse:
  (a) Cert drift — the audit starts acting as if Ines' owner certification requires Riley's routine approval. Symptom: Riley is asked to "co-sign" or "acknowledge" the cert; audit notes begin referencing "approval status" of Ines' cert; the audit note is filed against the routine packet rather than as a separate artifact. Drift source: well-meaning alignment pressure when evidence↔messaging-state findings surface. Per Ines' 2026-11-25 input, this is off the table — Ines' cert is Ines'. Mitigation: the Ines-boundary in §4 (audit inspects evidence↔messaging-state agreement and may surface a finding, but does not convert her cert into a request for Riley's routine approval); escalation (§3) as the only path for Riley to act on a cert finding; the audit artifact is filed separately, not against the routine packet.
  (b) Engineering-control drift — the audit starts acting as if it can release, suppress, restore, or roll back system state. Symptom: audit notes begin recommending or recording releases/suppressions/restores/rollbacks; Riley is asked to "authorize" a release from the audit; the audit is treated as a gate on engineering action. Drift source: scope creep when a finding touches live system state. Per Daniela's 2026-11-25 clarification, this is off the table — engineering controls remain in Daniela's lane. Mitigation: the Daniela-boundary in §4 (audit inspects reliability evidence only; cannot release/suppress/restore/roll back); audit findings about live system state route to Daniela for action, not to the audit for action; escalation (§3 trigger 5) covers Riley's involvement in incident decisions as a decision right, not as an operating lever.
  Both drift modes are detectable at the quarterly audit-vs-closure check (R9) and at the new audit-shape check (Q10). If either drift mode is detected, the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the audit design is reset, the same fallback as R9.

## 7. December 4 decision questions

The December 4 meeting should produce a recorded decision on each of the following.

Q1. Approve the model as drafted (delegation in §2, escalation in §3, audit in §4, rights retained in §5)?
- Options: approve / approve with amendments / defer / decline.

Q2. If approving: any amendments to the escalation trigger set (§3)? Adding a trigger requires Riley's sign-off; removing one is off the table.

Q3. If approving: any amendments to the audit (§4)? Specifically: sampling cadence (default monthly), sampling rule (Riley picks, defined stratum), checklist (fixed), artifact (one-page note, Lifecycle Systems folder).

Q4. If approving: any amendments to the decision rights (§5)? The five domains are fixed; the question is whether any are under-articulated and need sharper definition.

Q5. Effective date. Default = first Lifecycle Systems cycle of FY27, with a written handoff and a one-cycle overlap where Riley co-attends. Alternative = a later date. Earliest possible date is the first FY27 cycle, not before.

Q6. Re-decision cadence. Default = re-decide at end of Q2 FY27 (end of June 2027) based on audit notes and escalation volume. Alternative = earlier or later.

Q7. Vacancy / transition rule (R7). Confirm: if Owen or Ines role is vacant or in transition, default is *no delegation* and Riley re-attends until filled.

Q8. Cross-cycle synchronization (R5). Confirm Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar and that audit samples may land on cross-cycle months.

Q9. Cadence-preservation rules and audit-versus-closure sequencing (added 2026-11-24). Confirm each of the following as part of the proposal — not as implementation details:
  (a) The four preserved-cadence properties in §2 hold under the delegation: second-business-day snapshot preparation; named-owner certification before closure; explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing; one closure-and-exception summary instead of informal follow-up fragments. Any amendment to one of these properties requires an explicit decision.
  (b) The audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4: Riley declares the audit's evidence scope only after Owen's routine source-completeness decision for that month is recorded. The audit cannot shape the routine sample, and the audit cannot quietly become a second closure review.
  (c) Audit findings flow through the escalation set in §3 and are filed as a separate artifact in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not as an amendment to the routine closure packet.
  (d) A quarterly audit-vs-closure check (R9) at the end of Q1 FY27 and again at the re-decision point, on whether the audit is functioning as a system test or as a second closure review. If it is functioning as a second closure review, the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the audit design is reset.

Q10. Audit shape: most direct system contact, least duplicate work (added 2026-11-25). Confirm the shape of the monthly audit, with three properties already baked in from the §1a role boundaries: (i) inspects evidence↔messaging-state agreement but does not require Ines' cert to be re-approved by Riley; (ii) inspects reliability evidence only and cannot release/suppress/restore/roll back (engineering controls stay with Daniela); (iii) does not become a parallel closure review (§4 sequencing, R9).
  Open question for December 4: which audit shape gives Riley the most direct contact with the evidence system while doing the least duplicate work relative to Owen's source-completeness decision and Ines' lifecycle-governance certification? Options to compare:
    - Shape A — current draft (§4 as written): one named claim per month, six-step checklist, separate one-page note. Direct contact: claim, source, derivation, cert, message-state, instructional wording. Duplicate work risk: medium if Riley picks claims that overlap the routine sample; sequencing rule mitigates but does not eliminate.
    - Shape B — claim-pull + countercheck: Riley pulls the named claim and runs only the derivation + cert checks (steps 1–3 of the checklist) on a quarterly cadence, with a monthly light-touch message-state check on a different item. Direct contact: source and cert. Duplicate work risk: low; loses monthly cadence on derivation check.
    - Shape C — evidence-system walk: Riley picks a named system (e.g., the message-state ledger, the source-completeness register, the cert log) and walks a single artifact end-to-end, instead of picking a claim. Direct contact: the system itself, not a claim derived from it. Duplicate work risk: low; pivots the audit from "is this claim right" to "is this system reliable."
    - Shape D — hybrid: Shape A's monthly claim pick + Shape C's quarterly system walk. Direct contact: high (both claim and system); duplicate work risk: medium; needs an explicit rule that the system walk cannot revisit a claim the routine packet just closed.
  Each shape must be evaluated against the §1a boundaries (cert drift, engineering-control drift), the §4 sequencing rule, and the R9/R10 checks. The December 4 decision is to pick a shape, amend a shape, or defer the question. Default if discussion runs long: Shape A as drafted, with the option to revisit toward Shape D at the end of Q1 FY27 quarterly check.

---
End of draft. This document is the working input for the December 4 decision. It is not the decision.

arguments.body:
# 2027 Lifecycle Systems leadership model — December 4 decision draft

Author: Riley Tanaka
Status: PROPOSAL — decision draft, not approved. No role change is approved or effective. Riley continues current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance unless and until Priya approves a later effective date. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Update log
- 2026-11-18: Initial draft.
- 2026-11-24: Updated after today's 11:00am 1:1 with Owen. Added (a) four preserved-cadence properties in §2 (second-business-day snapshot preparation; named-owner certification before closure; explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing; one closure-and-exception summary instead of informal follow-up fragments); (b) audit-evidence sequencing rule in §4; (c) audit-versus-closure implementation risk R9 in §6; (d) consolidated decision question Q9 in §7.
- 2026-11-25: Updated after Ines and Daniela input. Added §1a "Four functions and their holders"; audit-role boundaries in §4 (Ines: evidence↔messaging-state inspection only, not a request for Riley's approval; Daniela: reliability-evidence inspection only, no release/suppress/restore/rollback); R10 audit-role boundary drift; Q10 on audit shape.
- 2026-12-01: Recommendation finalized after the drafting block. Replaced the §4 monthly hands-on audit shape with a quarterly rotating recheck of one evidence lane. Five inspection dimensions (denominator or coverage dates; outcome window; exclusions; reliability evidence; revenue and forecast treatment). Four safeguards (does not reopen source closure; does not approve Ines's owner certification; does not exercise Daniela's release or rollback controls; does not create a second approval queue). Lane selected only after Owen's routine packet closure is recorded. Implementation date left for Priya's decision; current routine prep and source-closure attendance continue unless and until she approves a later effective date.

## 1. Purpose & decision posture

Priya is requesting a 2027 role design that removes Riley from routine monthly Lifecycle Systems preparation and from source-closure attendance, while preserving a concrete independent verification activity so Riley can still test the evidence system directly. Escalation rights on a defined trigger set must be retained. Authority over causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions must not be narrowed.

No role change is approved today. This document is the working draft for the December 4 decision meeting. Riley continues current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance unless and until Priya approves a later effective date. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Input the model is built from:
- Owen's November 6 independent source closure (independent prep + source-completeness closure inside the unchanged definition + named-owner certification).
- Riley's November 13 bounded claims decision (bounded instructional wording, precise extension-authority language).
- The November 17 manager calibration was working notes only — not delivered feedback, no authority expansion, no company calibration closure. It is not part of the input set for this role design.
- 2026-11-24 1:1 with Owen: four cadence-preservation properties (see §2) and the audit-evidence sequencing rule (see §4); see also R9 in §6.
- 2026-11-25 input from Ines and Daniela: four-function boundaries (see §1a) and the audit-role boundaries for the recheck (see §4).
- 2026-12-01 recommendation finalized: the concrete shape of the independent verification activity is a quarterly rotating recheck of one evidence lane (see §4), selected only after Owen's routine packet closure is recorded. Implementation date left for Priya's decision.

## 1a. Four functions and their holders

The 2027 model keeps four functions separate. They are not collapsed into each other. The holders do not exchange their function.

- Source closure. Owen. Routine monthly preparation, source-completeness check, source-completeness closure, named-owner certification on the standard pack. Owen's source-completeness decision is recorded on a defined cadence (see §2).
- Owner certification (lifecycle governance). Ines. Routine message-state governance (sending/suppressed/queued state correctness), precise extension-authority language on outbound claims, bounded instructional wording (no expansion of claim scope beyond the approved surface), lifecycle-governance certification.
- Independent verification (the recheck). Riley. The concrete shape of this function is the quarterly rotating recheck of one evidence lane, as defined in §4. The recheck inspects evidence — it does not collapse into source closure, owner certification, or engineering controls.
- Final claim authority. Riley. Retained decision rights (see §5). The recheck is not a route for second approval of routine claims.

Why the four are kept separate
- If the recheck is treated as a request for Riley's routine approval of Ines's cert, source closure has effectively moved into the recheck function. That is the drift §6 R10 names.
- If the recheck exercises release/suppress/restore/rollback controls, engineering controls have moved into the recheck function. That is the other drift R10 names.
- If the recheck becomes a parallel closure review, the four-function model has been quietly reduced to three (with the recheck acting as a duplicate of source closure). That is the drift §6 R9 names.

## 2. Delegated monthly cadence

The four lanes and their owners are unchanged from FY26. What changes is *who carries routine prep and routine source-closure attendance*. Riley steps out of those two specific activities; everything else stays.

Lane A — Preparation and source-closure ownership: Owen
- Routine monthly preparation (data pulls, cycle definitions, source-completeness check, named-owner certification on the standard pack).
- Routine source-closure attendance: Owen owns the close on routine packets.
- Source of authority: unchanged from FY26 definition.

Lane B — Lifecycle governance and message-state discipline: Ines
- Routine message-state governance (sending/suppressed/queued state correctness).
- Precise extension-authority language on outbound claims.
- Bounded instructional wording (no expansion of claim scope beyond the approved surface).
- Lifecycle-governance certification.

Lane C — Cross-cycle/strategic: Priya
- Owns the cross-cycle narrative, the broader Lifecycle Systems roadmap, and the December 4 decision package.

Lane D — Final authority: Riley
- Retains decision rights (see §5).
- Stands out of routine prep and routine source-closure attendance.
- Stands in via the quarterly rotating recheck (§4) and via escalation (§3).

What the delegated cadence preserves (Owen's 11/24 1:1 input)
The delegation transfers *who carries* routine prep and source-closure attendance to Owen and Ines. It does not change the form of the cadence. The following four properties must continue to hold under the delegation; they are part of the proposal's definition of the cadence, not implementation details.

1. Second-business-day snapshot preparation. The monthly snapshot is prepared by the second business day of the cycle, not later, and not on a rolling "when ready" basis. This is a hard date against the calendar, not against completion of any other step.
2. Named-owner certification before closure. Every routine closure carries a named-owner certification — Owen for source completeness, Ines for lifecycle-governance — recorded before the closure is treated as final. No silent closures.
3. Explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing. If a required field is missing or a named-owner certification is not in place, the packet's status is recorded as explicitly incomplete. Not "ready with caveats." Not "closed with notes." Incomplete is incomplete. The closure cannot proceed in that state.
4. One closure-and-exception summary, not informal follow-up fragments. Closure is a single, written closure-and-exception summary per cycle. Disputes, exceptions, and follow-ups are folded into that summary, not carried as informal Slack threads, ad-hoc DMs, or email fragments that drift from the closure record.

Amending or dropping any of these four properties is a December 4 decision question (see §7 Q9), not an implementation detail.

## 3. Escalation triggers retained (not narrowed)

Riley is escalated into on any of the following six triggers. The set is closed. Adding a trigger is a December 4 decision question; removing one is not on the table.

1. Missing fields in a routine packet.
2. Disputed semantics on a defined term or claim surface.
3. Cross-surface discrepancies (e.g., a number that reconciles in one surface but not another).
4. Customer corrections (a customer has flagged an inaccuracy that affects a routine claim).
5. Incident stops (anything that pauses, rolls back, or quarantines a routine cycle).
6. Executive-language decisions (any claim headed to exec, board, investor, or external comms surfaces).

Escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request for re-prep. Owen/Ines remain the named owners; Riley arbitrates and decides.

## 4. Quarterly rotating recheck of one evidence lane (the recommendation)

This section replaces the prior monthly hands-on audit shape. The recommendation Priya decides on December 4 is a quarterly rotating recheck of one evidence lane. The recheck is the concrete independent verification activity that lets Riley test the evidence system directly without redoing routine prep.

Recommendation summary
- Cadence: quarterly. One recheck per quarter.
- Subject: one evidence lane per quarter.
- Lane selection: only after Owen's routine packet closure is recorded. The recheck does not select or shape the routine sample.
- Five inspection dimensions. Each recheck walks all five for the selected lane (see below).
- Four safeguards. Each recheck holds all four (see below). A recheck that breaches any safeguard is out of scope.
- Implementation date: for Priya to decide. Not pre-set in this draft. Until she approves a later effective date, Riley continues current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance.

Five inspection dimensions (each recheck walks all five)
1. Denominator or coverage dates. Confirm the lane's denominator and coverage dates are correct for the period under recheck. The recheck does not modify these — it inspects them.
2. Outcome window. Confirm the outcome window used by routine claims for the lane is the one the source supports. The recheck does not redefine the window — it inspects it.
3. Exclusions. Confirm any exclusions applied in the lane are documented and consistent with how routine claims treat them. The recheck does not authorize or remove exclusions — it inspects them.
4. Reliability evidence. Confirm the lane's reliability evidence is intact. Per Daniela's constraint: the recheck inspects reliability evidence only; it does not release, suppress, restore, or roll back anything. Engineering controls remain in Daniela's lane.
5. Revenue and forecast treatment. Confirm revenue and forecast treatment in the lane is consistent with how routine claims treat revenue and forecast. Per §5: causal/revenue/forecast decision rights remain with Riley; the recheck inspects treatment, it does not decide treatment.

Four safeguards (each must hold for every recheck)
1. Does not reopen source closure. The recheck does not revisit Owen's source-completeness decision or modify it. Source closure remains Owen's lane.
2. Does not approve Ines's owner certification. The recheck does not convert Ines's lifecycle-governance certification into a request for Riley's approval. Ines's cert stays Ines's.
3. Does not exercise Daniela's release or rollback controls. The recheck does not release, suppress, restore, or roll back anything. Engineering controls remain in Daniela's lane.
4. Does not create a second approval queue. The recheck produces an inspection artifact, not a separate approval. Findings, if any, flow through the existing escalation set (§3) or as input to the next cycle's source-completeness decision — never as an amendment to the current cycle's closure.

Sampling rule (lane selection)
- One evidence lane per quarter, picked by Riley from a defined set of evidence lanes eligible for recheck.
- Lane is named only after Owen's routine packet closure for the relevant cycle is recorded.
- Lane rotates by quarter (default). Repeated selection of the same lane requires an explicit decision and a written reason.
- The lane set is a December 4 decision question (see §7 Q10). It is not pre-set in this draft.

Recheck artifact
- A one-page recheck note per quarter, posted in the Lifecycle Systems folder by the second business day of the week following the quarter close.
- Format: lane selected, source of record, dimension-by-dimension result, safeguard confirmation, findings (if any), sign-off.
- The recheck note cites Owen's recorded source-completeness decision for the cycle the lane belongs to and is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not in the routine closure packet.

Time budget
- One recheck per quarter. Half-day at most. Not a substitute for routine prep, source closure, owner certification, or engineering controls.

Why this shape (and not the prior monthly audit)
- Quarterly matches the cadence at which Owen's routine closure is the meaningful boundary; a monthly recheck would either disrupt Owen's cycle or replicate it.
- One lane per quarter is broad enough to test the lane's integrity end-to-end (denominator, outcome, exclusions, reliability, revenue and forecast treatment) without re-litigating source closure.
- Selecting the lane only after Owen's routine closure is recorded ensures the recheck cannot shape the routine sample or quietly become a second closure review.
- The five dimensions and four safeguards are the answer to "what does the recheck actually inspect" and "what does the recheck explicitly not do" — both of which Owen, Ines, and Daniela need answered before December 4.

Implementation date
- For Priya to decide. Not pre-set in this draft.
- Until Priya approves a later effective date, Riley continues current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance. Nothing in this draft takes effect early.

## 5. Decision rights retained (not narrowed)

Riley retains final decision authority on the following five domains. The model must not narrow any of these.

- Causal: any claim of the form "X caused Y" or "because of X" in a routine or strategic surface.
- Revenue: ARR/MMR/expansion/contraction claims, including cohort cuts and segment reads.
- Forecast: forward-looking revenue, retention, or growth projections.
- Board-readiness: anything headed to the board pack or the board pre-read.
- Final-claim: any claim whose authority is the Lifecycle Systems function rather than a named owner.

Note on generalization: the Nov 13 decision was on a *bounded* surface. It is one data point. The model must not assume all routine claims will close the way Nov 13 did. This is why the recheck (§4) exists.

## 6. Implementation risks

R1 — False confidence from two clean closes. Nov 6 and Nov 13 are two data points. The model assumes a stable success rate that may not hold. Mitigation: recheck (§4) and the closed escalation set (§3).

R2 — Recheck becomes performative. If the recheck is predictable, it stops testing the system. Mitigation: Riley picks the lane from a defined set; lanes rotate by quarter; same-lane repetition requires an explicit decision.

R3 — Escalation under-triggering. Owen/Ines may resolve a trigger informally rather than escalating. Mitigation: the six triggers are closed and escalation is *into Riley's queue*, not a request to skip Riley.

R4 — Scope creep into causal/revenue/forecast language. Ines owns instructional wording but must not narrow or expand claim scope. Owen owns source closure but must not move into causal/revenue/forecast interpretation. Mitigation: §5 decision rights are explicit; the recheck's revenue and forecast dimension inspects treatment but does not decide it.

R5 — Cadence drift vs. cross-cycle obligations. Routine monthly cadence must not desynchronize from quarterly board-readiness, customer-correction cycles, or incident response. Mitigation: Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar; recheck lanes can land on a cross-cycle quarter.

R6 — Cert completeness decoupling. A named-owner cert can be signed while the underlying source-completeness is not actually complete (the failure mode Owen's Nov 6 close was built to prevent). Mitigation: recheck dimension 1 (denominator or coverage dates) and dimension 3 (exclusions) explicitly check that the lane's source supports the cert.

R7 — Key-person risk. The model depends on Owen and Ines continuing in their roles. Mitigation: if either role is vacant or transitioning, default to *no delegation* — Riley re-attends routine prep and source closure until the role is filled.

R8 — Confusion with the manager-calibration channel. The Nov 17 working notes were not delivered feedback and did not expand authority. The recheck is *not* a calibration instrument. Mitigation: the recheck note is filed in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not the calibration folder.

R9 — Recheck versus closure. Even with the sequencing rule in §4, the recheck can drift into a parallel closure review: Riley could pick lanes that effectively re-litigate Owen's source-completeness decision; Owen could shape the source-completeness decision in anticipation of Riley's recheck; or the recheck note could quietly become a second closure artifact the routine packet links to. The risk is not that any single recheck does this once — it's that over quarters the recheck becomes a structural duplicate of the closure review rather than a system test of it. Mitigation: the lane-selection sequencing rule in §4 (declare only after Owen's recorded decision; cite the decision; file the recheck note separately); the closed escalation set in §3 (recheck findings flow through escalation, not back into the routine packet); and a semi-annual recheck-vs-closure check (see §7 Q9) at the end of Q2 FY27 and again at the re-decision point, on whether the recheck is functioning as a system test or as a second closure review. If the latter, the model is failing and the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the recheck design is reset.

R10 — Audit-role boundary drift (cert drift, engineering-control drift). The recheck could drift into Ines's cert function (recheck findings become a request for Riley to approve or reject Ines's cert) or into Daniela's engineering-control function (recheck findings trigger release/suppress/restore/rollback actions). Mitigation: §1a explicitly names the four functions as separate; the four safeguards in §4 prohibit both drift modes; recheck findings flow through the existing escalation set (§3) or as input to the next cycle, not as direct action on certs or engineering controls. If either drift mode is observed, the default is to re-attend routine prep and source closure until the recheck design is reset.

R11 — Quarterly cadence too sparse (added 2026-12-01). A recheck only once per quarter means a lane's integrity could degrade for two months before inspection. Mitigation: the closed escalation set (§3) catches the most acute issues mid-quarter; the recheck is a system test, not real-time monitoring; the lane set can be amended at the re-decision point if quarterly proves too sparse for high-traffic lanes.

R12 — Lane set too narrow (added 2026-12-01). If the defined lane set does not cover enough of the routine claim surface, the recheck tests only a slice. Mitigation: lane set is defined as part of the proposal and is a December 4 decision question (see §7 Q10); expand or amend at re-decision point if coverage is too thin.

## 7. December 4 decision questions

The December 4 meeting should produce a recorded decision on each of the following.

Q1. Approve the model as drafted (delegation in §2, escalation in §3, recheck in §4, rights retained in §5)?
- Options: approve / approve with amendments / defer / decline.

Q2. If approving: any amendments to the escalation trigger set (§3)? Adding a trigger requires Riley's sign-off; removing one is not on the table.

Q3. If approving: any amendments to the recheck (§4)? Specifically: cadence (default quarterly), subject (one evidence lane per quarter), sequencing (lane named only after Owen's recorded closure), inspection dimensions (five, fixed), safeguards (four, fixed), artifact (one-page note, Lifecycle Systems folder).

Q4. If approving: any amendments to the decision rights (§5)? The five domains are fixed; the question is whether any are under-articulated and need sharper definition.

Q5. Implementation date. For Priya to decide. Not pre-set in this draft. Until Priya approves a later effective date, Riley continues current routine monthly preparation and routine source-closure attendance; nothing in this draft takes effect early.

Q6. Re-decision cadence. Default = re-decide at end of Q2 FY27 (end of June 2027) based on recheck notes and escalation volume. Alternative = earlier or later.

Q7. Vacancy / transition rule (R7). Confirm: if Owen or Ines role is vacant or in transition, default is *no delegation* and Riley re-attends until filled.

Q8. Cross-cycle synchronization (R5). Confirm Priya owns the cross-cycle calendar and that recheck lanes may land on cross-cycle quarters.

Q9. Cadence-preservation rules and recheck-versus-closure sequencing (added 2026-11-24, refined 2026-12-01). Confirm each of the following as part of the proposal — not as implementation details:
  (a) The four preserved-cadence properties in §2 hold under the delegation: second-business-day snapshot preparation; named-owner certification before closure; explicit incomplete status when any required field or owner certification is missing; one closure-and-exception summary instead of informal follow-up fragments. Any amendment to one of these properties requires an explicit decision.
  (b) The lane-selection sequencing rule in §4: Riley names the recheck lane only after Owen's routine source-completeness decision for that cycle is recorded. The recheck cannot shape the routine sample, and the recheck cannot quietly become a second closure review.
  (c) Recheck findings flow through the escalation set in §3 and are filed as a separate artifact in the Lifecycle Systems folder, not as an amendment to the routine closure packet.

Prior 30/13/43 two-pilot split is preserved for record only and explicitly NOT combined into the source-locked denominator. Claim stays descriptive — no causal, revenue, or forecast treatment.

---

## Scenario (read aloud)

On Monday morning, the Lifecycle Systems team opens the January sanitized campaign snapshot for review.
