February 14 family archive session — checklist
One-time remote session with Marcus, 6:00pm–7:00pm Central
Session #1 of 2 (second session: 3/14/27, same time)

Pre-session state (do not change before the session)
- 26 photographs scanned and in the archive.
- 14 photographs still undigitized, in sleeves, provenance intact.
- Marcus has confirmed the order of the selected seven-photo batch from the 14 undigitized. The order is locked; do not reorder, swap, or substitute before the session.
- Pre-session work is complete. Do not begin scanning, do not begin the session early, and do not record any scan or identification outcome ahead of the session.

During the session — ground rules
- Keep every photograph in its sleeve. Do not remove a photograph from its sleeve for any reason.
- Remove no residue. No cleaning, no brushing, no adhesive work, no chemical treatment of any photograph, sleeve, or envelope.
- Guess no dates. If a date is not corroborated against existing provenance, leave it unresolved.
- Preserve the originals, all sleeves, and all provenance. Nothing leaves its sleeve; nothing is discarded, trimmed, or altered.

Identity / provenance checks with Marcus (in real time)
For each of the seven photographs, in Marcus-confirmed order, confirm with Marcus:
- Names of people depicted, against existing provenance.
- Approximate year, against existing provenance.
- Location notes, against existing provenance.

Handling rule:
- If Marcus's recollection matches existing provenance → record as confirmed.
- If Marcus's recollection disagrees with existing provenance → preserve both as unresolved; do not pick a winner.
- If Marcus is uncertain, or provenance is silent → preserve as unresolved. Unresolved stays unresolved.

Capture
- For each photograph that has a back with content (writing, stamp, postmark, label, numbers, etc.):
  - Capture the front.
  - Capture the back separately, in the same orientation handling, before moving to the next photograph.
- Photographs with no back content: front capture only.

Filing and verification (before moving on from each photograph)
- Filename pair: front and back (when captured) are saved as a matched pair under one parent identifier per photograph. Front filename and back filename share the same base name with `-front` / `-back` suffixes.
- Readability check: open each captured file at full resolution and confirm the image is sharp, fully framed, and free of glare, finger, or sleeve artifact obscuring the subject. Re-capture if not readable.
- Provenance note: the sleeve, envelope, or accompanying note for that photograph is preserved unchanged and kept with the photograph.

End-of-session checks (must complete before 7:00pm Central)
- All seven photographs have a captured file (or front+back pair) saved.
- Every pair's filenames match the parent identifier and have `-front` / `-back` suffixes where a back was captured.
- Readability verification done for every captured file.

- Unresolved names / years / locations, if any, are recorded as unresolved — not guessed, not back-filled.
- Marcus's order, the originals, every sleeve, and every provenance item are accounted for and unchanged.

What not to do this session
- No early scan. No pre-session capture. No pre-session identification.
- No removing photographs from sleeves.
- No residue removal, no cleaning.
- No guessing dates, names, or locations.
- No reorganizing, reordering, or relabeling.
- No discarding sleeves, envelopes, or provenance notes.

- The remaining 7 undigitized photographs (14 minus 7 scanned this session).
- Any unresolved names / years / location notes preserved this session.

messages.content:
CONSERVATIVE HANDLING FOR P05

Framing. The residue is provenance, not dirt — it tells you P05 was once mounted in a black-paper album (common from the 1860s through about the 1960s), and any flakes that detach are evidence of that. The goal of interim handling is to stop further loss, not to clean. Anything you do to "fix" it now is a treatment; leave treatment to a photograph conservator.

DOCUMENT FIRST — BEFORE YOU TOUCH IT

  1. With P05 exactly where you found it, photograph:
       - the full front and full back
       - close-ups of both residue corners, with a ruler in frame for scale
       - the print in place among the other five so its position in the 01–06 sequence is recorded
  2. Add a line to your index: date, what you observed, position relative to the other prints, "dry black album-paper residue attached at two corners."
  3. Now — and only now — handle it.

HANDLING SEQUENCE (MOVE IT ONCE, MOVE IT CAREFULLY)

  1. Wash and dry hands thoroughly; no lotion, no rings. Clean nitrile gloves are the safer choice here — cotton gloves can snag dry flakes and pull them off. If you only have cotton, handle with extreme care around the residue corners and keep handling time short.
  2. Clear a flat workspace. Lay down a clean sheet of acid-free paper or a clean cotton cloth as a base.
  3. Slide a piece of acid-free paper or a clean piece of card UNDER the print rather than picking it up by the edges. The two residue corners are mechanically weakened; don't lift from those points or pinch them.
  4. Keep the print flat at all times. Don't flex, tilt, or wave it — barely-adhered flakes will drop.
  5. Set it on the prepared surface. Image-side up if the residue is on the back, residue-side up if the residue is on the front. Don't flip-flop it.

ISOLATION (KEEP FLAKES WITH THE PRINT)

  1. Best enclosure: a four-sided Mylar (polyester) sleeve. Detached flakes stay inside the sleeve with the print instead of falling into a drawer and being lost. Mylar is chemically stable.
  2. Acceptable fallback if you don't have Mylar: sandwich the print between two sheets of unbuffered, acid-free tissue inside a rigid acid-free folder. Place the print face-up on the lower tissue, then lift and lay the upper tissue on top — don't slide it.
  3. Any flakes you find detached during enclosure go into a small labeled paper envelope (unbuffered, acid-free), kept with the print. Do not throw them away. They are provenance; a conservator may be able to match them to a specific album page.
  4. Keep P05 physically with the 01–06 set in the same drawer/box, but in its own enclosure so flakes can't migrate onto the other five.

STORAGE — ENVIRONMENT AND POSITION

  1. Flat. Never on edge, never stacked under heavy objects.
  2. Cool: roughly 65–70°F (18–21°C).
  3. Dry: 30–50% RH. Stability matters more than hitting a specific number — avoid swings.
  4. Dark. Light damage is cumulative; even brief direct sun matters.
  5. In a closed cabinet or drawer, away from exterior walls, radiators, water pipes, and any window.
  6. Inside its enclosure, ideally inside a rigid archival box. A clean, dry, lidded plastic or metal container is fine for now. Avoid cardboard food boxes (acidic, off-gas) and avoid any unsealed wood drawer (wood off-gases acids).
  7. Not in a bathroom, kitchen, attic, basement, or garage.

LABELING

  On the OUTSIDE of the enclosure, in pencil only: "P05 — DO NOT CLEAN — dry black album-paper residue, two corners — observed 2025-09-14 — [your initials]."

MATERIALS TO AVOID

  - PVC / vinyl sleeves, "magnetic" photo album pages, self-adhesive album pages
  - Plain office paper, copy paper, newsprint, paper towels, tissue with lotion
  - Paperclips, rubber bands, staples, binder clips
  - Any kind of tape, even "archival" tape — adhesion is a treatment, not a step
  - Lamination, dry-mounting, glue sticks, photo corners (the triangular stick-on kind)
  - Markers or pens on the print or its back; pencil directly on the print

During the session — ground rules
- Keep every photograph in its sleeve. Do not remove a photograph from its sleeve for any reason.

----------------------------------------------------------------
ARCHIVE-NOTE UPDATE — 2025-08-23 (rescan, two-photo dedup hold removed)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Subject of this update: the two physical family photographs that
were on a deduplication hold because their older scan files had
identical bytes despite different handwriting on their backs.

This update is added to the family-photo archive note on
2025-08-23. It supersedes any prior dedup hold on this pair.
Nothing in this update narrows or resolves identity, date,
occasion, or location fields for either photograph — those
remain unresolved as recorded elsewhere in this note.

----------------------------------------------------------------
1. Status of the dedup hold
----------------------------------------------------------------

The deduplication hold on these two photographs is REMOVED,
effective 2025-08-23.

Reason for removal: the earlier hold rested on the byte-
identity of the older scan files (fronts and backs hashed
identically between the two photographs). The byte-identity
was an artifact of the older scan workflow, not evidence that
the two physical photographs are the same image. The new scan
pairs have distinct bytes (fronts and backs both), and the two
backs carry visibly different handwriting, which is itself a
distinguishing physical artifact that the older scan had
flattened.

----------------------------------------------------------------
2. Both photographs are retained as separate sources
----------------------------------------------------------------

Photograph A and Photograph B are each retained as a separate
source object in the archive. Neither is merged into the other.
Neither is removed in favor of the other. They are linked in
the archive as a possible-near-duplicate PAIR, not as a single
record.

Per the duplicate-prints rule from the photo archive filename
and metadata convention (session 20260914_092659_abc86c):
  - Two physical prints that may depict the same image stay as
    separate, linkable objects.
  - In metadata, each record's `possible_duplicate_print_of`
    field points to the other.
  - Do NOT collapse based on visual similarity until a reviewer
    confirms they are the same image.

That rule now governs this pair explicitly. The byte-identity
test that previously suggested collapse is retired; the new
byte-distinct scan pairs are the canonical scans going forward.

----------------------------------------------------------------
3. Distinct backs (the evidence that survives the rescan)
----------------------------------------------------------------

The two backs are distinct artifacts. Each back carries its
own handwriting. The backs are not the same artifact and are
not interchangeable.

What is preserved on the record for each back:
  - The new back scan (distinct bytes from the new front scan
    for the same photograph).
  - The back's handwriting, as visible on the new back scan.
  - The fact that the other photograph's back carries
    DIFFERENT handwriting, so the two backs are not the same
    artifact.

What is NOT recorded here:
  - Transcription of either back's handwriting. The rescan
    preserved the handwriting on the scan, but no one has
    read it aloud or transcribed it as of 2025-08-23. The
    backs are stored as scanned evidence; their text content
    remains to be read.
  - Any attribution of either back's handwriting to a specific
    family member or date.
  - Any inference that the two backs were written by the same
    hand or by different hands — the visual similarity of the
    fronts does not imply either conclusion for the backs.

----------------------------------------------------------------
4. What the rescan did and did not establish
----------------------------------------------------------------

Established by the 2025-08-23 rescan:
  - Photograph A has a separate front scan and a separate back
    scan, with the back's handwriting preserved. The new front
    and back for Photograph A have distinct bytes.
  - Photograph B has a separate front scan and a separate back
    scan, with the back's handwriting preserved. The new front
    and back for Photograph B have distinct bytes.
  - The new scan pairs (front + back) for Photograph A and
    Photograph B have distinct bytes from each other.
  - The two physical backs carry different handwriting.

NOT established by the 2025-08-23 rescan:
  - That the two photographs depict different scenes or the
    same scene. The fronts remain visually similar; the rescan
    did not produce a verdict on whether the two fronts are of
    the same image or of two near-duplicate images.
  - Any new identity, date, occasion, or location evidence.
    The user explicitly reported no new evidence of this kind
    on 2025-08-23.
  - Any reading of the back handwriting on either photograph.
  - Any attribution or authorship claim for either back.

----------------------------------------------------------------
5. Unresolved fields — unchanged
----------------------------------------------------------------

The following remain UNRESOLVED for both Photograph A and
Photograph B, and are not changed by this update:

  - Identity of the people in the front image
  - Identity of the writer(s) of the back handwriting
  - Date (year, season, occasion) for either photograph
  - Location depicted in the front image
  - Whether the two fronts depict the same scene or two
    different scenes
  - Whether the two photographs were taken at the same event
    or different events

These fields are left unresolved because no new evidence has
been added. Resolving them requires either:
  - A reading of the back handwriting (still pending)
  - A family-side identification of the people, date, or
    location in the front image (not provided on 2025-08-23)
  - Visual or contextual evidence distinguishing the two
    fronts as the same scene or different scenes (not
    established by the rescan)

Any future narrowing of these fields must follow the same
discipline as the rest of this archive note: recorded as-is,
not promoted to a precise claim, and not collapsed across the
two photographs unless independent evidence supports doing so.

----------------------------------------------------------------
6. Filename and metadata (operational)
----------------------------------------------------------------

Per the photo archive filename and metadata convention, the
two photographs are stored as separate files using the
`_print-A` / `_print-B` suffix convention, sharing the same
date and slug fields so a casual listing reveals the pair. The
older byte-identical scan files are superseded by the new
distinct-byte scan pairs; the older files are retained in
quarantine (per the convention's duplicate-prints rule) until
a reviewer confirms whether the two fronts are the same
image, but they are NOT the working scans going forward.

----------------------------------------------------------------
7. Audit trail
----------------------------------------------------------------

  - 2025-08-23: Rescan completed. Two physical family
    photographs (Photograph A and Photograph B) rescanned.
    Each now has a separate front scan and a separate back
    scan with the back's handwriting preserved. The new scan
    pairs have distinct bytes. The fronts remain visually
    similar. No new identity, date, occasion, or location
    evidence found.
  - 2025-08-23: Deduplication hold on this pair REMOVED. Both
    photographs retained as separate source objects. Distinct

session_meta.title: Handle flaking album residue on photograph

messages.content: [2025-09-14T14:10:00-05:00] While checking the six loose family photographs, I found dry, flaking black album-paper residue attached at two corners of temporary-index pair 05. The photograph isn’t currently stuck to another surface, the image layer appears intact, and the handwriting on the back needs to remain readable. I don’t want to scrape, clean, or restore it myself. Give me a conservative handling, isolation, and storage sequence that preserves the front, back, order, and provenance; tell me what materials and actions to avoid and what signs would justify involving a photograph conservator.

CONSERVATIVE HANDLING FOR P05

Framing. The residue is provenance, not dirt — it tells you P05 was once mounted in a black-paper album (common from the 1860s through about the 1960s), and any flakes that detach are evidence of that. The goal of interim handling is to stop further loss, not to clean. Anything you do to "fix" it now is a treatment; leave treatment to a photograph conservator.

DOCUMENT FIRST — BEFORE YOU TOUCH IT

  1. With P05 exactly where you found it, photograph:
       - the full front and full back
       - close-ups of both residue corners, with a ruler in frame for scale
       - the print in place among the other five so its position in the 01–06 sequence is recorded
  2. Add a line to your index: date, what you observed, position relative to the other prints, "dry black album-paper residue attached at two corners."
  3. Now — and only now — handle it.

HANDLING SEQUENCE (MOVE IT ONCE, MOVE IT CAREFULLY)

  1. Wash and dry hands thoroughly; no lotion, no rings. Clean nitrile gloves are the safer choice here — cotton gloves can snag dry flakes and pull them off. If you only have cotton, handle with extreme care around the residue corners and keep handling time short.
  2. Clear a flat workspace. Lay down a clean sheet of acid-free paper or a clean cotton cloth as a base.
  3. Slide a piece of acid-free paper or a clean piece of card UNDER the print rather than picking it up by the edges. The two residue corners are mechanically weakened; don't lift from those points or pinch them.
  4. Keep the print flat at all times. Don't flex, tilt, or wave it — barely-adhered flakes will drop.
  5. Set it on the prepared surface. Image-side up if the residue is on the back, residue-side up if the residue is on the front. Don't flip-flop it.

ISOLATION (KEEP FLAKES WITH THE PRINT)

  1. Best enclosure: a four-sided Mylar (polyester) sleeve. Detached flakes stay inside the sleeve with the print instead of falling into a drawer and being lost. Mylar is chemically stable.
  2. Acceptable fallback if you don't have Mylar: sandwich the print between two sheets of unbuffered, acid-free tissue inside a rigid acid-free folder. Place the print face-up on the lower tissue, then lift and lay the upper tissue on top — don't slide it.
  3. Any flakes you find detached during enclosure go into a small labeled paper envelope (unbuffered, acid-free), kept with the print. Do not throw them away. They are provenance; a conservator may be able to match them to a specific album page.
  4. Keep P05 physically with the 01–06 set in the same drawer/box, but in its own enclosure so flakes can't migrate onto the other five.

STORAGE — ENVIRONMENT AND POSITION

  1. Flat. Never on edge, never stacked under heavy objects.
  2. Cool: roughly 65–70°F (18–21°C).
  3. Dry: 30–50% RH. Stability matters more than hitting a specific number — avoid swings.
  4. Dark. Light damage is cumulative; even brief direct sun matters.
  5. In a closed cabinet or drawer, away from exterior walls, radiators, water pipes, and any window.
  6. Inside its enclosure, ideally inside a rigid archival box. A clean, dry, lidded plastic or metal container is fine for now. Avoid cardboard food boxes (acidic, off-gas) and avoid any unsealed wood drawer (wood off-gases acids).
  7. Not in a bathroom, kitchen, attic, basement, or garage.

LABELING

  On the OUTSIDE of the enclosure, in pencil only: "P05 — DO NOT CLEAN — dry black album-paper residue, two corners — observed 2025-09-14 — [your initials]."

MATERIALS TO AVOID

  - PVC / vinyl sleeves, "magnetic" photo album pages, self-adhesive album pages
  - Plain office paper, copy paper, newsprint, paper towels, tissue with lotion
  - Paperclips, rubber bands, staples, binder clips
  - Any kind of tape, even "archival" tape — adhesion is a treatment, not a step
  - Lamination, dry-mounting, glue sticks, photo corners (the triangular stick-on kind)
  - Markers or pens on the print or its back; pencil directly on the print
  - Household cleaners, water, saliva, solvents, erasers (even soft white plastic), furniture polishes
  - Anything labeled "acid-free" only by a maker you don't trust — when in doubt, food-grade unbuffered tissue from a conservation supplier is the safer bet

ACTIONS TO AVOID

  - Touching the residue with bare fingers (oils and salts accelerate deterioration and can detach flakes)
  - Brushing, blowing on, or "dusting" the residue
  - Scraping, picking, peeling, or pressing flakes back down
  - Pressing anything onto either surface of the print
  - Folding, bending, rolling, or standing the print on edge
  - Photocopying or scanning with a flatbed that presses the lid onto the print (scan through the Mylar sleeve or with the lid raised, and only after the print is fully enclosed)
  - Leaving it in direct sun, near a heat source, or anywhere with humidity swings
  - Writing on the print or its back — write on the enclosure

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY INVOLVING A PHOTOGRAPH CONSERVATOR (ANY ONE IS ENOUGH)

  - Residue sits on or overlaps the image layer, not just the corners
  - Flakes continue to detach between handling sessions (active loss)
  - Image layer shows damage: silver mirroring (a bluish/purplish sheen on B&W prints), fading, yellowing, staining, tears, creases, cracking or flaking of the emulsion itself
  - The handwriting on the back is at risk or already partially abraded/smudged
  - You find mold (often looks like fuzzy spots, sometimes white/green/black), foxing (small reddish-brown spots), or any biological growth
  - Water damage, tide-line staining, or warping
  - The print is one-of-a-kind and you want it preserved across generations rather than just stabilized for now
  - You'd like the residue removed, the back safely cleaned, or the surface cleaned
  - Any time you feel tempted to do something beyond enclosing and storing

WHEN YOU INVOLVE ONE

  Ask specifically for a photograph conservator — paper conservators don't always specialize in photographic processes, and the chemistry (silver gelatin, albumen, platinum, chromogenic, etc.) matters. The American Institute for Conservation (conservation-us.org) maintains a "Find a Conservator" directory searchable by specialty and region. University art-conservation programs and the photo collection at a regional archive or museum can also refer. Expect an initial consultation to be modest in cost; full treatment is quoted after examination.

WHAT A CONSERVATOR CAN DO THAT YOU SHOULD NOT

  - Consolidate lifting flakes in place so they stop falling off
  - Safely reduce or remove the album-paper residue if that's appropriate for the specific photographic process
  - Surface-clean the print without damaging the emulsion or the back inscription
  - Stabilize tears, creases, or other damage
  - Re-house it in materials matched to the actual photographic process (buffered vs. unbuffered, etc.)
  - Tell you what the print is (process, approximate date) and whether the residue matches a known album, which can recover lost provenance

A small note on the index: when you do update the pair index for P05, it's worth recording this residue observation alongside the unresolved identification — it doesn't move P05 closer to being identified, but it does pin down one piece of its history (album-mounted, black paper), and it tells future-you (or a conservator) that this print was treated as evidence, not cleaned.

tests.request: Create a concise two-stage evidence-maturation case note for Lifecycle Systems training about the onboarding-timing analysis. Contrast the initial provisional cut with the later sharpened read, preserving the group definitions, observed churn rates, sample-strength context, and the reason the first read was not yet decision-ready. Close by explaining how the later interpretation informed the test direction, while clearly avoiding a causal claim from the cohort cut alone. Use a clear title and a skimmable structure.
tests.answer:
================================================================
ONBOARDING-TIMING ANALYSIS — TWO-STAGE EVIDENCE MATURATION
Lifecycle Systems training case note
================================================================

SUM (read first):
The first cut suggested late onboarders churned roughly 2x
early onboarders. After conditioning on signup source and
pre-signup intent, the gap collapsed (weighted avg from
+11.3 pp to +2.0 pp) and the residual signal concentrated in
a different population than the original hypothesis pointed
to. Test direction shifted from "accelerate everyone" to a
targeted, source-differentiated re-engagement design.

================================================================
STAGE 1 — PROVISIONAL CUT  (initial read)
================================================================

Groups:
  Early onboarders — completed first key action within 7 days
                     of signup (n = 412)
  Late onboarders  — completed between days 8–30 (n = 186)

Observed 60-day churn:
  Early:  11.8%
  Late:   23.1%
  Gap:    +11.3 pp on late

Sample-strength context:
  - Early cohort 2.2x larger than late
  - Paid-source users disproportionately landed in "early"
  - No conditioning on source or pre-signup intent
  - 60-day observation; activation-dependent behaviors not
    yet fully expressed

Why this read was NOT decision-ready:
  Self-selection confound. Users who onboard quickly are also
  users with stronger pre-signup intent signals. The late
  cohort is enriched for organic / low-intent signups. The
  cut cannot distinguish "later onboarding causes higher
  churn" from "lower-intent users both onboard late and
  churn more."

================================================================
STAGE 2 — SHARPENED READ  (follow-up cut)
================================================================

Re-cuts applied:
  - Split by signup source (paid vs organic)
  - Split by pre-signup intent score (high vs low)
  - Window extended to 90 days
  - 30% holdout for validation

Observed 90-day churn, source + intent conditioned:

  Paid,     high intent:   early  9.4%   late 11.1%   +1.7 pp (n.s.)
  Paid,     low  intent:   early 14.2%   late 13.8%   -0.4 pp (n.s.)
  Organic,  high intent:   early 12.1%   late 19.4%   +7.3 pp (sig.)
  Organic,  low  intent:   early 18.7%   late 21.0%   +2.3 pp (n.s.)

Sample-strength context:
  - Cell sizes smaller after conditioning (smallest n = 39);
    holdout corroborated direction in the one significant cell
  - Within-source conditioning absorbed most of the headline
    gap
  - The single surviving signal is in organic + high-intent —
    NOT the population the Stage 1 framing pointed at

What changed:
  - Headline +11.3 pp gap  →  weighted avg +2.0 pp
  - Surviving effect localized to organic high-intent users
    onboarding past day 7
  - "Accelerate everyone" no longer justified by the evidence

================================================================
TEST DIRECTION (informed by Stage 2)
================================================================

Moved FROM:  generic push to onboard everyone by day 7
Moved TO:    targeted re-engagement for organic high-intent
             users who have not onboarded by day 10, plus
             onboarding-path differentiation by source

Why this direction:
  Stage 2 identified the population in which late onboarding
  still co-occurs with elevated churn. The test is designed
  around that population rather than the original "late =
  bad" framing.

================================================================
CAVEAT — read carefully
================================================================

The cohort cut alone does NOT establish that changing
onboarding timing changes churn. Stage 2 finds an association
between late onboarding and elevated churn within one
conditioned subgroup. Whether re-timing onboarding for that
subgroup actually moves churn is what the test measures.
This case note trains the maturation discipline; it does
not authorize a causal claim from the cohort cut.

================================================================
TRAINING TAKEAWAY
================================================================

A large unconditioned gap is not a decision. The obvious
confounder (self-selection into the timing cohort) collapsed
most of the signal and moved the target population. The test
that followed is qualitatively different from the one the
first read would have produced.
================================================================

messages.content: [2023-05-10T15:00:00-05:00] ok so all-hands deck is basically there. 15 for the talk, 10 q+a, and i'm trying not to make it feel like a postmortem for a thing we already fixed. title right now is "Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned". Priya pushed me to cut two slides that were just me re-proving the segmentation change and she's right. keeping the before/after seat-band table, the Apr 10 break, and one slide on what goes in the doc vs what stays tribal if nobody writes it down. leaning pretty plain on delivery -- what we saw, what was noise, what changed, what rule we use now. no Friday ships stays in there bc otherwise someone will do it again lol

The "what was noise" frame does the lifting — signals you've got the data discipline to sort signal from coincidence rather than just relitigating what already got fixed. And the doc-vs-tribal slide is the soft one that actually prevents the next incident, since the segmentation def going into the playbook is exactly the kind of thing that quietly rots if nobody owns writing it down.

One small thing to flag: is the seat-band table going in as "here's what moved" or "here's why we trust v2"? Both work but the framing changes what people take away — the first is the postmortem read, the second is the "we have a defensible definition now" read, which is more aligned with where the rest of the deck is pointing.

ARCHIVE NOTE — for internal five-year retrospective
Subject: The onboarding-trigger result as presented at the May 12, 2023 company all-hands
Author: Riley Tanaka
Date prepared: 2028-01-01
Citation-ready — use verbatim or paraphrase; source note at end.

SCOPE OF THIS NOTE
This note documents the onboarding-trigger result only as it was presented at the formal May 12, 2023 company all-hands. It is not a record of the underlying investigation in general, nor is it a credit roster for the work overall. Recognition is scoped to what that specific presentation did and did not name. Do not extend these credits into a universal attribution rule for the project — other artifacts (the institutional doc circulated 2023-04-29, later retrospective briefs, the Expansion Assist and Helio Start decision records) carry their own contributor lists and should be cited separately.

THE RESULT, AS PRESENTED
- Talk title on the deck: "Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned." The onboarding-trigger result sat inside this broader investigation talk; it was not a standalone headline in the all-hands setting.
- Result named in the talk: the v2 onboarding trigger shipped 2023-04-10, after the team waited one stabilization cohort (the standing rule locked 2023-03-26) before calling anything. The April 10 break was kept as a slide.
- Surrounding content that framed the result: a before/after seat-band table, one slide on what belongs in the written doc vs. what stays tribal if nobody writes it down, and the "no Friday ships" rule (kept on a slide specifically so the recurrence risk was visible to the room).

AUDIENCE SCALE
The talk was allocated 15 minutes for the presentation and 10 minutes for Q&A, consistent with a company-wide all-hands slot. A precise attendee headcount for the May 12, 2023 session is not recorded in the contemporaneous notes I have on hand (deck-prep messages from late April and early May 2023, plus the institutional doc circulated 2023-04-29). The presentation was framed and delivered to the full company, not to a sub-team. If a specific attendance figure is needed for citation, pull it from the company's all-hands attendance record for that date rather than from this note.

HOW THE RESULT WAS FRAMED
- Plain delivery, not a postmortem of a thing already fixed. The explicit framing in prep was: "what we saw, what was noise, what changed, what rule we use now."
- The "what was noise" frame was deliberate — it positioned the team as having the data discipline to separate signal from coincidence, rather than re-litigating what had already been fixed.
- Two slides that re-proved the segmentation change (50-200 → 75-200 cohort redef, 2023-04-26) were cut on Priya's push before delivery, because they read as defensive rather than informative in the all-hands setting.
- The seat-band table was presented as "here's why we trust v2" — a defensible-definition read, not a "here's what moved" postmortem read.
- The doc-vs-tribal slide was the soft preventive: it explicitly called out which decisions belonged in the institutional doc so they would not quietly rot into folklore.

CONTRIBUTORS EXPLICITLY CREDITED IN THAT PRESENTATION
The contemporaneous record of the May 12, 2023 all-hands does not contain a captured credit slide or a captured verbal roll-call of contributors from the talk itself. The deck-prep messages document Priya's framing input (she pushed to cut the two re-proving slides) and the presenter's own delivery; they do not document a named-contributors slide in the final deck.

What this note can responsibly say about recognition in that specific setting:
- Presenter: Riley Tanaka delivered the talk.
- Framing credit attributable to the all-hands prep: Priya, for the cuts and the "what was noise" framing push.
- That is the full set of named contributions I can tie to the May 12, 2023 all-hands setting from the contemporaneous record.

What this note does NOT claim:
- It does not claim a full contributor roster for the underlying mid-segment churn investigation. That belongs in the institutional doc circulated 2023-04-29, which carried ticket IDs, cohort dates, and "who checked what" by design.
- It does not extend the May 12 credits to Owen, Daniela, Ines, Tomas, Marcus Vail, or anyone else on the basis of their involvement in adjacent workstreams — they were involved in the broader investigation and in later decisions (sub-50-seat tier, Helio Start, Expansion Assist), but the contemporaneous all-hands record does not place them in the May 12, 2023 talk's recognition. Cite those contributions against the relevant artifacts (the institutional doc, the sub-50-seat tier scoping record, the Helio Start and Expansion Assist decision records), not against this all-hands.

SOURCE NOTE
- Deck title, time allocation, and framing language: drawn from the 2023-04-29 message beginning the institutional doc ("Mid-segment churn investigation Feb-Apr 2023 -- what we learned ... aiming to have that circulate today and use it for May 12 all-hands") and the 2023-05-10 deck-tightening message (15 talk / 10 Q&A, "what we saw, what was noise, what changed, what rule we use now," cut two re-proving slides on Priya's push, kept the before/after seat-band table, the Apr 10 break, and the doc-vs-tribal slide; "no Friday ships" kept to prevent recurrence).
- v2 onboarding-trigger ship date (2023-04-10) and stabilization-cohort rule (locked 2023-03-26): drawn from the same deck-prep record and the standing-rule memory entry.
- Cohort redef 50-200 → 75-200 (2023-04-26): drawn from the standing mid-segment cohort definition; not on the deck's kept-slide list per the 2023-05-10 message.
- Audience scale: limited to what the deck-prep record supports (15 + 10 minute company-wide slot). A specific headcount for May 12, 2023 is not in the contemporaneous notes I have on hand and is not asserted here.
- Contributors credited in the presentation: limited to what the deck-prep record supports (presenter and Priya's framing credit). No other names are asserted as credited in the May 12, 2023 talk itself.

HONEST LIMITS
If a future reader needs a fuller credit roster, an attendance figure, or a verbatim transcript of the May 12, 2023 talk, those should be pulled from the company's archived all-hands recording and the institutional doc (circulated 2023-04-29) rather than reconstructed from this note. This note is scoped on purpose to what the contemporaneous prep record actually says about the talk.

[2027-07-20T10:15:00-05:00] After Owen delivered the reconciled one-time aggregate sizing cut, Customer Success followed up with:

`Could Owen cross-tab renewal month against active-CS-work yes/no and refresh it weekly through the renewal cycle? We still do not need workspace IDs, but a recurring version would be useful for prioritization.`

That would turn the bounded one-time answer into an iterative feed.

Ruling — CS request to convert Owen's reconciled one-time aggregate cut to a weekly feed

Summary
Decline the standing weekly feed. Either keep as one-time, or reopen as a bounded 4-week pilot gated on CS naming the decision threshold and the update cadence of the active-CS-work flag.

Why
- The one-time cut was bounded by design and answered the question as posed. Recurrence presumes underlying instability or that the decision needs ongoing calibration; neither is established.
- "Useful for prioritization" is not a decision threshold. Recurring Owen capacity shouldn't be committed against an unspecified action.
- Growth-method discipline (eff 7/6/27) requires primary metric + min effect pre-launch. CS has named neither.
- Per the sequential-workstream preference, layering a recurring cohort cut onto Owen's queue needs justification against whatever is already running, not a quiet add-on.
- Aggregate + no workspace IDs preserves the privacy boundary, but it doesn't reduce the analytical burden of justifying a recurring workstream.

Cuts (preconditions before revisiting)
1. What concrete CS action does the week-N read change that the week-1 read didn't?
2. What is the smallest shift in active-CS-work share within a renewal month that flips CS behavior — i.e., the operational effect threshold?
3. Is active-CS-work status event-driven or refresh-cadenced? If event-driven, weekly undersamples; if weekly-stable, weekly is mostly noise.

P (powered read)
Not applicable — this is an operational feed, not an experiment, so the 21-day rule doesn't bind. Pilot duration should still span one full renewal month so we cross at least one month boundary — ~4 weekly cuts.

Effect
- Owen: bounded 4-week commitment vs. open-ended weekly; the pilot is revocable, a standing feed isn't.
- CS: forced to specify decision threshold and flag cadence before any recurring capacity is committed — same discipline we'd apply to a launch.
- Signal: keeps the cohort cut clean by not running it concurrently with the rest of the growth queue.

Call
Decline as stated. Reply to CS via Priya in #lifecycle-systems: happy to keep the one-time cut as the deliverable, or run a 4-week pilot if CS can answer the three cuts above — especially the action threshold and the cadence of the active-CS-work flag itself. Offer a short sync to scope it if that's easier than writing it up.

Posture for the reply: short, specific, no softening of the gate. The aggregate cut is already a generous deliverable; recurring capacity is a separate commitment.

arguments.body:
Riley Tanaka — 2027 year-end self-review working draft

Reviewer: Priya. First draft due 2027-11-19. Working version — sections tightened before submission. No distribution, no Slack reference.

FRAME — DECISION-LED

Priya's calibration frame for this draft: lead with each decision I made and each claim limit I held, surface the credits inside the decision (not in a separate "team" section), and surface the exclusions inside the decision (not in a separate "out of scope" section). Lane boundaries are preserved as facts, not as defense language. The 1-pager ruling format holds at the section level: decision / bounded claim / credits / exclusions / status. December development outcomes stay open; the current paid batch is live operational work, not mature evidence.

This is a decision-led self-review. The four-lane year-end evidence framing is referenced inside each decision, not as a header above them. Owen, Ines, and Daniela's execution work is named in the credits line of each decision and is not re-described as my work in the body.

SUMMARY (DECISION-LED, SUM-FIRST)

In 2027 I held the operating-model and made the bounded calls below. Each is stated as a decision with its claim limit, who else owned what, and what is explicitly excluded from my lane.

1. Bounded Helio Start proposal. I drafted the bounded proposal and held the claim limits (no second-batch trigger, no pipeline/forecast credit, no activation or support-effort read into the descriptive numbers). Credit: Priya's batch approval; Daniela's November 1 launch authorization. Excluded: measurement execution (Owen), lifecycle-governance and message-state execution (Ines), engineering release and rollback execution (Daniela). Status: authorized November 1; live operational, not mature.

2. Five-consumer shared-state reminder operation. I held the decision that the reminder operates as the fifth prod consumer of the shared-state feed, with the incomplete-setup case treated as a reminder target rather than a routed workflow. Credit: Daniela's reliability and release work on the feed; Ines's lifecycle-governance meaning on the incomplete-setup state; Owen's denominator work on the shared-state surfaces. Excluded: the consumers' own execution, including any operational outcomes from consumer #5. Status: in flight — the fifth consumer is operating; the read on its effect is not closed.

3. Operating-model decisions held. Channel routing (Priya routes; I do not second-guess). Ruling 1-pager format (sum-first / why / cuts / p / effect / call). Expansion Assist stays descriptive — disputed / cross-team / exec-facing lines stay; routine line-edits do not; release and rollback routes to Daniela. Growth workstreams run sequentially, not in parallel, to keep signal clean. Monday cohort cuts with Owen, mid-segment, read locks first. Credit: the format is Priya's; lane splits are named, not invented. Excluded: any claim that the format itself moved outcomes.

4. Evidence and claim discipline held. Source completeness = Owen (bounded); claim, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, executive language = Riley. I did not absorb measurement, governance, release, or rollback into my lane, and I did not let my lane be absorbed into theirs. Excluded: any causal, revenue, forecast, or executive-language claim that has not gone through the standing review pathway.

5. Team development — December cycle. Owen and Ines both have October–December Q4 development focuses. These are open as of this draft and will be read against in the December cycle. I am not closing them here, and I am not pre-empting the December read. Credit: Owen's measurement/denominator/source-completeness/exception work is his; Ines's lifecycle-governance/message-state work is hers. Excluded: any characterization of Owen's or Ines's Q4 outcomes as my execution or as completed in this draft.

6. Next-cycle focus. Carry-forward placeholder — to be tightened before submission.

DECISIONS — DETAIL

Decision 1 — Bounded Helio Start proposal and claim limits.

What I decided. The proposal I drafted held three limits that I am not relaxing in this draft: (a) no automatic second-batch trigger from the day-7 leading read, (b) no pipeline or forecast credit against the cohort, (c) no read of the descriptive numbers into activation or support-effort claims. The launch posture I set was staged: staging first; isolated real-platform test campaign with no eligibility-flow entry; written Daniela ack; CS hours honored (M–F 8a–6p Central; after-hours route to the next opening); "paused" is not a bypass for V11.

Bounded claim. The launch is authorized and the gating rules are documented. The proposal does not prove acquisition, scale, pipeline, or forecast, and the bounded claim stays bounded.

Credits.
- Priya — batch approval.
- Daniela — November 1 launch authorization.
- Owen — measurement, denominator, source-completeness, and exception work on the proposal's numbers (his lane, not mine).
- Ines — lifecycle-governance and message-state meaning on the proposal's eligibility and routing (her lane, not mine).
- Daniela — engineering release and rollback on the launch itself (her lane, not mine).

Exclusions.
- The day-7 leading read, the cohort's mature-window read, and any support-effort classification — Owen's numbers, not mine.
- Lifecycle suppression, governed state meaning, and owner-state semantics — Ines's, not mine.
- Release preflight, connector-specific conditions, replay coverage, and rollback posture — Daniela's, not mine.
- Mature-outcome claims on the paid batch. The current paid batch is live operational work; the post-launch review runs after the batch clears.

Status. Authorized November 1. Live operational. Mature read pending the post-launch review; this draft does not claim mature outcomes.

Decision 2 — Five-consumer shared-state reminder operation (consumer #5 = incomplete-setup reminder).

What I decided. The shared-state feed has five prod consumers. Consumer #5 is the incomplete-setup reminder: a reminder targeted at the incomplete-setup case, operating off the shared-state feed without becoming a routed workflow. I held the decision that consumer #5 stays a reminder and does not absorb routing or governance responsibilities that belong to other lanes.

Bounded claim. The reminder operates as the fifth consumer. This draft does not claim operational outcomes from consumer #5; the read on its effect is in flight.

Credits.
- Daniela — reliability, release, and rollback on the shared-state feed (her lane).
- Ines — lifecycle-governance meaning on the incomplete-setup state (her lane).
- Owen — denominator and source-completeness on the shared-state surfaces (his lane).

Exclusions.
- Consumer #5's operational outcomes — not claimed here.
- The four prior consumers' execution — their lanes, not mine.
- Any causal or activation read off consumer #5's reminder traffic — out of scope for this draft.

Status. In flight. Consumer #5 is operating; the effect read is not closed.

Decision 3 — Operating-model decisions held.

What I decided.
- Channel routing: I own #growth-investigations (churn/cohort) and #lifecycle-systems (kickoff/certification). Priya routes cross-stream work; I do not second-guess that path.
- Ruling 1-pager format: sum-first, then why / cuts / p / effect / call.
- Expansion Assist: descriptive. Disputed, cross-team, exec-facing lines stay; routine line-edits do not; release and rollback routes to Daniela.
- Sequential growth workstreams: activation/retention, lifecycle email, feature-flag work do not all run hot at the same time. Workstreams run sequentially to keep signal clean.
- Monday cohort cuts with Owen, mid-segment. Read locks come first.

Bounded claim. The format and routing held through the year. This draft does not claim that the format itself moved outcomes.

Credits. Priya owns the format and the cross-stream routing. Lane splits are named; lane execution belongs to the named owners.

Exclusions. Any claim that format discipline alone drove a metric. Any claim about another owner's lane that is not explicitly credited above.

Status. Held through 2027. Continued into 2028 unless Priya redirects.

Decision 4 — Evidence and claim discipline held.

What I held. Source completeness = Owen (bounded). Claim, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, executive language = Riley. The split is preserved in every readout: I do not put a number on the page without naming the source-completeness lane it came from, and I do not put a causal or executive claim on the page without routing it through the standing review pathway.

Bounded claim. The discipline held under pressure through the year. This draft does not claim that the discipline by itself produced an outcome.

Credits. Owen — source-completeness review pathway and the bounded source lane. Ines — lifecycle-governance and message-state. Daniela — source-reliability, engineering-release, rollback.

Exclusions. Any read that conflates source completeness with claim, revenue, forecast, or executive language. Any read that lets my lane absorb theirs, or vice versa.

Status. Held through 2027. Carry-forward into 2028 unchanged unless Priya redirects.

Decision 5 — Team development: Owen and Ines Q4 focuses open through December.

What I held. Owen and Ines both have October–December Q4 development focuses. I am not closing them in this draft. The December cycle is where they get read against. I do not pre-empt that cycle here.

Bounded claim. This draft does not characterize Owen's or Ines's Q4 outcomes as complete. It does not characterize their execution as mine.

Credits. Owen's measurement/denominator/source-completeness/exception work is his; Ines's lifecycle-governance/message-state work is hers. Their Q4 development is theirs.

Exclusions.
- Any statement that Owen's Q4 focus is closed or on track — closed in the December cycle, not here.
- Any statement that Ines's Q4 focus is closed or on track — closed in the December cycle, not here.
- Any inflation of my role in Owen's, Ines's, or Daniela's execution.

Status. Owen Q4 focus — open through December cycle. Ines Q4 focus — open through December cycle.

Decision 6 — Next-cycle focus.

Placeholder. Two to three concrete 2028 focuses to be added before the 11/19 send. Carry-forward candidates: hold the claim-boundary discipline under next-cycle pressure; keep sequential workstream discipline; keep the December-cycle read intact for Owen and Ines; carry the bounded Helio Start posture into any 2028 paid-batch conversation.

EVIDENCE AND CLAIM DISCIPLINE — HELD

Source completeness = Owen (bounded). Claim, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, executive language = Riley. The split is preserved in every readout. I do not claim another owner's number, posture, or release as mine, and I do not let mine be absorbed into theirs. The standing review pathway is unchanged. Routine monthly preparation and source-closure reviews still flow through me as exception review; I have not left that work.

Where a system is still being set up, I say so. The five-consumer reminder operation is in flight, not mature. The current paid batch is live operational work, not mature evidence. The descriptive four-week reads on the authority-setup checklist are descriptive operating evidence, not activation or support-effort claims.

TEAM DEVELOPMENT — DECEMBER CYCLE

Owen Q4 focus — open. To be read in the December cycle. I will not pre-empt that read in this draft. Owen's lane is measurement, denominator, source-completeness, and exception reporting; his work is his.

Ines Q4 focus — open. To be read in the December cycle. I will not pre-empt that read in this draft. Ines's lane is lifecycle-governance and message-state; her work is hers.

Daniela's lane is source-reliability, engineering-release, and rollback. Her work is hers; I do not describe her release or rollback decisions as my execution.

I have not stopped routine monthly preparation or source-closure exception review. Both still flow through me.

SYSTEM RELIABILITY — BY LANE

This section names systems by decision authority. Other systems are reported by their owners.

- Shared-state feed — five-consumer reminder operation. Five prod consumers in production. Consumer #5 (incomplete-setup reminder) operates off the shared-state feed; the reminder operation is in flight, not mature. Reliability and release on the feed: Daniela. Lifecycle-governance meaning on the incomplete-setup state: Ines. Denominator on the shared-state surfaces: Owen. I hold the decision that consumer #5 stays a reminder and does not absorb routing or governance responsibilities.

- Controlled November paid-batch launch. Launch posture gated: staging first; isolated real-platform test campaign with no eligibility-flow entry; written Daniela ack; CS hours honored (M–F 8a–6p Central; after-hours route to the next opening); "paused" is not a V11 bypass. Launch authorized November 1 by Priya's batch approval and Daniela's launch authorization. The current paid batch is live operational work; mature outcomes are not claimed here. Measurement on the batch: Owen. Lifecycle-governance on the batch: Ines. Engineering release and rollback on the batch: Daniela.

- Bounded Helio Start posture. No second-batch trigger from the day-7 leading read. No pipeline or forecast credit against the cohort. No read of the descriptive numbers into activation or support-effort claims. Posture held.

NEXT-CYCLE FOCUS

Placeholder — to be tightened before 11/19.

OPEN BEFORE 11/19

1. Two to three concrete 2028 focuses (Next-cycle focus section).
2. Any 2027-specific decision you want anchored by name (one per lane is usually enough for a self-review of this shape).
3. Confirm whether the December cycle closes Owen's and Ines's Q4 focuses before or after the final feedback conversation; the draft assumes the cycle closes them after.

ROUTING

This doc stays in Growth until edited down to a 1-pager for Priya. No distribution, no Slack reference until then.

FRAME — DECISION-LED

# Riley Tanaka — H1 2027 self-review working notes

For: Priya. Draft due June 4. Center: outcomes, operating leverage, one development edge. Style: summary first; why / cuts / p / effect / call.

One-line summary: H1 was the half I stopped doing the work and started ruling on it — operating model reset in January, exception-only hands-on through Q1, bounded Q2 paid test, and one deliberate growth edge.

## 1. January operating-model transition

What changed: briefs became descriptive, not prescriptive. I rule on disputed / cross-surface / exec asks only; routine line-edits stay with the owner. Release and rollback authority moved to Daniela. Kickoff and certification flow through Priya. The point was to push variance out of the routine path and concentrate my judgment where it's actually load-bearing.

Effect: fewer rewrites mid-flight, cleaner signal in #growth-investigations and #lifecycle-systems, and I regained hours I'd been losing to second-opinion reviews.

Call: the model held. Don't relitigate it this half.

## 2. Exception-only involvement + quarterly hands-on audit

Day-to-day, I'm out of the routine path — I read locks before recurring meetings and I weigh in on the cohort cuts Owen and I walk through Mondays. Once per quarter I run a hands-on audit anyway, to keep my eye calibrated and to catch what the dashboards miss.

[TBD — fill: which audit (e.g. mid-segment churn cohort), dates, the one finding that changed a decision.]

The audit is leverage, not a deliverable: it lets me stay credible in exceptions without re-entering the queue.

## 3. Q2 Helio Start paid test — bounded execution

Closed 5/17 (Owen '27 cohort, CS-led paid-source lane):
- 25-admin enrollment cap; $7.6K committed; 61 screened → 25 active / 18 assistant / 18 ineligible.
- Attribution reconciles end-to-end (no double-count vs. organic).
- Support load: 2 of 25 = 8% exceeded 90-min support. No pause triggered. No unsupported admin.
- Day-90 window still open as of 5/20 — retention and downstream ARR impact are NOT yet established by this test.

What this test establishes:
- Paid-source mechanics work: enrollment gating, eligibility filter, attribution, support-cost baseline.
- The 25-admin cap is operationally safe at this support ratio.

What this test does NOT establish (read these out loud if asked):
- Day-90 retention, expansion, or net revenue — window incomplete.
- Generalizability to organic-source cohorts or other tiers.
- Authority for an eligibility or lifecycle change.
- That paid is preferable to organic at scale — that's a different experiment.

Decision lane: I signed off on the bounded scope and the NOs. Source mechanics, screening rules, and day-to-day enrollment are Owen's routine ownership. Lifecycle and certification governance are Ines's lane. Engineering controls on release/rollback are Daniela's. I did not, and should not, edit those layers mid-test.

## 4. Team development

[Fill in 2–3 concrete moments. Suggested frame: who grew into what, what I stopped doing so they could do it, what I unblocked. Avoid generic "supportive manager" language — Priya wants the moves.]

Working frame I'd use: Owen took full source ownership on Helio Start with me only on exceptions — that's the development, not a status update. Ines ran lifecycle kickoff and certification end-to-end without escalation. Daniela held release authority and I stayed out of it. [Add one moment where I explicitly got out of the way and it landed.]

## 5. One growth edge

The edge I want to name: learning to stop reading every brief end-to-end and only reading the locks + exceptions. Half 1 was the operational version of this (the model transition). Half 2 is the personal version — pushing my own floor on what I'll touch, and trusting the lanes.

Why it matters: if I keep drifting into the routine path under load, the model erodes quietly. The edge is keeping the model intact when it's inconvenient, not when it's easy.

## Boundaries to keep clean in the draft

- My decisions: scope of Helio Start paid test, the NOs (no lifecycle bypass, no 5th shared-state, no eligibility change), quarterly audit calls, disputed/cross-surface/exec rulings.
- Owen: routine source ownership — mechanics, screening, enrollment ops.
- Ines: lifecycle governance — kickoff, certification, journey rules.
- Daniela: engineering controls — release, rollback, feature-flag gating.

Don't let the draft blur these. If a sentence could be read as me owning Owen's, Ines's, or Daniela's lane, rewrite it as my ruling on a question they brought me.

---

arguments.body:
# Workload brief — Aug 21 contractor pre-read

Frame: Priya wants the decision structure explicit without a recommendation. This brief describes; Priya decides. Lane ownership (Owen, Ines, Riley, Daniela) is fixed by the 2025-03-24 audit-roles ruling (reaffirmed 2025-08-05) and is not on the table.

---

## 1. Lane anchors (fixed, not negotiated)

- Owen: shape + experiments + Lifecycle Systems semantics + exception readouts + Helio Start report.
- Ines: lifecycle-aud-risk; routine education is higher-risk; review-closure authority unchanged; 2 approved refs.
- Riley: judgment-esc + disputed semantics + cross-surface + exec language.
- Daniela: eng release / rollback control (incl. midsegment tagging controls).
- Expansion Assist: descriptive lane (not prescriptive); not eligible for contractor ownership.
- Standing-lane cap on lifecycle neutrals: ≤3 neutral emails / week.

Workshop out-of-scope (per 2025-08-21 agenda body): adding a fifth consumer; funding Helio Start paid acquisition; broadening Ines's review authority.

---

## 2. Side-by-side matrix

Dimensions are the same across all three cases. Where a case does not apply, the cell is marked n/a.

| Dimension | A. No contractor | B. $36K half-time (Oct 1 start) | C. $48K 4-mo FTE-eq (Nov 1 earliest) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost through Dec | $0 | $36K fixed | $48K prorated; ~$24K through Dec (2 of 4 mo) |
| Start | n/a | 2025-10-01 | 2025-11-01 (no earlier) |
| End horizon | n/a | open-ended at half-time | 4 months from start (~2026-03-01) |
| Capacity through Dec | 0 contractor-hrs | ~13 wks × ~20 hrs/wk ≈ 260 hrs | ~9 wks × ~40 hrs/wk ≈ 360 hrs (2 of 4 mo elapsed by 12/31) |
| Standing-lane lifecycle neutrals (≤3/wk) | stays with current owners | can absorb all 3/wk (≈ 39 hrs through Dec at neutral cadence) | can absorb all 3/wk plus headroom |
| Routine-education enumeration for Ines review | stays with current owners | covers enumeration; Ines retains review-closure | covers enumeration + first-pass review scaffolding; Ines retains review-closure |
| Support-load bucket refresh (no-contact / light / heavier / manual) | stays with current owners | full refresh cycle | full refresh + weekly top-up |
| Cohort-cut prep (Mon mid-segment cuts w Owen) | Owen | prep delegated; Owen keeps the cut | prep delegated; Owen keeps the cut |
| Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration | stays descriptive; no owner change | enumeration only; lane stays descriptive | enumeration + cross-link spotting |
| Owner-leverage gain (qualitative) | none | small: Ines + Owen get the largest time return | larger: Ines + Owen + light pressure-release on Riley's queue for routine enumeration |
| Coordination overhead added (est. hrs/wk) | 0 | ~3–5 hrs/wk (Ines 1–2 review; Owen 1 sign-off; Riley ≤1 dispute escalations; Daniela light touch) | ~5–8 hrs/wk (Ines 2–3 review; Owen 1–2 sign-off; Riley 1 dispute escalations; Daniela 1 cross-check) |
| Net leverage (gain − coord) through Dec | 0 | ≈ 260 − ~170 ≈ ~90 net hrs | ≈ 360 − ~280 ≈ ~80 net hrs (capacity higher, leverage similar because coordination scales) |
| Stays categorically with Owen / Ines / Riley / Daniela | yes — all of it | yes — see §4 | yes — see §4 |
| Risk: stale fail closure | baseline | contractor closes neutral-check fails under Ines sign-off | same, plus weekly stale-fail sweep |
| Risk: crossing into disputed semantics | n/a | watch: contractor must escalate, not adjudicate | same watch, higher volume of edge cases |

---

## 3. Sampled repeatable work each paid case could remove by December

Inputs: 8/5 CS support-load cut on the 52-ws mature cohort (31 no-contact / 15 light ~16-min median / 6 heavier ~41-min median / 0 manual billing-import-migration); standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk; routine education higher-risk under Ines; Expansion Assist descriptive.

B. $36K half-time, Oct 1 start — by 2025-12-31:
- Lifecycle neutral coverage: 3 neutrals × 13 wks ≈ 39 neutrals authored.
- Routine-education enumeration draft for Ines review: ~1 set / 2 wks ≈ 6–7 enumerations.
- Support-load bucket refresh: 1 full cycle ≈ 12–16 hrs; weekly top-ups ≈ 1 hr/wk.
- Mon cohort-cut prep (mid-segment): 1 prep packet / wk ≈ 2 hrs/wk.
- Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration: ~1 pass / 2 wks.
- Total absorbed: ~260 hrs. After coordination overhead (§2), ~90 net hrs land with the four owners.

C. $48K 4-mo FTE-eq, Nov 1 start — by 2025-12-31:
- Lifecycle neutral coverage: 3 neutrals × 9 wks ≈ 27 neutrals authored (more in Jan–Feb).
- Routine-education enumeration draft for Ines review: ~1 set / wk ≈ 9 enumerations + scaffolding.
- Support-load bucket refresh: 1 full cycle + weekly top-ups.
- Mon cohort-cut prep: 1 prep packet / wk.
- Expansion Assist descriptive enumeration: ~1 pass / wk + cross-link spotting.
- Total absorbed: ~360 hrs. After coordination overhead (§2), ~80 net hrs land with the four owners (more capacity, similar net leverage because coordination scales).

---

## 4. Work that remains categorically with each owner

Categorical = by audit-roles ruling, not by case selection. A contractor does not absorb these regardless of hours or cost.

Owen (stays):
- Lifecycle Systems semantic definitions and exception readouts.
- Mon mid-segment cohort cuts (contractor may prep; Owen owns the cut).
- Helio Start report content and shape + experiment design.
- Disputed-semantics calls on Lifecycle Systems semantics.

Ines (stays):
- Lifecycle-audit-risk rulings.
- Review-closure authority on routine education (2 approved refs); contractor enumerates.
- Higher-risk education escalations.
- Stale-fail sign-off (contractor may run the sweep; Ines closes).

Riley (stays):
- Judgment escalations.
- Disputed-semantics calls across surfaces.
- Cross-surface consistency claims.
- Executive language / positioning.
- Final sign-off on Q3 "stop line-editing routine work once checks pass" boundary (reaffirmed 2025-08-05).

Daniela (stays):
- Engineering release and rollback control.
- Midsegment tagging controls and related schema decisions.
- Boundary between release/rollback and lane ownership.

Out-of-scope at the workshop (2025-08-21 agenda body):
- Adding a fifth consumer.
- Funding Helio Start paid acquisition.
- Broadening Ines's review authority.

---

## 5. Evidence tests — owner leverage vs added coordination

For each paid case, run these tests in the first 4 weeks. Pass/fail thresholds are stated; Priya can sharpen them.

Common tests (B and C):
- T1. Lifecycle-neutral coverage. Did the contractor author all 3 standing-lane neutrals in wk 1 without crossing into disputed semantics? Pass = 3/3 wk 1, ≤1 Ines override / wk.
- T2. Routine-education enumeration. Did the contractor produce 1 enumeration set / 2 wks (B) or / wk (C) that Ines signs off without rework? Pass = ≤1 rewrite / enumeration.
- T3. Support-load bucket refresh. Did the full-cycle refresh reproduce the 8/5 cut shape (31 / 15 / 6 / 0) within ±10%? Pass = within ±10%, manual bucket still 0.
- T4. Cohort-cut prep. Did the Mon prep packet reduce Owen's cut time without changing the cut's conclusion? Pass = Owen's cut time ↓ ≥30%, conclusion unchanged.
- T5. Disputed-semantics escalation rate. Of escalations reaching Riley, what fraction originated in contractor-drafted work? Pass = ≤15% (B), ≤25% (C) — higher volume allowed in C.

Coordination tests (both B and C, watching the ceiling):
- T6. Ines review-hours / wk. B target ≤2; C target ≤3. Breaching = leverage has been eaten.
- T7. Owen sign-off-hrs / wk. B target ≤1; C target ≤2. Breaching = same.
- T8. Riley dispute-hrs / wk triggered by contractor work. B target ≤1; C target ≤1.5. Breaching = the contractor is adjudicating when it should be escalating.
- T9. Daniela cross-check / wk. B target ≤0.5; C target ≤1. Cross-check exists because midsegment-tagging edges can show up in enumeration; Daniela stays the release authority.

Decision read at week 4:
- B passes T1–T5 and stays under T6–T9 ceilings → keep.
- C passes T1–T5 and stays under T6–T9 ceilings → keep.
- Either fails T5 ceiling by ≥10 pts OR breaches any coordination ceiling → revisit at the next standing-lane review; do not auto-expand.
- A (no contractor) baseline: tests do not run; standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk cap stays binding on current owners; Expansion Assist stays descriptive.

---

## 6. No-preselection boundary

This brief describes three cases and the evidence that would discriminate between them. It does not select a case. The decision is Priya's, made at or after the 2025-08-21 workshop. Any reading of this brief that treats it as a recommendation is a misread.

Notes for the workshop:
- Priya owns the call. Owen, Ines, Riley, Daniela retain lane ownership under any case.
- The standing-lane ≤3 neutral/wk cap and the descriptive-only Expansion Assist lane are not relaxed by selecting a paid case.
- The audit-roles ruling (2025-03-24, reaffirmed 2025-08-05) is the boundary on what can move; the case choice is the boundary on how much can move.
